lessons.title: How the web works & your first HTML page
lessons.content:
## Key points - When you open a website, your browser sends a request to a server and receives HTML, CSS and JavaScript files back, which it then turns into the page you see. - HTML gives a page its structure and meaning, CSS controls how it looks, and JavaScript controls how it behaves. - Every HTML document starts with `` and has a `` (information about the page) and a `` (what users actually see). - The `` tag is mandatory for mobile-friendly sites; without it phones render a zoomed-out desktop page. - You only need VS Code, the Live Server extension and Chrome to start building real websites today. ## Transcript Namaste everyone, I'm Rahul. I've built more than 120 websites for clients — bakeries, coaching institutes, startups in Pune and Bengaluru — and every single one of them started with the exact file we're about to write. So first, what actually happens when you type a URL? Your browser asks a server, "bhai, give me this page." The server sends back some files. The most important one is HTML. Think of HTML as the skeleton of a building: walls, rooms, doors. CSS is the paint and furniture. JavaScript is the electricity — the things that move and respond. Chalo, let's open VS Code. Create a folder called `my-first-site`, and inside it a file called `index.html`. Type an exclamation mark and press Tab — VS Code gives you a starter template. Let's read it line by line. ```html Sharma Sweets, Jaipur

Sharma Sweets

Fresh ghewar and mawa kachori since 1987.

``` The `lang` attribute helps screen readers and Google. The `charset` line makes sure the ₹ symbol and Hindi text display correctly. And dekho, this viewport line — never delete it. Most of your client's customers will visit from a phone, and without this line the site looks tiny and broken. Now right-click and choose "Open with Live Server." Your page opens in Chrome, and every time you save, it refreshes automatically. Congratulations — you're a web developer now. In the next lesson we'll make this structure meaningful.

lessons.title: Quiz: HTML structure & semantics
lessons.content: Let's check that your HTML foundations are solid. These questions are about decisions you will make on real client pages.

questions.prompt: A client's site looks zoomed-out and tiny on phones even though the CSS is responsive. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The page uses too many div tags
The viewport meta tag is missing from the head
The images are not in WebP format
The lang attribute is set to en instead of hi

questions.explanation: Without <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">, mobile browsers render the page at a desktop width and shrink it down, ignoring your responsive CSS.

questions.prompt: You want the menu section title to look smaller than other section titles. What should you do?

options.text: Change it from h2 to h5 so it renders smaller
Wrap it in a small tag
Keep it as h2 and reduce its size with CSS
Replace it with a bold paragraph

questions.explanation: Heading levels describe the document outline, not visual size. Keep the correct level for structure and SEO, and control size in CSS.

questions.prompt: Which link is best for letting a homestay guest message the owner directly from their phone?
questions.explanation: A wa.me link with the country code opens a WhatsApp chat in one tap, and the link text clearly describes the action. Clickable divs are not keyboard-accessible.

questions.prompt: Why should every form input have a label connected with for and id?

options.text: It is required for the form to submit
It makes the field bigger on desktop
It lets screen readers announce the field and makes the label tappable to focus the input

questions.explanation: Linked labels are an accessibility essential and improve usability on small touch screens. Submission and validation work without them, which is why people forget them.

questions.prompt: Where does the main unique content of a page belong?

options.text: Inside multiple main elements, one per section

questions.explanation: Use one <main> per page for its unique content; split it into <section> and <article> elements inside.

Assignment: Responsive landing page for a Jaipur bakery
lessons.content: Small local businesses are the most common first clients for freelancers in India. A clean, fast, mobile-friendly landing page that drives WhatsApp orders is a project you can realistically sell for ₹5,000-₹12,000. This assignment is that project.

assignment.brief:
## The client

**Ghar Ki Bakery**, a home bakery in Malviya Nagar, Jaipur, run by Meera Agarwal. She sells eggless cakes, cookies and festive hampers, mostly through Instagram DMs and WhatsApp. She wants a simple website she can put in her Instagram bio.

## Your task

Build a single-page, responsive landing page using only HTML and CSS.

## Required sections

1. **Header** with the bakery name and a nav linking to the sections below.
2. **Hero** with a clear headline, one line about same-day delivery, and a WhatsApp "Order now" button (use a `wa.me` link).
3. **Menu** — at least 6 items in a CSS Grid, each card with name, short description, price in ₹ and an image with proper `alt` text.
4. **Why us** — 3 features laid out with Flexbox.
5. **Footer** with address, phone (`tel:` link) and Instagram link.

## Steps

1. Sketch the layout on paper for a phone first, then for a laptop.
2. Write semantic HTML (one `h1`, proper `section` elements).
3. Set up CSS variables for brand colours and `box-sizing: border-box`.
4. Style mobile-first, then add at least one `min-width` media query.
5. Test at 360px, 768px and 1280px in DevTools.

## Deliverable

Push the code to a public GitHub repository and submit the repository link (deployment comes in Module 4, but you can deploy early if you know how).

## Tips

- Use free images from Unsplash or Pexels and compress them to WebP.
- Keep it to one or two fonts from Google Fonts.
- Make the WhatsApp button impossible to miss on mobile.

Selecting and changing the DOM

Quiz: JavaScript & the DOM
lessons.content: Five questions on JavaScript fundamentals and DOM manipulation. Think about what the code actually does before you pick an answer.

questions.prompt: Given const prices = [650, 750, 550], what does prices.filter((p) => p > 600) return?
questions.explanation: filter keeps the original items for which the callback returns true. It does not return booleans (that would be map) or a sum (that would be reduce).

questions.prompt: You need to show a customer's name, typed into a form, on the page. Which is the safest approach?
questions.explanation: textContent inserts plain text and never parses HTML, so a malicious script in the input cannot run. innerHTML with user input is an XSS risk.

questions.prompt: Your script runs document.querySelector('.card') but gets null, even though the card exists in the HTML. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The script runs in the head before the HTML is parsed, without defer
Cards cannot be selected by class

questions.explanation: A script in the head without defer runs before the body exists. Use defer or place the script at the end of the body.

questions.prompt: Why do we call event.preventDefault() in a form submit handler?

options.text: To stop the browser's default page reload or navigation so JavaScript can handle the data
To prevent the user from typing invalid data

questions.explanation: By default, submitting a form navigates or reloads the page. preventDefault stops that so your code can process the data, for example by building a WhatsApp link.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to open and close a mobile nav with JavaScript?

options.text: Set nav.style.display in JavaScript each time
Delete and recreate the nav element on each click
Toggle a class like 'open' and define the visible styles in CSS
Reload the page with a URL parameter

questions.explanation: Keeping styles in CSS and toggling a class keeps responsibilities separate, is easier to animate, and is easier for the next developer to maintain.

modules.title: Ship It: Git, GitHub, Deployment & Client Handoff

lessons.title: Git and GitHub: save points for your code
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Git records snapshots (commits) of your project, so you can always go back if something breaks.
- The everyday loop is: edit files, `git add`, `git commit -m "message"`, `git push`.
- GitHub hosts your repositories online, acts as your public portfolio, and connects directly to Netlify and Vercel.
- Write commit messages that describe what changed and why, like "Add WhatsApp order form to menu section".
- Use a `.gitignore` file so secrets and bulky folders like `node_modules` never get uploaded.

## Transcript
Let me tell you a story. In my second year of freelancing, I was editing a client's site directly on the server. I made a "small change", broke the whole homepage, and had no copy of the old version. The client was a coaching institute, it was admission season, and I spent the whole night fixing it. That night I learned Git properly.

Git is a time machine for your code. Every commit is a save point. Break something? Go back.

Install Git from git-scm.com, then set your identity once:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

Now inside your project folder:

```bash
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial bakery landing page"
```

`git add` chooses what goes into the snapshot, and `git commit` takes the snapshot. Run `git status` anytime to see what's changed — I type it probably a hundred times a day.

Next, GitHub. Create a free account, click "New repository", name it `ghar-ki-bakery`, and GitHub shows you commands like these:

```bash
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/ghar-ki-bakery.git
git push -u origin main
```

Refresh the page — your code is online. From now on, your loop is: make changes, add, commit, push.

Two professional habits. First, commit messages: "update" tells nobody anything. "Fix menu cards overflowing on 360px screens" tells future-you exactly what happened. Second, create a `.gitignore` file and never commit passwords, API keys or `node_modules`.

And here's a bonus: your GitHub profile is your resume. When a Pune startup is deciding between you and someone else, a green contribution graph and clean repos say a lot. Chalo, push your bakery project now.

lessons.title: Deploy to Netlify or Vercel (with a custom domain)
lessons.content:
## Why these two?

Netlify and Vercel both host static sites **free** on generous plans, give you HTTPS automatically, and redeploy every time you push to GitHub. For small-business sites and portfolios, you rarely need anything else.

## Deploying on Netlify

1. Sign in at netlify.com with your GitHub account.
2. Click **Add new site → Import an existing project → GitHub**.
3. Pick your repository.
4. For a plain HTML/CSS/JS site: leave the build command **empty** and set the publish directory to the folder containing `index.html` (often just the root).
5. Click **Deploy**. In under a minute you'll have a URL like `ghar-ki-bakery.netlify.app`.

Change the site name under **Site configuration** to something readable before sending it to the client.

## Deploying on Vercel

1. Sign in at vercel.com with GitHub and click **Add New → Project**.
2. Import the repository. Vercel detects "Other" for static sites — that's correct.
3. Click **Deploy**. You get `your-project.vercel.app`.

Both platforms create a **preview deployment** for every branch or pull request. Send preview links to clients for approval before merging changes into `main`. It looks very professional.

## Connecting the client's domain

Most Indian small businesses buy domains from GoDaddy, Hostinger or BigRock (a `.in` domain is usually ₹500-₹900 per year). The steps:

1. In Netlify/Vercel, open **Domains** and add `gharkibakery.in`.
2. The platform shows the DNS records to add — typically an **A record** for the root domain and a **CNAME** for `www`.
3. Log into the registrar's DNS panel and add exactly those records.
4. Wait. DNS can take a few minutes to a few hours. HTTPS is issued automatically once it resolves.

> **Tip:** Always buy the domain in the **client's** name and account, not yours. Ask them to add you as a collaborator or share access temporarily. This avoids awkward disputes later and builds trust.

## Before you announce "it's live"

Run through this list every time:

- Open the live URL on your phone over mobile data, not just Wi-Fi.
- Test every link: WhatsApp, `tel:`, Instagram, nav anchors.
- Submit the contact form and confirm the client receives it.
- Run Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse) and aim for 90+ on Performance and Accessibility.
- Add a `favicon` and a proper `<title>` and `<meta name="description">` for Google.
- Check that `www` and non-`www` both work and HTTPS shows a padlock.

## Updating the site later

Edit locally, commit, push. The site redeploys automatically in about 30 seconds. If something breaks, both platforms let you instantly roll back to a previous deploy from their dashboard — one more reason to commit often.

lessons.title: Client handoff: docs, access and getting paid
lessons.content:
## The project isn't done when the site is live

The handoff is where you turn a one-time project into referrals and repeat work. A sloppy handoff ("bhai, link bhej diya") leaves the client confused. A clean one makes them recommend you to every business owner they know.

## Before handoff: get paid properly

The standard structure many Indian freelancers use for small sites:

- **50% advance** before you start (protects you from ghosting).
- **50% on completion**, before you transfer final access or point the domain.

Share a simple invoice with your name, the client's business name, scope, amount in ₹ and your UPI ID or bank details. Razorpay Payment Links or a direct UPI request works well. If you are GST-registered, include GST; most beginners aren't required to register until they cross the turnover threshold, but check current rules.

## The handoff checklist

1. **Access**: The client owns the domain account. Transfer or share the GitHub repo and add the client (or their next developer) to Netlify/Vercel as a team member.
2. **A one-page guide**: Written in simple language, ideally with screenshots — how to request changes, where the site is hosted, renewal dates for the domain.
3. **Credentials sheet**: Shared securely (not in a WhatsApp group). List every account and who owns it.
4. **Final QA proof**: Lighthouse scores, mobile screenshots, a test form submission.
5. **Support terms**: For example, "14 days of free bug fixes; content changes after that at ₹500 per small update or ₹2,000/month for up to 5 updates."

## A sample handoff message

> Hi Meera ji, your website is live at gharkibakery.in. I've attached a short guide with your domain renewal date (12 March), how orders reach your WhatsApp, and how to request changes. All accounts are in your name. I'll fix any bugs free for the next 14 days. It was a pleasure working with you — if you're happy with the site, a Google review or a referral to another business owner would mean a lot!

## Ask for the testimonial now

The best time to ask for a review is the day the client is happiest — launch day. Ask for:

- A **Google review** on your business profile, or a LinkedIn recommendation.
- Permission to add the site to your **portfolio** with a one-line quote.
- **Referrals**: "Do you know anyone else who needs a website?" Business owners in the same market or WhatsApp group are your best leads.

## Keep a project log

For every client, note the price, time spent, what went well and what you'd change. After five projects, you'll know your real hourly rate — and you'll be ready to charge more.

lessons.title: Final assignment: Ship your portfolio and a handoff kit
lessons.content: Clients hire freelancers they can verify. A live portfolio on your own URL, backed by a clean GitHub profile, is the single most important asset for getting your first paid web project. This capstone puts everything from the course together.

assignment.brief:
## Your task

Build and deploy your personal portfolio website, then prepare a client-style handoff kit for it.

## Requirements

1. **Semantic HTML**: header, nav, main with sections, footer. One `h1`.
2. **Sections**: Hero (who you are, what you build), Projects (at least 2, including your Jaipur bakery page), Skills, and Contact.
3. **Responsive CSS** with Flexbox and/or Grid, mobile-first, no horizontal scroll at 360px.
4. **JavaScript**: at least one real interaction, such as a mobile menu toggle or a contact form that builds a WhatsApp message.
5. **Git**: at least 5 meaningful commits pushed to a public GitHub repo.
6. **Deployment** on Netlify or Vercel with a readable site name.
7. **Handoff kit** in the repo's `README.md`: live URL, how to run locally, how to deploy updates, and a short "support terms" paragraph as if this were a client project.

## Steps

1. Write your content first: a two-line intro, project descriptions with your role and outcome.
2. Build and commit section by section.
3. Deploy, then run Lighthouse and fix anything below 90 on Performance or Accessibility.
4. Test the live site on your phone over mobile data.

## Deliverable

Submit your **live site URL**. Make sure the GitHub repo is linked from the site footer.

## Tips

- Recruiters and clients spend seconds, not minutes. Put your best project first.
- Add `<meta name="description">` and a favicon. Small details signal care.
- Share it on LinkedIn when it's done — tag Catalance Campus, we love seeing student launches.

lessons.title: Why React for client work (and when not to use it)
lessons.content:
## Key points
- React lets you build interfaces from reusable components, which saves huge amounts of time once a site has repeated pieces like cards, menus and forms.
- React is a great fit for interactive projects: dashboards, booking flows, carts, admin panels and multi-page startup sites.
- A five-section brochure site for a local shop is often faster, cheaper and better for SEO in plain HTML or a site builder.
- Knowing when not to use React is a professional skill that clients trust and pay for.
- Most React freelance work in India comes from startups, agencies and D2C brands needing someone who can ship and maintain an app.

## Transcript
Welcome to React for Freelancers. I'm Rahul, and before we write a single component, I want to answer the question my students always ask: "Sir, should every website be in React?" Honestly — no.

Dekho, React's superpower is components. You build a `MenuCard` once, and reuse it fifty times with different data. You build a cart once, and its state stays in sync across the page. For interactive products — a booking flow for a Kochi homestay, a dashboard for a Pune startup, an ordering system for a cloud kitchen — React saves you days of work and makes changes painless.

But if a Jaipur boutique wants a five-section page with photos and a WhatsApp button, React is overkill. You'd add a build step, a JavaScript bundle and SEO complications for no real benefit. I've seen freelancers lose clients because a simple site became slow and hard to update.

So here's my rule of thumb. Choose React when the site has real state — things users add, filter, log into, or submit through multiple steps. Or when the client already has a React codebase and needs someone to maintain it. That second one is a huge market, by the way. Agencies in Bengaluru and Gurugram constantly look for freelancers who can jump into an existing React project.

In this course we'll build one real project end to end: a website for "Malabar Bites", a café in Fort Kochi. Menu, cart, table booking, live opening hours, Tailwind styling, deployment on Vercel — and finally, how much to charge for it. By the end, you won't just know React; you'll know how to sell it. Chalo, let's set up the project.

lessons.title: Set up with Vite and understand JSX
lessons.content:
## Creating the project Vite is the standard way to start a React project today. It's fast and produces small production builds. In your terminal: ```bash npm create vite@latest malabar-bites -- --template react cd malabar-bites npm install npm run dev ``` Open the local URL Vite prints (usually `http://localhost:5173`). Edit `src/App.jsx`, save, and the page updates instantly. ## The files that matter - `index.html` — the single HTML page. It has a `
`. - `src/main.jsx` — mounts your React app into that root div. - `src/App.jsx` — your top-level component. Start here. - `public/` — static files like the favicon and images served as-is. Delete the demo content in `App.jsx` and `App.css` so you start clean. ## JSX: HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript ```jsx export default function App() { const cafeName = "Malabar Bites"; const isOpen = true; return (

{cafeName}

Kerala breakfast and filter coffee in Fort Kochi.

{isOpen ?

Open now

:

Closed — see you tomorrow at 7 AM

}
); } ``` JSX looks like HTML but compiles to JavaScript. The rules that trip people up: 1. **One parent element.** A component returns a single root. If you don't want an extra div, use a fragment: `<>...`. 2. **`className`, not `class`** — because `class` is a reserved word in JavaScript. Similarly `htmlFor` instead of `for` on labels. 3. **Curly braces for JavaScript expressions.** `{cafeName}`, `{price * 2}`, `{isOpen ? "Yes" : "No"}`. Expressions only — no `if` statements or `for` loops inside the braces. 4. **Close every tag**, including self-closing ones: ``, ``, `
`. 5. **Inline styles are objects**: `style={{ color: "teal", marginTop: 16 }}`. You'll rarely need them once we add Tailwind. ## Conditional rendering patterns ```jsx {isOpen && Open now} {items.length === 0 ?

Your cart is empty

: } ``` `&&` renders the right side only when the left is true. The ternary picks between two options. > **Tip:** Watch out for `{count && }`. If `count` is `0`, React renders the number 0 on the page. Use `{count > 0 && }` instead. ## Install the React DevTools Add the "React Developer Tools" Chrome extension. It shows your component tree, props and state — you'll use it constantly from the next lesson onward. ## Commit early ```bash git init git add . git commit -m "Scaffold Malabar Bites with Vite + React" ``` Vite's template already includes a `.gitignore` that excludes `node_modules` and `dist`. Push to GitHub now — Module 4 deploys straight from there.

questions.prompt: A cart badge is written as {cartCount && <Badge count={cartCount} />}. When the cart is empty, a stray '0' appears on the page. Why?

options.text: Badge has a bug that renders 0
When cartCount is 0, the expression evaluates to 0 and React renders numbers
JSX does not support the && operator

questions.explanation: && returns the left value when it is falsy. React skips false, null and undefined, but it renders 0. Use cartCount > 0 && ... instead.

questions.prompt: Which is the best key when rendering menu items that the client can reorder and delete from an admin panel?

options.text: A stable unique id stored with each item

questions.explanation: Keys must be stable and unique so React can match items between renders. Indexes break when items move; random values change every render; prices are not unique.

questions.prompt: A MenuCard component wants to show a discounted price. What should it do?

options.text: Compute a new value, e.g. const finalPrice = price * 0.9, and render that
Ask the parent to re-mount it
Store the price in a global variable

questions.explanation: Props are read-only. Derive new values from props inside the component instead of mutating them.

questions.prompt: Which JSX is valid?
questions.explanation: JSX uses htmlFor and className, requires self-closing tags like , and only allows expressions (not if statements) inside curly braces.

Assignment: Menu, filters and cart for a Kochi café
lessons.content: Menus with filters and a cart are among the most requested React features from restaurants, cloud kitchens and D2C brands. Getting state right here — no mutation, derived totals, persistence — is what separates a demo from something a client can actually run their business on.

assignment.brief:
## The client

**Malabar Bites**, a café in Fort Kochi. The owner, Anitha, wants customers to browse the menu on their phones, build an order and send it to the café's WhatsApp.

## Your task

Build the menu and cart in React using what you learned in Modules 1 and 2.

## Requirements

1. Menu data (at least 10 items across 3+ categories) in `src/data/menu.js` with stable `id`s, prices in ₹ and a veg/non-veg flag.
2. A reusable `MenuCard` component that receives data through props.
3. Category tabs and a "Veg only" toggle, both driven by `useState`. Filtered results must be **derived**, not stored.
4. A cart with add, increase, decrease and remove. Total formatted with `toLocaleString("en-IN")`.
5. Cart persisted to `localStorage` with `useEffect`.
6. A "Send order on WhatsApp" button that builds a readable order message from the cart.
7. Empty states: an empty cart and a filter with no results.

## Deliverable

Push to GitHub and submit the **repository link**. Include a short README with screenshots of the mobile view.

## Tips

- Keep cart state in `App` and pass `onAdd` / `onChangeQty` down.
- Test by refreshing the page mid-order — the cart should survive.
- Run the React DevTools Profiler once and make sure clicking a tab doesn't cause errors in the console.

rubric.criterion: Component design: reusable MenuCard, clean props, sensible file structure
State correctness: no mutation, derived filters and totals, working quantity controls
Effects: localStorage persistence implemented correctly without loops
UX details: empty states, WhatsApp message quality, mobile usability

lessons.title: React Router: multi-page client sites
lessons.content:
## Key points
- React Router maps URLs like `/menu` and `/book` to components, so a single-page React app behaves like a normal multi-page website.
- Use `Link` or `NavLink` for internal navigation instead of `<a href>`, so the page doesn't fully reload.
- A shared layout with `<Outlet />` keeps the header and footer consistent across every page.
- Dynamic segments like `/menu/:itemId` let one component render many detail pages, read with `useParams`.
- Always add a catch-all 404 route; clients and Google both hit broken URLs.

## Transcript
Most client sites aren't one page. Malabar Bites needs Home, Menu, Book a Table and Contact. Each needs its own URL, so customers can share `malabarbites.in/menu` on WhatsApp. That's what React Router does.

```bash
npm install react-router-dom
```

```jsx
import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, NavLink, Outlet } from "react-router-dom";

function Layout() {
  return (
    <>
      <header>
        <nav>
          <NavLink to="/">Home</NavLink>
          <NavLink to="/menu">Menu</NavLink>
          <NavLink to="/book">Book a table</NavLink>
        </nav>
      </header>
      <main>
        <Outlet />
      </main>
      <footer>Fort Kochi · Open 7 AM to 10 PM</footer>
    </>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <Routes>
        <Route element={<Layout />}>
          <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
          <Route path="/menu" element={<MenuPage />} />
          <Route path="/menu/:itemId" element={<MenuItemPage />} />
          <Route path="/book" element={<BookingPage />} />
          <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
        </Route>
      </Routes>
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}
```

Dekho the structure. `Layout` holds the header and footer, and `<Outlet />` is the slot where the current page renders. Change the header once, it changes everywhere.

`NavLink` is like `Link` but adds an `active` class to the current page's link, so you can highlight it in CSS. Never use a plain `<a href="/menu">` for internal pages — it reloads the whole app and your cart state disappears.

The `:itemId` route is dynamic. Inside `MenuItemPage`, you call `useParams()` to get the id, find the item in your data, and render it. One component, fifty dish pages. If the item doesn't exist, render a friendly "Dish not found" message.

And the star path — that's your 404. Clients mistype links in Instagram bios all the time; a helpful 404 with a link back home keeps visitors from bouncing.

One warning for deployment: on a static host, refreshing `/menu` can give a 404, because the server looks for a `menu` file. We'll fix that with a rewrite rule in Module 4.

lessons.content: Five scenario questions drawn from real bugs in client React projects.

questions.prompt: A customer adds items to the cart, then clicks a header link written as Menu. The cart empties. Why?

options.text: React Router does not support the /menu path
A plain anchor triggers a full page reload, resetting in-memory React state
The cart component was not wrapped in Outlet
useState only works on the home page

questions.explanation: Internal navigation should use Link or NavLink, which change the URL without reloading the app. A full reload discards state that is not persisted.

questions.prompt: Your fetch to an API returns a 500 error, but the catch block never runs. What is happening?

options.text: fetch only rejects on network failures; you must check res.ok and throw yourself
500 errors are cached by the browser

questions.explanation: fetch resolves successfully for HTTP error statuses. Check res.ok (or res.status) and handle errors explicitly.

questions.prompt: You need to add a Razorpay secret key so the frontend can create orders. Where should it go?

options.text: On a server or serverless function, never in the frontend bundle

questions.explanation: Everything shipped to the browser is public, including VITE_ variables. Secrets belong on a backend; the frontend only uses the public key.

questions.prompt: In a controlled input, what happens if you set value={form.name} but forget the onChange handler?

options.text: The input becomes read-only because React keeps resetting it to the state value
React converts it to an uncontrolled input silently

questions.explanation: React controls the displayed value from state. Without onChange to update state, typing has no effect, and React warns in the console.

questions.prompt: Which route renders a helpful page for mistyped URLs like /menuu?
questions.explanation: The * path matches any URL not matched by other routes, making it the catch-all 404.

Deploying React apps on Vercel: env vars, SPA routes and domains
lessons.content:
## Build first, locally

Before deploying, always run the production build on your machine:

```bash
npm run build
npm run preview
```

`build` creates an optimised `dist/` folder. `preview` serves it locally. Many bugs — a wrong image path, a missing environment variable — only show up here. Fix them before the client sees anything.

## Deploying to Vercel

1. Push your code to GitHub.
2. On vercel.com, **Add New → Project**, import the repo.
3. Vercel detects **Vite**: build command `npm run build`, output directory `dist`. Leave these as-is.
4. Under **Environment Variables**, add each `VITE_` variable from your local `.env` file (for example `VITE_SPECIALS_URL`).
5. Click **Deploy**.

Every push to `main` now deploys to production, and every other branch gets a preview URL. Send preview links to the client for approval before merging.

## Fix the refresh-404 problem

With React Router, refreshing `/menu` asks the server for a file called `menu`, which doesn't exist. Tell the host to serve `index.html` for every route. On Vercel, add `vercel.json` at the project root:

```json
{
  "rewrites": [{ "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" }]
}
```

On Netlify, create `public/_redirects` containing:

```text
/*    /index.html   200
```

Test it: open a deep link like `/menu/appam-stew` directly in a new tab on the live site.

## Environment variables, the right way

- Keep a `.env.example` in the repo listing variable **names** without values, so the next developer knows what to set.
- Add `.env` to `.gitignore`.
- Remember that `VITE_` variables are baked into the public bundle at build time. If you change one in Vercel, **redeploy** for it to take effect.
- Secrets (payment keys, admin tokens) go into **serverless functions** (a file in an `api/` folder on Vercel), never the frontend.

## Custom domain

In the project's **Settings → Domains**, add `malabarbites.in` and `www.malabarbites.in`. Vercel shows the DNS records; add them in the client's GoDaddy, Hostinger or BigRock panel. HTTPS is automatic.

## SEO for single-page apps

Client-rendered React apps start with a nearly empty HTML file. Google can render JavaScript, but social previews on WhatsApp and LinkedIn often can't. At minimum:

- Set a good `<title>`, `<meta name="description">` and Open Graph tags (`og:title`, `og:image`) in `index.html`.
- Update `document.title` per page.
- If SEO is a core business goal (a blog, a marketplace), recommend **Next.js** or **Astro** to the client instead. Saying this upfront builds trust.

## Pre-launch checklist

- Lighthouse on the live URL: aim for 90+ Performance, Accessibility and SEO on mobile.
- Test deep links, the booking form and the WhatsApp order on a real phone over mobile data.
- Check the console for errors and remove stray `console.log` calls.
- Confirm the client owns the domain and has access to the Vercel team.

lessons.title: Pricing a React project for an Indian client
lessons.content:
## Price the outcome, not the technology

Clients don't buy "React". The café owner buys **more orders and fewer phone calls**. A Pune startup buys **a working MVP before their investor demo**. Start every pricing conversation by understanding that outcome — it decides how much the project is worth to them.

## Step 1: Scope in writing

Break the project into features and estimate hours honestly. For Malabar Bites:

- Design adaptation and component setup — 8 hours
- Home, Menu, Contact pages with routing — 10 hours
- Filterable menu and cart with WhatsApp checkout — 12 hours
- Booking form with validation and email delivery — 6 hours
- Google Sheet-powered specials with loading/error states — 6 hours
- Tailwind polish and responsive QA on real devices — 8 hours
- Deployment, domain, SEO basics and handoff docs — 5 hours

That's about **55 hours**. Add a **20-25% buffer** for feedback rounds and surprises: roughly **68 hours**.

## Step 2: Know your hourly floor

As a beginner-to-intermediate React freelancer in India, ₹400-₹800 per hour is a realistic range; experienced developers charge ₹1,500+ per hour. At ₹600/hour, 68 hours is about **₹40,800**. Round it to a clean number.

## Step 3: Offer three packages

Indian clients almost always negotiate. Packages let them choose instead of bargaining your one price down.

- **Basic — ₹28,000**: Home, Menu with filters, Contact, WhatsApp button, deployment. 1 revision round.
- **Standard — ₹42,000** (recommended): Everything in Basic, plus cart with WhatsApp checkout, booking form and Google Sheet specials. 2 revision rounds.
- **Premium — ₹65,000**: Everything in Standard, plus Razorpay online payments, an admin view for orders and 1 month of support.

Most clients pick the middle option. Make it the one you actually want to build.

## Step 4: Payment terms

- **40% advance** to start, **30%** at the design/demo milestone, **30%** before final handoff and domain switch.
- Accept UPI, bank transfer or a Razorpay payment link. Send a proper invoice every time.
- If you're GST-registered, add 18% GST and say so in the quote. If you're not, state that prices are without GST.

## Step 5: Protect yourself from scope creep

Write these into the quote:

- **Revision rounds** included, and the rate for extra changes (for example ₹800/hour).
- **What's out of scope**: content writing, photography, paid plugins, third-party fees like domain and Razorpay charges.
- **Timeline** that depends on the client sending content on time.

> **Tip:** When a client asks "just one small change" after sign-off, reply warmly: "Happy to! That's outside the current scope — it'll take about 3 hours, so ₹2,400. Shall I add it?" Most clients respect a clear, friendly boundary.

## Step 6: Recurring income

Offer a **maintenance retainer**: ₹3,000-₹8,000 per month for updates, upgrades and small content changes. Five retainers can cover a student's monthly expenses.

Send every quote as a clean PDF with your portfolio link. That alone beats most competing quotes on Instagram and Internshala.

## Your task

Complete the **Malabar Bites** site (or a real local business of your choice — a Pune bakery, a Jaipur boutique, a Kochi homestay) and prepare a client quote for it.

## Build requirements

1. **Routing**: at least 4 routes with a shared layout, active nav links and a 404 page.
2. **Components & state**: menu/catalogue with filters and a cart (from Module 2).
3. **Form**: a validated booking or enquiry form with sending, success and error states.

## Tips

lessons.title: Why Flutter, and setting up your machine
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Flutter lets you build Android, iOS and web apps from one Dart codebase, which is why small Indian startups and agencies love it.
- You need three things installed: the Flutter SDK, Android Studio (for the Android SDK and emulator) and VS Code with the Flutter extension.
- `flutter doctor` is your best friend; it tells you exactly which piece of the setup is missing.
- Enable Developer Options and USB debugging on your phone to run apps on a real device, which is faster than the emulator on low-RAM laptops.
- `flutter create` generates a working counter app, and hot reload (press `r`) shows your changes in under a second.

## Transcript
Namaste everyone, I'm Kiran. Over the last eight years I've shipped more than thirty apps with Flutter, from a delivery app for a Nashik grocery chain to a booking app for a Pune fitness studio. Almost every one of those started exactly the way we'll start today: an empty folder and one command.

Why Flutter? Dekho, most clients in India have a small budget. They want Android first, iOS maybe later. With Flutter I write the code once in Dart and I can ship both, plus a web version if they ask. That is a real cost saving you can pitch to clients.

Chalo, setup. Download the Flutter SDK from the official site and unzip it somewhere without spaces in the path, like `C:\src\flutter`. Add its `bin` folder to your PATH. Then install Android Studio, open the SDK Manager once, and accept the licences. Finally install VS Code and the Flutter extension.

Now open a terminal and run this:

```bash
flutter doctor
flutter doctor --android-licenses
flutter create hello_kiran
cd hello_kiran
flutter run
```

If `flutter doctor` shows a red cross, read the message slowly. Ninety percent of the time it is a missing licence or Android Studio not found. On a 4 or 8GB laptop, I strongly suggest using your own phone instead of the emulator. Go to Settings, About phone, tap Build number seven times, then turn on USB debugging.

When the counter app opens on your phone, change the title text in `lib/main.dart`, save, and press `r` in the terminal. That instant update is hot reload, and it is the reason you will enjoy this course. See you in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Dart essentials: variables, types and null safety
lessons.content:
## Dart in one sentence

Dart is a typed, object-oriented language that feels familiar if you have seen Java, JavaScript or C. You can practise everything in this article on **dartpad.dev** without installing anything.

## Variables: var, final and const

Every Dart program starts at `main()`. Inside it you declare variables in three main ways:

```dart
void main() {
  var city = 'Pune';          // type inferred as String
  final int orders = 42;      // assigned once, can be decided at runtime
  const gstRate = 0.18;       // compile-time constant
  double price = 1499;        // ints are promoted to double here

  print('Course in $city costs Rs. $price');
  final total = price * (1 + gstRate);
  print('With GST: Rs. $total');
}
```

- Use `final` by default for values that should not change after being set.
- Use `const` for values known while writing code, like tax rates or padding sizes. Flutter rewards `const` with better performance.
- Use `var` or an explicit type only when the value will change.

> **Tip:** `$name` inserts a variable into a string. For anything more complex than a plain variable, compute it into a local variable first (like `total` above) and insert that; it keeps strings readable.

## The core types

- `int` and `double` for numbers, `num` if you accept either.
- `String` for text, with single or double quotes.
- `bool` for `true` / `false`.
- `List<T>` for ordered items and `Map<K, V>` for key-value pairs.

```dart
final menu = <String>['Samosa', 'Vada Pav', 'Poha'];
final prices = <String, int>{'Samosa': 20, 'Vada Pav': 25, 'Poha': 30};

for (final item in menu) {
  final itemPrice = prices[item];
  print('$item: Rs. $itemPrice');
}
```

## Null safety: the feature that saves your app

In Dart, a normal variable **cannot be null**. If something might be missing, you say so with a `?`:

```dart
String? upiId;                    // may be null
print(upiId?.length);             // safe access, prints null
print(upiId ?? 'UPI not set');    // fallback value
upiId = 'kiran@okaxis';
print(upiId!.toUpperCase());      // ! means "trust me, not null"
```

The compiler forces you to handle the null case before using the value. That one rule removes the most common crash in Android apps: the null pointer exception.

### Rules of thumb

1. Prefer `?.` and `??` over `!`. Every `!` is a promise; break it and the app crashes.
2. Use `late` only when a value is guaranteed to be set before it is read, such as in `initState`.
3. Keep types explicit in public APIs (function parameters, class fields) and let inference handle local variables.

Try changing `upiId` back to `null` before the last line and watch DartPad throw the error. Breaking things on purpose is how these rules stick.

lessons.title: Functions, classes and async code in Dart
Quiz: Dart fundamentals
lessons.content: Five questions on variables, null safety, functions and async. If you miss one, revisit the article and try the snippet in DartPad.

questions.prompt: You fetch a user's name from a server once when a screen opens and never change it. Which declaration fits best?
questions.explanation: final is for values set once at runtime. const only works for values known at compile time, so it cannot hold a network result.

questions.prompt: Given String? phone; what does print(phone ?? 'Not added') print when phone is null?
questions.explanation: The ?? operator returns the right-hand value whenever the left side is null.

questions.prompt: Why is using the ! operator on a nullable variable considered risky?

options.text: It is not allowed inside classes
It converts the value to a String
If the value is actually null at runtime, the app throws an error

questions.explanation: ! tells the compiler to trust you. If the value turns out to be null, Dart throws at runtime, which is exactly the crash null safety tries to prevent.

questions.prompt: A function is declared as double addGst(double amount, {double rate = 0.18}). Which call is valid?
questions.explanation: amount is positional and required; rate is named, so it must be passed as rate: value.

questions.prompt: You print the result of fetchTodaySpend() and see 'Instance of Future<double>'. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Change the return type to String
Add await before the call inside an async function
Remove the async keyword from fetchTodaySpend
Wrap the call in a for loop

questions.explanation: Without await you get the Future itself, not the value it eventually completes with.

lessons.title: Everything is a widget: StatelessWidget and the widget tree
Layouts that work on every phone: Row, Column, Expanded and friends
lessons.content:
## The layout mindset

Indian users have everything from a 5-inch budget Redmi to a large Samsung. Never place widgets at fixed pixel positions. Instead, describe **relationships**: "these go side by side", "this takes the remaining space".

## Column and Row

- `Column` stacks children **vertically**.
- `Row` places children **horizontally**.
- `mainAxisAlignment` controls spacing along the main direction; `crossAxisAlignment` controls the other direction.

```dart
Column(
  crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
  children: [
    Text('Shree Ram Bakery', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineSmall),
    const SizedBox(height: 4),
    const Text('Johari Bazaar, Jaipur'),
  ],
)
```

> **Tip:** Use `SizedBox(height: 8)` or `SizedBox(width: 8)` for gaps. It is cleaner than padding every child.

## Expanded and Flexible

The most common beginner error is the yellow-and-black striped "RenderFlex overflowed" banner. It means children asked for more space than the row has. The fix is usually `Expanded`:

```dart
Row(
  children: [
    const Icon(Icons.cake_outlined),
    const SizedBox(width: 12),
    Expanded(
      child: Text(
        'Mawa Kachori with extra dry fruits',
        overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis,
      ),
    ),
    const Text('Rs. 40'),
  ],
)
```

`Expanded` tells the text: "take whatever space is left, no more". The price stays visible on every screen size. Use `flex: 2` on one `Expanded` and `flex: 1` on another to split space in a ratio.

## Padding, Container and Card

- `Padding` adds space around one child.
- `Container` combines padding, margin, colour, borders and rounded corners. Use it when you need decoration, not just for spacing.
- `Card` gives a Material surface with elevation, perfect for list items.

```dart
Card(
  child: Padding(
    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
    child: Row(
      children: [
        const CircleAvatar(child: Icon(Icons.bakery_dining)),
        const SizedBox(width: 12),
        const Expanded(child: Text('Ghevar (250g)')),
        Text('Rs. 180', style: TextStyle(fontWeight: FontWeight.bold)),
      ],
    ),
  ),
)
```

## Stack for overlays

`Stack` places children on top of each other. Use it for a "Bestseller" badge on a product image, with `Positioned(top: 8, right: 8, ...)` for the badge.

## A debugging checklist

1. Overflow in a Row? Wrap the flexible child in `Expanded`.
2. Column inside a scroll view not showing? Check you did not put an unbounded `ListView` inside a `Column` without `Expanded`.
3. Not sure where space comes from? Turn on "Show guidelines" in the Flutter inspector.

Master these few widgets and you can build roughly eighty percent of the screens clients will ever ask for.

From debug build to Play Store: signing, App Bundles and testing tracks
lessons.content:
## Debug vs release

The app you run with `flutter run` is a **debug** build: large, slow, and signed with a debug key. The Play Store needs a **release** build signed with your own upload key.

## Step 1: Pick a permanent application ID

Open `android/app/build.gradle` (or `build.gradle.kts` in newer projects) and change `applicationId` from `com.example...` to something you own, like `in.kiranpatil.kharcha`. You **cannot** change it after publishing, so choose carefully. Also set a proper app name in `AndroidManifest.xml` and generate launcher icons with the `flutter_launcher_icons` package.

## Step 2: Create an upload keystore

```bash
keytool -genkey -v -keystore upload-keystore.jks -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 -alias upload
```

Keep this file and its passwords safe and **out of Git**. Create `android/key.properties`:

```properties
storePassword=your-store-password
keyPassword=your-key-password
keyAlias=upload
storeFile=../upload-keystore.jks
```

Then follow the official Flutter "Build and release an Android app" guide to load `key.properties` in your Gradle file and add a `release` signing config. Add both `key.properties` and `*.jks` to `.gitignore`.

> **Tip:** Back up the keystore to a private cloud folder. With Play App Signing, Google holds the final app signing key, so a lost upload key can be reset, but it costs you days.

## Step 3: Build

```bash
flutter build appbundle --release
flutter build apk --release --split-per-abi
```

- The **.aab** (Android App Bundle) in `build/app/outputs/bundle/release/` is what you upload to Google Play. New apps must use App Bundles.
- The split **APKs** are handy for sharing a test build directly with a client over WhatsApp or Google Drive.

Bump `version: 1.0.0+1` in `pubspec.yaml` before every upload. The number after `+` is the version code and must always increase.

## Step 4: Google Play Console

1. Create a developer account. There is a one-time registration fee of 25 US dollars (roughly ₹2,100) and identity verification.
2. Create the app, fill in the store listing: short description, full description, screenshots, feature graphic and an icon.
3. Complete the **App content** section: privacy policy URL, data safety form, content rating questionnaire and target audience. A free privacy policy page on GitHub Pages works fine for a simple offline app.
4. Upload your `.aab` to a **testing track**.

## The testing requirement for new personal accounts

Google requires newly created personal developer accounts to run a **closed test** with a minimum number of testers (currently 12) opted in for 14 continuous days before you can apply for production access. Plan for this:

- Line up classmates, family and friends early and collect their Gmail IDs.
- Share the opt-in link in a WhatsApp group and ask testers to keep the app installed.
- Fix the feedback you get; this period makes your app better.

Once production access is approved, promote the release, and your app is live for anyone in India to install.

lessons.title: Final project: Ship Kharcha, your expense tracker
lessons.content: This is your portfolio piece. A working app with a real Play Store testing link or signed build tells clients and recruiters far more than any certificate, and it gives you a codebase you can reuse for paid projects.

assignment.brief:
## The task

Build and release version 1.0 of **Kharcha**, an offline expense tracker for students and young professionals.

## Required features

1. **Home screen** with the current month's total and a list of expenses (newest first) using `ListView.builder`.
2. **Add and edit** an expense through a validated form: title, amount, category (dropdown) and date (date picker).
3. **Delete** an expense with swipe-to-delete (`Dismissible`) and an Undo `SnackBar`.
4. **Category summary** screen showing totals per category.
5. **Offline persistence** with `shared_preferences` and JSON, so data survives app restarts.
6. A custom app name, launcher icon and `applicationId` (no `com.example`).

## Release steps

- Create an upload keystore and configure release signing (keystore **not** committed).
- Build a release App Bundle and a release APK.
- Upload the bundle to a Play Console internal or closed testing track. If you do not yet have a developer account, upload the signed release APK to Google Drive instead.

## Deliverable

Submit **one link** to your public GitHub repository. The README must include:

- Three or more screenshots
- A link to the Play testing track or the signed APK
- A short "What I would build next" section

## Tips

- Commit after each feature with clear messages; reviewers do read history.
- Test on the smallest screen you can find.
- Ask two friends to use the app without help, and fix whatever confuses them.

lessons.title: Connecting Flutter to Firebase with the FlutterFire CLI
lessons.content:
## Key points
- The FlutterFire CLI registers your Android and iOS apps with Firebase and generates `firebase_options.dart` for you.
- Always call `Firebase.initializeApp` before `runApp`, after `WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized()`.
- Add only the Firebase packages you actually use; each one increases app size.
- Start on the free Spark plan, and set a budget alert before ever switching to Blaze.

## Transcript
Hello again! In this course we'll give our apps a real backend without writing a server. Chalo, let's connect Flutter to Firebase.

Create a project in the Firebase console, then in your terminal:

```bash
npm install -g firebase-tools
firebase login
dart pub global activate flutterfire_cli
flutterfire configure
flutter pub add firebase_core firebase_auth
```

`flutterfire configure` asks which project and platforms to use, then writes `lib/firebase_options.dart`. Now update `main`:

```dart
Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await Firebase.initializeApp(options: DefaultFirebaseOptions.currentPlatform);
  runApp(const MyApp());
}
```

Run the app. No red errors means you're connected. One habit from client work: create two Firebase projects, one for development and one for production, so your testing never touches real customer data. Next, let's make users log in.

lessons.title: Email and Google sign-in with authStateChanges

lessons.content: Three quick questions to check your setup and auth flow understanding.

questions.prompt: Your app crashes on launch with 'No Firebase App has been created'. What is the likely fix?
questions.explanation: Firebase must be initialized before any Firebase service is used, which means awaiting initializeApp in main before runApp.

questions.prompt: Why use a StreamBuilder on authStateChanges() instead of checking currentUser once?

options.text: It is the only way to read the user's email
The UI automatically switches screens whenever the user signs in or out
currentUser does not work on Android

questions.explanation: The stream emits on every sign-in and sign-out, so the right screen is always shown without manual navigation.

questions.prompt: Google sign-in works on your teammate's laptop build but fails on yours. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether your machine's SHA-1 fingerprint is added in the Firebase console
Whether your phone has enough storage

questions.explanation: Each debug keystore has its own SHA-1. Google sign-in on Android fails if the fingerprint of the signing key is not registered.

lessons.title: Modelling data in Firestore: collections, documents and queries
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Firestore stores documents (small JSON-like maps) inside collections, and documents can hold subcollections.
- Design your data around the screens and queries you need, not around SQL-style tables.
- Duplicating a little data, like a homestay name inside each booking, is normal and saves extra reads.
- You pay per document read, so avoid loading whole collections when a filtered query will do.

## Transcript
A homestay owner in Fort Kochi asked me for a booking app. Guests pick dates, the owner sees all bookings live. Perfect Firestore use case.

Dekho, Firestore is not SQL. Think about screens first. A guest needs "my bookings". The owner needs "all bookings for my property, by date". So I created a `bookings` collection where each document has `guestId`, `homestayId`, `homestayName`, `checkIn`, `checkOut` and `status`.

Yes, I copied `homestayName` into every booking. In SQL that's a sin; in Firestore it saves a read on every list screen, and reads cost money.

The guest's list is one query:

```dart
FirebaseFirestore.instance
    .collection('bookings')
    .where('guestId', isEqualTo: uid)
    .orderBy('checkIn')
    .snapshots();
```

Combining `where` and `orderBy` on different fields needs a composite index. Don't panic when you see the error; it includes a link that creates the index in one click.

Shipping safely: Crashlytics, App Distribution and budgets
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Crashlytics reports real crashes from users' phones with stack traces, so you fix problems before reviews mention them.
- Firebase App Distribution sends test builds to a client by email, without going through the Play Store.
- Set a budget alert in Google Cloud the day you move to the Blaze plan.
- Tighten security rules and remove test-mode access before handing over a project.

## Transcript
Last lesson, and it's the one that protects your reputation.

First, Crashlytics. Add `firebase_crashlytics` and route Flutter errors to it:

```dart
FlutterError.onError = FirebaseCrashlytics.instance.recordFlutterFatalError;
```

Now every crash on a guest's phone in Kochi appears in your console with the exact line.

Second, App Distribution. When the homestay owner wants to try a build, I upload the APK there and add her email. No Play Store review, no waiting.

Third, money. Dekho, a missing `where` clause in a loop once cost a friend of mine a few thousand rupees overnight. Set a budget alert, even for ₹500.

Before handover, check your Firestore rules once more so nothing still allows open reads and writes, and transfer project ownership to the client's Google account while keeping yourself as an editor. Ship with all this in place, and clients will trust you with their next app too.

modules.title: Design Fundamentals That Make Screens Feel Right

lessons.title: What clients actually pay a UI designer for
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Clients don't pay for "pretty screens"; they pay for screens that help their customers finish a task, like booking a room or placing an order.
- Good UI rests on four fundamentals: hierarchy, spacing, typography and color. Figma is just the tool you use to apply them.
- Most beginner designs fail because everything looks equally important, not because of a lack of creativity.
- In this course you'll design a real booking app for a Kochi homestay, from rough wireframes to a clickable prototype.
- Your goal by the end: a portfolio-ready project and the confidence to quote for your first ₹15,000 to ₹40,000 freelance UI gig.

## Transcript
Hi everyone, I'm Priya. I've been a product designer for about seven years, first at Swiggy and then as a full-time freelancer working with startups in Bengaluru, Pune and Kochi. Welcome to the course.

Let me start with something nobody told me when I was in college. Clients are not paying you for pretty screens. A homestay owner in Fort Kochi doesn't care if you used a trendy gradient. She cares that a family from Delhi can open her app, see the rooms, pick dates and pay through UPI without calling her five times. If your design makes that happen, you're worth every rupee.

So how do we make screens that work? Dekho, it comes down to four fundamentals. Hierarchy: what should the eye see first? Spacing: how do elements group and breathe? Typography: is the text readable and does it have a clear structure? And color: does it guide action and stay accessible? Almost every bad screen I review breaks one of these four. Usually it's hierarchy, where everything is bold and everything is shouting.

Once those basics click, Figma becomes your workshop. We'll learn frames, auto layout and components properly, not just by clicking around. Then we'll take one real project, a booking app for a homestay called Backwater Nest, all the way from wireframes to hi-fi screens to a prototype you can show a client.

My promise: if you do the assignments, you'll finish with a project you can put in your portfolio and pitch with. Chalo, let's start with hierarchy.

lessons.title: Visual hierarchy: telling the eye where to go
lessons.content:
## What is visual hierarchy?

Visual hierarchy is the order in which a person notices things on a screen. Every screen has a job, and hierarchy makes sure the most important thing for that job is seen first. On a homestay listing, that's usually the room photo, the price per night and the **Book now** button, not the cancellation policy.

When everything has the same weight, users scan, get confused and leave. When the hierarchy is clear, they don't even notice the design. They just complete the task.

## The tools you use to create hierarchy

### 1. Size
Bigger things get noticed first. Your screen title might be 24px, section headings 18px and body text 14 to 16px. A clear jump between levels matters more than the exact numbers.

### 2. Weight
Bold versus regular text creates contrast without changing size. Use bold sparingly: if five things are bold, nothing is.

### 3. Color and contrast
A saturated primary color on the main button pulls the eye. Secondary actions should be quieter, like an outline or text-only button. Grey text (for example `#6B7280` on white) signals "supporting information".

### 4. Position
People scan top to bottom, left to right. Put key information near the top and keep the primary action where thumbs can reach it, usually at the bottom on mobile.

### 5. Space
An element surrounded by empty space feels important. Crowding reduces importance.

## A quick exercise: the squint test

Open any screen you've designed and squint at it, or blur it slightly. What stands out? If the answer isn't the most important element, your hierarchy needs work.

> **Tip:** Write down the "one thing" each screen must achieve before you design it. For a room details screen: "Help the guest decide to book this room." Then rank every element by how much it helps that goal.

## Common beginner mistakes

- **Too many font sizes.** Stick to 4 or 5 sizes across the whole app.
- **Two primary buttons on one screen.** Pick one primary action. "Book now" is primary; "Save to wishlist" is secondary.
- **Bold labels and bold values.** In a price row, make the value (₹2,400 / night) bold, not the label.
- **Decoration competing with content.** Icons, dividers and badges should support content, not fight it.

## Real example

Imagine the Backwater Nest room card. A weak version shows the room name, amenities, rating, price and two buttons all in 14px regular. A strong version leads with a large photo, then the room name at 18px semibold, a muted line of amenities, a bold price, and a single clear button. Same information, completely different experience.

Hierarchy is the foundation for everything else in this course. Spacing, typography and color are all ways of expressing it.

lessons.title: Spacing and the 8-point grid
lessons.content:
## Why spacing matters so much

Spacing is the most underrated design skill. Two designs can use the same fonts and colors, yet one feels professional and the other feels "college project". Nine times out of ten, the difference is spacing.

Spacing does two jobs: it **groups** related things together and it **separates** unrelated things. This is the Gestalt principle of proximity. If the price sits closer to the room name than to the next card, users instantly understand it belongs to that room.

## The 8-point grid

Instead of picking random values like 13px or 22px, use multiples of 8: **8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64**. For tight spots, 4px is allowed as a half-step.

Why 8?
- Most screen sizes divide cleanly by 8, so layouts scale well on Android and iOS.
- Developers can map your spacing to tokens easily (`space-2 = 8px`, `space-4 = 16px`).
- It removes decision fatigue. You choose from a small set instead of guessing.

## A simple spacing scale to start with

- **4px**: icon to its label
- **8px**: between lines of related text, like room name and location
- **16px**: padding inside cards, gap between form fields
- **24px**: between groups inside a section
- **32 to 48px**: between major sections of a screen

> **Rule of thumb:** inner spacing should be smaller than outer spacing. The padding inside a card should be smaller than the gap between cards, otherwise the grouping breaks.

## Margins and layout grids on mobile

For a 360px or 390px wide mobile frame, use **16px side margins** (20px also works). In Figma, add a layout grid to your frame: 4 columns, 16px margin, 16px gutter. This keeps content aligned across every screen.

## How to apply it in Figma

1. Set your nudge amount: in Preferences, change "Big nudge" to 8. Now `Shift + Arrow` moves things by 8px.
2. Use auto layout (you'll learn it in Module 2) and set gaps and padding only from your scale.
3. Hold `Alt` (or `Option` on Mac) while hovering to measure distances between elements.

## Spot the problem

A booking summary screen has 12px between the dates and the guest count, 20px between guest count and price, and 14px padding inside the card. It "feels off" but you can't say why. The fix: 8px between related lines, 24px before the price block, 16px card padding. Consistent, intentional and calm.

Spacing is invisible when it's right. Users just feel the screen is easy to read, and that's exactly what you want.

lessons.title: Typography and color for screens
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Use one typeface (two at most) for an app; a good sans-serif like Inter, Poppins or Manrope covers 95% of projects.
- Build a type scale with 4 to 6 sizes and fixed line heights, for example 12, 14, 16, 20, 24 and 32px.
- Body text on mobile should be at least 14px, ideally 16px, with line height around 1.4 to 1.5 times the size.
- A practical color palette has one primary color, neutrals (greys), and semantic colors for success, warning and error.
- Check contrast: normal text needs a ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background to meet WCAG AA.
- Use color to signal meaning and action, never as the only way to convey information.

## Transcript
Okay, let's talk about type and color, the two things beginners love to play with and usually overdo.

Typography first. I'll be honest, for most client apps I use one font family. Inter, Manrope or Poppins are free on Google Fonts and work beautifully on screens. Instead of switching fonts, I create contrast using size and weight. My usual mobile scale looks like this: 32 for big display moments, 24 for screen titles, 20 for section headings, 16 for body, 14 for secondary text and 12 for captions and labels. That's it. Six sizes for an entire app.

Line height matters as much as size. Body text at 16px gets a 24px line height. Headings can be tighter, like 24px text on a 32px line. Notice how these are all on our 8-point grid? Not an accident.

Now color. Dekho, the mistake I see in portfolios is a rainbow. Seven bright colors, none of them meaning anything. For Backwater Nest, I'd pick one primary color, maybe a deep backwater teal like #0F766E, which feels calm and Kerala-ish. Then a set of greys for text, borders and backgrounds. Then semantic colors: green for "booking confirmed", amber for "only 2 rooms left", red for errors.

The primary color goes on things people should act on: the main button, selected dates, active tabs. If you also put it on random headings and icons, it stops meaning "tap here".

And please, check contrast. Light grey text on white might look elegant on your 27-inch monitor, but a guest checking the app on a budget phone in bright sunlight won't be able to read it. Use a contrast checker plugin in Figma and aim for 4.5:1 for normal text.

One more thing: never use color alone. An error field should have red color plus an icon and a message, because some users are colour-blind. Next up, a quick quiz to lock this in.

lessons.title: Quiz: Design fundamentals
lessons.content: Let's check that hierarchy, spacing, type and color have really clicked. These questions are based on real situations you'll face on client projects.

questions.prompt: A room details screen has a 'Book now' button and a 'Share with friends' button, both filled with the primary color. What's the best fix?

options.text: Make both buttons bigger so they're easier to tap
Keep 'Book now' as the filled primary button and make 'Share' a secondary outline or text button
Change 'Share' to a different bright color so both stand out
Remove the 'Book now' button and rely on the price to drive bookings

questions.explanation: A screen should have one primary action. Making the secondary action visually quieter keeps the hierarchy clear and pushes users toward the main goal.

questions.prompt: Inside a room card you use 24px padding, but the gap between cards is 16px. Why does this feel wrong?

options.text: Cards should never have a gap between them
Inner spacing is larger than outer spacing, so the grouping of each card gets weaker

questions.explanation: Proximity drives grouping. When the space inside a card is bigger than the space between cards, content visually 'leaks' into neighbouring cards. Inner spacing should be smaller than outer spacing.

questions.prompt: Which type setup is most suitable for body text in a mobile booking app?
questions.explanation: 16px text with roughly 1.5x line height is comfortable to read on phones and fits the 8-point grid. 12px is too small for body copy and tight line heights hurt readability.

questions.prompt: A form shows an invalid phone number by turning the field border red, nothing else. What's the main problem?

options.text: Red is not on-brand for a homestay app
Color is the only signal, so colour-blind users may miss the error and nobody knows how to fix it
Errors should only be shown after the form is submitted

questions.explanation: Never rely on color alone. Add an icon and a clear message like 'Enter a 10-digit mobile number' so every user understands what went wrong and how to fix it.

questions.prompt: You squint at your screen and the first thing you notice is a decorative wave illustration, not the price or the button. What does this tell you?

options.text: The illustration is well designed and should stay as is
You need to add more colors to the button
Decoration is competing with content, so the hierarchy needs to be rebalanced

questions.explanation: The squint test reveals what dominates visually. If decoration wins over the key information and action, reduce its size, contrast or position so the important elements lead.

modules.title: Figma Essentials: Frames, Auto Layout and Components

lessons.title: Figma tour: frames, layers and constraints
lessons.content:
## Key points
- A frame is a container that represents a screen or a section; always design inside frames, not on the bare canvas.
- Use the right preset size for your target device, for example Android Compact (360 x 800) or iPhone 14 (390 x 844).
- Name your layers and frames clearly, like "Room details / Default", because messy files cost time and look unprofessional to clients.
- Constraints decide how a child element behaves when its parent frame resizes, such as sticking a button to the bottom.
- Pages help organise a file: keep separate pages for wireframes, UI, components and handoff.

## Transcript
Chalo, let's open Figma. If you haven't yet, sign up with your college email and apply for the Education plan. It's free and gives you everything we need.

The first thing to understand is the frame. Press F, and on the right you'll see device presets. For Backwater Nest, most guests will be on Android, so I'll pick Android Compact, which is 360 by 800. A frame is like a sheet of paper for one screen. Anything you put inside it becomes its child and shows up nested in the layers panel on the left.

Why does this matter? Because beginners often draw rectangles directly on the canvas and group them with Ctrl+G. Groups are dumb containers, they just wrap things. Frames are smarter. They can clip content, have their own fill and corner radius, hold layout grids, and later, auto layout. My rule: if it's a screen or a meaningful block, make it a frame.

Next, naming. Double-click a layer and rename it. I know it's boring, but when a developer opens your file and sees "Rectangle 247" and "Frame 1093", they lose trust immediately. Name screens with a pattern like "02 Room details" and layers by role, like "Price row" or "CTA".

Now constraints. Select the "Book now" button inside your frame. On the right panel, set the vertical constraint to Bottom and horizontal to Left and Right. Now resize the frame to a taller phone. See how the button stays pinned to the bottom and stretches? That's how real apps behave.

Finally, pages. At the top left, create pages called Wireframes, UI, Components and Handoff. Your future self, and your client, will thank you. In the next lesson we'll tackle the most important Figma feature of all: auto layout.

lessons.title: Auto layout, explained properly
lessons.content:
## What auto layout does

Auto layout turns a frame into a flexible container that arranges its children automatically, like CSS flexbox. Instead of manually nudging every element when the text changes, the frame grows, shrinks and re-spaces itself.

If a client says "change 'Book' to 'Book this room'", a manually drawn button breaks. An auto layout button simply gets wider. This is why every professional Figma file uses auto layout everywhere.

## Creating auto layout

Select one or more layers and press `Shift + A`. Figma wraps them in a frame with auto layout. In the right panel you now control:

- **Direction**: vertical (stacked) or horizontal (side by side), or wrap
- **Gap**: the space between children, for example 8 or 16
- **Padding**: space between the frame's edge and its children
- **Alignment**: where children sit, like top left or center

> **Tip:** Only use values from your spacing scale (4, 8, 16, 24, 32). Auto layout makes it easy to stay consistent.

## Resizing: hug, fill and fixed

This is where most beginners get stuck, so read slowly.

- **Hug contents**: the frame is exactly as big as its children plus padding. Perfect for buttons and tags.
- **Fill container**: the element stretches to take available space in its parent. Perfect for a full-width button or a text block in a card.
- **Fixed**: a set width or height that doesn't change. Use for icons, avatars and screen frames.

A typical room card: the card itself is **Fill** width inside the screen, its padding is 16, its text column is **Fill** so long room names wrap, and the "₹2,400 / night" tag is **Hug**.

## Nesting: auto layout inside auto layout

Real UI is built by nesting. Here's the room card structure for Backwater Nest:

```text
Room card (vertical, gap 12, padding 16)
  Photo (fill width, fixed height 180)
  Info (vertical, gap 4)
    Room name
    Location row (horizontal, gap 4)
      Pin icon
      "Fort Kochi, 1.2 km from beach"
  Footer (horizontal, space between)
    Price
    Book button (horizontal, padding 12 x 20, hug)
```

Once you can read and build a structure like this, you can build almost any screen.

## Handy shortcuts and tricks

- `Shift + A` adds auto layout; `Ctrl + Alt + G` (`Cmd + Option + G` on Mac) wraps a selection in a plain frame.
- Set gap to **Auto** for "space between" layouts, like price on the left and button on the right.
- Use **absolute position** for a badge that overlaps a photo corner without breaking the flow.
- Toggle **Canvas stacking** when you need overlapping avatars.
- Hide a layer and auto layout closes the gap. Great for optional elements like a "Free breakfast" tag.

## Why developers love it

Auto layout maps closely to how developers build interfaces with flexbox. Gap, padding and alignment translate almost one to one into code, so your designs get built exactly as intended.

lessons.title: Components, variants and properties
lessons.content:
## Key points
- A component is a reusable master element; every copy you place is an instance that updates when the master changes.
- Create a component with Ctrl+Alt+K (Cmd+Option+K on Mac) and keep all masters on a dedicated Components page.
- Variants group related versions of a component, like a button's Primary, Secondary and Disabled states, into one set.
- Component properties (text, boolean and instance swap) let you change labels, show or hide icons, and swap icons without detaching.
- Never detach instances to make small edits; add a property or variant instead so the system stays consistent.

## Transcript
This lesson is the one that changed how fast I work. Components.

Imagine Backwater Nest has a "Book now" button on six screens. The client calls and says, "Priya, can we make the buttons a bit rounder?" Without components, you'd edit six buttons by hand and probably miss one. With components, you edit the master once and every instance updates. That's the whole idea.

Let's build one. Take the auto layout button from the last lesson, select it and press Ctrl+Alt+K. The icon turns into a four-diamond shape. That's your main component. Move it to the Components page. Now when you copy it into a screen, you get an instance, shown with a hollow diamond.

Next, variants. A button isn't one thing. It has types, Primary, Secondary and Ghost, and states, Default, Pressed and Disabled. Select your main component and click "Add variant". Figma creates a component set with a purple dashed border. Rename the properties to "Type" and "State", and design each combination. Now on any instance, you can switch from Primary to Secondary from a dropdown on the right. Beautiful, right?

Then properties. Add a text property called "Label" so you can change "Book now" to "Check availability" from the panel. Add a boolean property called "Show icon" so the leading icon can be turned on and off. And an instance swap property so you can change the icon itself.

One rule I'm strict about: don't detach instances. When you detach, the link to the master breaks and your system slowly falls apart. If you need something new, add a variant or property.

In the assignment, you'll build a button set and a room card component for Backwater Nest. Take your time, this is the foundation for everything we do in Module 3.

lessons.title: Assignment: Build a button and room card component set
lessons.content: On real client projects, you rarely design a screen from scratch. You assemble it from components. Freelancers who show a clean, well-structured component set in their files get repeat work, because their designs are faster to change and easier for developers to build.

assignment.brief:
## Your task

Create a small, reusable component library for the Backwater Nest homestay app in Figma.

## Steps

1. Create a new Figma file called **Backwater Nest - Components** with pages: Components, Playground.
2. **Button component set** with two properties:
   - Type: Primary, Secondary, Ghost
   - State: Default, Pressed, Disabled
   - Add a text property **Label** and a boolean property **Show icon**.
   - Use auto layout with padding 12 x 20, hug width, corner radius 8 or 12.
3. **Room card component** built with nested auto layout:
   - Photo, room name, location row, amenities line, price, and a Button instance.
   - Variants: Default and Sold out (sold out greys the photo and disables the button).
4. On the Playground page, place 3 room card instances with different room names (for example "Kayal View Deluxe", "Coconut Grove Cottage", "Heritage Attic Room") and prices in ₹.
5. Test it: change a long room name and confirm the card text wraps instead of overflowing.

## Deliverable

Share a **view link** to your Figma file (Share > Copy link, set to "Anyone with the link can view").

## Tips

- Name layers properly. Reviewers will open the layers panel.
- Only use spacing from your 8-point scale.
- Don't detach any instances on the Playground page.

rubric.criterion: Button component set has correct Type and State variants with working Label and Show icon properties
Room card uses nested auto layout with correct hug and fill behaviour (long names wrap cleanly)
Consistent spacing on the 8-point grid and clear visual hierarchy within the card
