File hygiene: named layers, organised pages, no detached instances

modules.title: Wireframe to Hi-fi: The Kochi Homestay Booking App

lessons.title: The brief: Backwater Nest and its users
lessons.content:
## Meet the client

**Backwater Nest** is a 6-room family-run homestay near Fort Kochi, Kerala, owned by Anna Mathew. Right now, bookings come through phone calls, WhatsApp messages and a listing on a big travel site that takes a hefty commission. Anna wants a simple mobile app (and later a website) where guests can browse rooms, check availability, and pay a booking advance via UPI or card through Razorpay.

Her budget for design is ₹35,000, and she wants to show the prototype to a developer in two weeks.

## Who are the users?

Before opening Figma, a good designer asks: who will use this, and what are they trying to do?

### Primary user: the domestic family traveller
- Booking a 3 to 4 night trip from Bengaluru, Chennai or Delhi
- Compares photos and price per night carefully
- Wants to know: is breakfast included, is it safe for kids, how far is the beach
- Prefers paying through UPI

### Secondary user: the solo or couple backpacker
- Often foreign or young Indian travellers
- Cares about location, Wi-Fi and reviews
- Books last minute, sometimes the same day

### Admin user: Anna herself
- Needs to see upcoming bookings and block dates. We'll keep this out of scope for the first version.

## Defining the core flow

For version one, we focus on a single happy path:

1. **Home**: search by dates and guests, see featured rooms
2. **Room listing**: browse all available rooms for those dates
3. **Room details**: photos, amenities, house rules, price breakdown
4. **Booking summary and payment**: guest details, advance amount, pay with UPI
5. **Confirmation**: booking ID, check-in instructions, WhatsApp contact

> **Tip:** Write the flow as a list before drawing anything. If you can't describe the flow in five steps, the design will be confused too.

## Constraints that shape the design

- **Budget phones and patchy networks.** Many guests travel through areas with weak signal, so screens must be light and clear even before images load.
- **Trust.** A small homestay has no big brand behind it. Real photos, reviews, a clear cancellation policy and visible contact options build trust.
- **Language.** Keep copy simple English; avoid jargon like "inventory" or "SKU".
- **Payment.** Show the advance amount and balance clearly, for example "Pay ₹3,000 now, ₹6,600 at check-in".

## Success criteria

Agree on success with the client upfront. For Anna: fewer phone calls asking about availability, and guests completing a booking in under two minutes. Every design decision in this module should help one of those goals.

In the next lesson, we'll turn this flow into rough wireframes, fast.

lessons.title: Low-fi wireframes in 30 minutes
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Wireframes are for thinking about structure and flow, not looks, so use greys, boxes and real-ish text only.
- Start on paper or with simple Figma rectangles; speed matters more than polish at this stage.
- Use real content wherever possible, like actual room names and ₹ prices, because placeholder text hides layout problems.
- Wireframe all five screens of the flow before refining any single screen.
- Share wireframes with the client early so you catch wrong assumptions before investing hours in hi-fi.

## Transcript
Okay, time to wireframe Backwater Nest. Set a timer for 30 minutes. Seriously. The timer stops you from obsessing over one screen.

I usually start on paper. Five rectangles for five screens, a pen, and I sketch the flow from Home to Confirmation. Then I move to Figma on the Wireframes page. Rules for this stage: only greys, one font, no icons except simple boxes, no images, just a grey box with an X through it.

Let's do the Home screen. At the top, a short greeting and the homestay name. Then the most important thing, a search block: check-in date, check-out date, number of guests, and a "Check availability" button. Below that, two or three featured room cards and a small trust section, like "4.8 rating from 320 guests" and "5 min walk to Fort Kochi beach".

Notice I wrote real text. Not lorem ipsum. Dekho, when you write "Kayal View Deluxe Room with Balcony", you immediately see that the title wraps to two lines on a 360px screen. With lorem ipsum you'd never notice that until the developer complains.

Room details: big photo area at the top, room name, a quick facts row like "2 adults, 1 child, AC, Breakfast included", amenities, house rules, cancellation policy, and a sticky bottom bar with total price and a "Book now" button.

For booking summary, keep it boring and clear. Dates, guests, price breakdown, advance to pay now, guest name and phone, and a pay button. Boring is good when money is involved.

Once all five are done, I'd send Anna a quick link and ask two questions: is anything missing, and is anything here wrong for your guests? In my experience, this one message saves at least a day of rework.

lessons.title: Building a mini design system: styles and variables
lessons.content:
## Why a mini design system?

Before you jump to hi-fi, set up the building blocks. A design system sounds like something only big companies like Swiggy or Razorpay need, but even a 5-screen freelance project benefits from a small one. It keeps every screen consistent and makes client changes take minutes instead of hours.

For Backwater Nest, our mini system has four parts: color, typography, spacing and components.

## 1. Color variables

In Figma, open the **Local variables** panel and create a collection called **Color**. Separate raw colors (primitives) from how they're used (tokens):

```text
Primitives
  teal/700   #0F766E
  teal/50    #F0FDFA
  sand/100   #FEF3C7
  grey/900   #111827
  grey/500   #6B7280
  grey/200   #E5E7EB
  red/600    #DC2626
  green/600  #16A34A

Tokens
  bg/default        -> white
  bg/subtle         -> teal/50
  text/primary      -> grey/900
  text/secondary    -> grey/500
  border/default    -> grey/200
  action/primary    -> teal/700
  feedback/error    -> red/600
  feedback/success  -> green/600
```

Always apply **tokens** in your designs, not primitives. If Anna later wants a deeper teal, you change one primitive and every button updates. Tokens also make a dark mode possible later.

## 2. Text styles

Create text styles that match your type scale. Name them by role, not size:

- **Display**: 32 / 40, Bold
- **Title**: 24 / 32, Semibold
- **Heading**: 20 / 28, Semibold
- **Body**: 16 / 24, Regular
- **Body small**: 14 / 20, Regular
- **Caption**: 12 / 16, Medium

The format "16 / 24" means 16px size with a 24px line height.

## 3. Spacing and radius variables

Create a **Number** variable collection with spacing (4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48) and radius (8 for inputs and buttons, 16 for cards). Bind these to your auto layout gaps and padding. Developers can then read exact values in Dev Mode.

## 4. Update your components

Go back to your button and room card from Module 2 and replace hard-coded values with your variables and text styles. Now your components and your system are connected.

> **Tip:** Keep a "Foundations" page in your file showing the palette, type styles and spacing scale. Clients love seeing this; it makes your work look thoughtful and professional, and it helps justify your fee.

## A note on brand feel

Backwater Nest should feel calm, local and trustworthy. That's why we picked a backwater teal as the primary color and a warm sand tone for highlights like "Breakfast included". Your system is not just technical, it carries the brand personality across every screen.

lessons.title: From wireframe to hi-fi, screen by screen
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Duplicate your wireframes onto the UI page and upgrade them step by step instead of starting from a blank frame.
- Apply the fundamentals in order: hierarchy first, then spacing, then type styles, then color, then imagery.
- Use real, high-quality photos (from the client or free sources like Unsplash) because photos sell a homestay more than any UI detail.
- Design the important states, not just the happy path: empty results, loading, sold-out rooms and payment failure.
- Review every screen against the brief's success criteria before calling it done.

## Transcript
This is the fun part. Let's take our grey wireframes and make them hi-fi.

First, I duplicate the five wireframes onto the UI page. I never start hi-fi from a blank canvas, because the structure decisions are already made. Now I upgrade in layers.

Layer one is hierarchy. On Home, I ask: what's the hero? It's the search block. So I give it a white card with a soft shadow sitting over a beautiful photo of the backwaters. The "Check availability" button becomes my Primary button instance.

Layer two is spacing. I wrap everything in auto layout, 16px side margins, 24px between sections, 16px card padding. Instantly it looks calmer.

Layer three, type. I apply the text styles: Title for "Find your stay in Fort Kochi", Body small in text secondary for helper lines.

Layer four, color. I apply tokens. Teal only on the primary actions and selected dates. Sand for the "Breakfast included" tag. Everything else is neutral.

Layer five is imagery. Ask your client for real photos. Real rooms, real verandah, real breakfast appam and stew. For practice, Unsplash is fine. Use the same corner radius on all images.

Now the part most students skip: states. What happens when no rooms are available for the selected dates? Design that empty state with a friendly message and a suggestion like "Try 14 to 17 Dec instead". What about a sold-out room card? We already have that variant. Payment failed? A clear message, the amount, and a "Try again with UPI" button. Clients notice when you've thought about these, and developers really notice.

Finally, I put the brief next to my screens and check: can a guest book in under two minutes? Is the advance amount crystal clear? Is there a visible WhatsApp contact for trust? If yes, we're ready for the assignment.

lessons.title: Assignment: Design the hi-fi booking flow
lessons.content: This is your portfolio centrepiece. A complete, consistent booking flow built on a design system is exactly what clients and hiring managers look for, because it proves you can take a real brief from rough idea to polished, buildable screens.

assignment.brief:
## Your task

Design the hi-fi mobile booking flow for **Backwater Nest**, the Kochi homestay from the brief.

## Screens required (360 x 800 or 390 x 844)

1. Home with date and guest search
2. Room listing for selected dates
3. Room details with photos, amenities, house rules and a sticky "Book now" bar
4. Booking summary and payment (advance via UPI shown clearly, for example "Pay ₹3,000 now")
5. Booking confirmation with booking ID and WhatsApp contact

Plus at least **two edge states**: for example "No rooms for these dates", "Room sold out", or "Payment failed".

## Steps

1. Duplicate your wireframes onto a UI page.
2. Set up the Foundations page: color variables (primitives and tokens), text styles and spacing variables.
3. Build each screen using your components from Module 2, updated with variables.
4. Use real content: room names, ₹ prices, Fort Kochi landmarks, realistic reviews.
5. Run the squint test and a contrast check on every screen.

## Deliverable

A Figma **view link** with pages: Foundations, Wireframes, UI, Components.

## Tips

- Consistency beats creativity here. Same margins, same radius, same button everywhere.
- Add a short sticky note on each screen explaining one design decision. Reviewers love seeing your thinking.

rubric.criterion: All 5 screens plus 2 edge states complete, with a logical, easy booking flow
Strong visual hierarchy: one clear primary action per screen and readable price/advance information
Design system usage: color tokens, text styles, spacing variables and components applied consistently
Realistic content and accessibility (contrast, touch targets, no color-only signals)

modules.title: Prototype, Handoff and Presenting to the Client

lessons.title: Prototyping: making your screens clickable
lessons.content:
## Key points
- A prototype lets clients and users experience the flow, which gets you far better feedback than static screens.
- Connect screens in Prototype mode using triggers (On tap, While pressing, After delay) and actions (Navigate to, Open overlay, Back).
- Use Smart Animate between frames with matching layer names for smooth transitions like expanding cards.
- Build interactive components, such as a button with a pressed state, once at the component level so every instance works.
- Set the flow starting point and test the prototype on your phone using the Figma mobile app.

## Transcript
Static screens are great for you, but clients don't think in screens. They think in experiences. "What happens when I tap this?" That's why we prototype.

Switch to the Prototype tab on the right. Select the "Check availability" button on Home, and you'll see a little plus circle. Drag it to the Room listing frame. Figma creates a connection: trigger On tap, action Navigate to, animation Instant. Change the animation to Smart Animate or Move in from right for a natural feel.

Do this for the whole happy path. Room card to Room details. "Book now" to Booking summary. "Pay ₹3,000 now" to Confirmation. On the back arrows, use the Back action so it works from anywhere.

For the date picker, I prefer an overlay. Select the date field, set the action to Open overlay, choose a bottom sheet frame, position it at the bottom and add a background dim. Now it feels like a real app.

Here's a trick: interactive components. Go to your Button component set, select the Default variant and connect it to the Pressed variant with a While pressing trigger. Now every button in your entire file has a pressed effect, automatically. That's the power of components again.

Smart Animate works by matching layer names between frames. If the room photo is called "Room photo" on both the listing and details screens, Figma animates it growing. Name your layers, I keep saying it!

Finally, set a flow starting point on Home, click Present, and then open the Figma app on your phone to test it. Hand it to a friend or your cousin and say "Book a room for this weekend". Don't help them. Just watch where they hesitate. That's free usability testing.

lessons.title: Developer handoff that developers thank you for
lessons.content:
## Why handoff matters for freelancers

Your design isn't done when it looks good. It's done when it's built correctly. Most freelance disputes I've seen don't come from bad design, they come from confused handoff: "the developer built it differently", "where's the error state?", "which icon file is this?". A clean handoff protects your reputation and gets you referrals.

## The handoff checklist

### 1. Organise the file
- A **Handoff** page with final screens only, in flow order, left to right.
- Mark frames as **Ready for dev** so they show up clearly in Dev Mode.
- Remove experiments, or move them to an Archive page.

### 2. Annotate behaviour
Developers can see sizes, but they can't read your mind. Add short notes for:
- What happens on tap, on error and while loading
- Validation rules, for example "Phone: 10 digits, starts with 6 to 9"
- Sticky elements, like the bottom booking bar
- Content limits, for example "Room name: max 2 lines, then truncate"

### 3. Share tokens, not random values
Because you used variables, Dev Mode shows names like `action/primary` and `space/16` instead of raw hex codes. You can also hand over a simple token list your developer can drop into CSS:

```css
:root {
  --color-action-primary: #0F766E;
  --color-text-primary: #111827;
  --color-text-secondary: #6B7280;
  --color-border-default: #E5E7EB;
  --space-2: 8px;
  --space-4: 16px;
  --space-6: 24px;
  --radius-card: 16px;
}
```

Even if the developer uses Flutter or React Native, the same names and values transfer easily.

### 4. Export assets properly
- Icons as **SVG**, photos as **WebP** or JPG at 2x.
- Select a layer, add an export setting in the right panel, and name files clearly like `ic-location.svg`.
- Don't export things that can be built in code, like buttons or card backgrounds.

### 5. Include all states
Link the edge states next to each screen: empty, loading, error and sold out. If it's not in the file, assume it won't be built.

> **Tip:** Schedule a 30-minute walkthrough call (Google Meet is fine) with the developer. Share your screen, go through the flow, and record it. That single call prevents dozens of WhatsApp messages later.

## After handoff

Ask for a staging build or APK and do a **design QA** pass. Compare the build with your screens and list issues in a shared doc with screenshots: "Price on room card should be Body/Bold, currently Regular." Be specific and polite. Most freelancers skip this step, which is exactly why doing it makes you stand out.

lessons.title: Presenting your design to the client
lessons.content:
## Presenting is part of the job

You can design the best screens of your life and still lose the client if you present them badly. A good presentation explains **why** each decision was made, connects it to the client's goals, and makes it easy for them to give useful feedback.

## Structure of a 20-minute client presentation

### 1. Recap the goal (2 minutes)
Start with what you agreed: "Anna, the goal was fewer availability calls and guests booking in under two minutes, with the advance paid through UPI." This frames everything that follows.

### 2. Walk through the user's journey (10 minutes)
Present the prototype as a story, not a list of screens: "Meet Divya, flying in from Bengaluru with her husband and daughter for a long weekend..." Then tap through the flow. Clients connect with people, not with "Screen 3".

### 3. Explain key decisions (5 minutes)
Pick three or four decisions and link each to a goal:
- "The search is the first thing on Home, because availability questions were your biggest time drain."
- "The advance and balance are shown separately, so guests aren't surprised at check-in."
- "A WhatsApp button stays on the details screen, because trust matters for a small homestay."

### 4. Ask for focused feedback (3 minutes)
Avoid "So, do you like it?". Ask specific questions:
- "Is anything in the booking summary missing for your guests?"
- "Does the room information match how you describe rooms on calls?"

## Handling feedback like a professional

- **Listen fully before responding.** Write everything down.
- **Separate problems from solutions.** If Anna says "make the button red", ask "What makes you feel it needs to change?" Maybe the real issue is that it's not noticeable enough.
- **Don't defend every pixel.** Push back only when a change hurts the user, and explain it in terms of her goals.
- **Summarise in writing.** Send a short message after the call listing agreed changes.

> **Tip:** Agree on revision rounds in your proposal, for example "2 rounds of revisions included, additional rounds at ₹2,000 each". This one line protects you from endless changes.

## Pricing and proposals, briefly

For a 5 to 8 screen mobile app design with a prototype and handoff, beginner freelancers in India typically charge ₹15,000 to ₹40,000 depending on complexity. Ask for a 40 to 50 percent advance through UPI or a Razorpay payment link before starting. Mention deliverables clearly: Figma file, prototype link, handoff page and one design QA pass.

## Your presentation deck

Keep it short: the goal, the user journey, three key decisions, the foundations page, and next steps. Five or six slides plus the live prototype is plenty. Confidence comes from preparation, so rehearse once out loud before the call.

lessons.title: Quiz: Prototyping, handoff and client work
lessons.content: A quick check on the last mile of a design project: prototyping, developer handoff and working with clients.

questions.prompt: You set up Smart Animate between the room listing and room details screens, but the photo just fades instead of growing. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: Smart Animate only works on desktop prototypes
The photo layers have different names on the two frames
The photo needs to be exported as SVG
The trigger must be While pressing instead of On tap

questions.explanation: Smart Animate matches layers by name (and hierarchy) across frames. If the names differ, Figma can't pair them, so it falls back to a dissolve.

questions.prompt: You want every button in the file to show a pressed effect in the prototype. What's the most efficient approach?

options.text: Add a prototype connection to each button instance on every screen
Create a separate pressed-state screen for each tap
Detach all buttons and animate them manually
Connect the Default and Pressed variants inside the component set using a While pressing trigger

questions.explanation: Interactive components let you define the interaction once in the component set, and every instance inherits it automatically.

questions.prompt: Which of these should usually NOT be exported as an image asset for developers?

options.text: The primary button and card backgrounds

questions.explanation: Buttons and card backgrounds are built in code with colors, radius and padding. Exporting them as images makes the app heavier and harder to change.

questions.prompt: During the presentation, the client says 'Make the Book now button bigger and red.' What's the best first response?

options.text: Agree immediately to keep the client happy
Explain that red is bad design and refuse
Ask what makes them feel it needs to change, to understand the underlying concern
Say you'll consider it and quietly ignore the feedback

questions.explanation: Clients often describe solutions rather than problems. Understanding the real concern (for example 'guests don't notice the button') lets you solve it properly, maybe without red.

questions.prompt: Why include a line like '2 rounds of revisions included, additional rounds at ₹2,000 each' in your proposal?

options.text: It's a legal requirement for freelancers in India
It sets clear expectations and protects you from unlimited, unpaid changes
It encourages clients to request more revisions
It replaces the need for an advance payment

questions.explanation: Defining revision scope upfront keeps the project profitable and avoids awkward conversations later. It's one of the simplest ways to protect your time.

lessons.title: Capstone: Prototype and client presentation
lessons.content: This capstone simulates the end of a real freelance project: a working prototype, a developer-ready handoff page and a short presentation. Completing it gives you a full case study to show future clients, not just pretty screens.

assignment.brief:
## Your task

Turn your Backwater Nest hi-fi screens into a complete, client-ready delivery.

## Steps

1. **Prototype** the full happy path from Home to Confirmation:
   - Navigate, Back and Open overlay (for the date picker) actions
   - Interactive pressed state on your Button component
   - At least one Smart Animate transition
2. **Handoff page**:
   - Final screens in flow order, marked Ready for dev
   - Annotations for tap behaviour, validation rules and edge states
   - Export settings on icons (SVG) and photos (2x)
3. **Test it**: ask one friend or family member to "book a room for this weekend" on their phone. Note where they hesitated and fix one issue.
4. **Present**: record a 3 to 5 minute Loom or screen recording presenting to "Anna" (the client): goal, user journey, three key decisions, next steps.

## Deliverable

A single link to a Google Doc or Notion page containing: your Figma prototype link, Figma file link, recording link, and 3 to 4 lines on what you changed after testing.

## Tips

- Tell the user's story in your recording. Avoid "this is screen one, this is screen two".
- Keep the recording under 5 minutes. Clients are busy.

rubric.criterion: Prototype covers the full happy path with overlays, interactive components and smooth transitions
Handoff page is organised, annotated and includes edge states and correct exports
Evidence of user testing and a sensible fix based on what was observed
Presentation is clear, story-led and links design decisions to client goals

courses.title: UX Research & Case Studies that Get Hired
courses.subtitle: Run real research, turn it into decisions, and write a case study recruiters actually read.
courses.description: Most student portfolios show pretty screens and skip the thinking, which is exactly what hiring managers want to see. In this course you'll run lean user interviews and usability tests on a student budget, synthesise what you learn into clear decisions, and package it all into a tight, honest case study. You'll finish with a published case study and a plan for sharing it on LinkedIn and with startups.
whatYouBuild: An interview guide and notes from 5 real user interviews
An affinity map with prioritised insights and problem statements
A published UX case study on Behance, Notion or your portfolio site
requirements: Comfort with Figma basics (frames, auto layout, components)
One past design project, even a college or practice project, that you want to strengthen
Access to 5 people you can interview over a call or in person
courses.outcome: Run quick research and present it as a clear case study.
courses.whoFor: Learners who can use Figma and want to work from client-style briefs.

modules.title: Research That Is Real, Not Decorative

lessons.title: Why most UX case studies get ignored
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Recruiters spend about a minute on a case study, so the problem and outcome must be clear in the first scroll.
- Fake research, like a persona with a stock photo and invented quotes, is easy to spot and hurts your credibility.
- Hiring managers look for your reasoning: what you learned, what you decided, and what you'd change.
- Small but real research with 5 people beats an impressive-looking process you didn't actually do.

## Transcript
I've reviewed hundreds of portfolios while hiring at startups, and I'll tell you a secret. Most case studies look the same. Double diamond diagram, a persona called "Rahul, 24, loves travel", a stock photo, and then twenty screens. I scroll for thirty seconds and close it.

Why? Because I can't see the person's thinking. I don't know what problem they found, how they found it, or why they designed what they designed.

What makes me stop scrolling? Something real. "I spoke to six home bakers in Jaipur and found that four of them lose orders because WhatsApp messages get buried." Now I'm interested. That's one real insight, from real people, and it changes the design.

So in this course we'll do research that's small, honest and useful. Five interviews. One usability test round. Clear decisions. Then we'll write it up so a recruiter gets it in one minute. Chalo, let's learn how to run interviews that don't just confirm what you already believe.

lessons.title: Running 5 user interviews on a student budget
lessons.content:
## Why five is enough

For early discovery, five to six interviews with the right people surface most of the major patterns. You don't need a research budget, just a plan.

## Recruit the right people

Interview people who actually do the thing. Designing for home bakers? Find them through Instagram, local WhatsApp groups or your relatives' network. Offer a small thank-you like a ₹200 UPI transfer or a coffee.

## Write a short interview guide

- **Warm-up**: "Tell me about how you started your bakery."
- **Past behaviour**: "Walk me through the last time you took a custom cake order."
- **Pain points**: "What was the most frustrating part of that?"
- **Workarounds**: "How do you handle that today?"

> **Tip:** Ask about what people **did**, not what they **would** do. "Would you use an app for orders?" gets a polite yes. "How did you track last week's orders?" gets the truth.

## During the call

- Record with permission, and take notes too.
- Ask "why?" and "can you show me?" often.
- Stay silent after an answer; people fill silence with honest details.
- Never pitch your solution during the interview.

Write up key quotes and observations within an hour, while it's fresh.

lessons.title: Quiz: Interviewing well
lessons.content: Three scenario questions to check you can run an unbiased, useful interview.

questions.prompt: Which interview question is most likely to give you reliable insight?

options.text: Would you use an app that manages your cake orders?
Walk me through the last custom order you received, from the first message to delivery.
Don't you think WhatsApp is bad for managing orders?
How much would you pay for an order management app?

questions.explanation: Questions about real past behaviour give concrete, honest answers. Hypothetical, leading or pricing questions mostly produce polite guesses.

questions.prompt: Midway through an interview, the participant describes a problem your app idea solves. What should you do?

options.text: Tell them your app will fix this
End the interview since you've validated the idea
Ask them to tell you more about how they deal with it today

questions.explanation: Pitching biases the rest of the conversation. Digging into current workarounds reveals how painful the problem really is and what any solution must beat.

questions.prompt: Why is a persona with invented quotes and a stock photo a problem in a case study?

options.text: It signals research wasn't actually done, which reduces trust in all your decisions
Personas are never used in industry
Recruiters only want to see final UI

questions.explanation: Hiring managers value evidence-based reasoning. Fabricated research is easy to spot and undermines everything that follows in the case study.

lessons.title: Affinity mapping and sharp problem statements
lessons.content:
## Affinity mapping in FigJam

After your interviews, you have pages of notes. Affinity mapping turns them into patterns.

1. Write **one observation per sticky**: a quote, a behaviour or a pain point. Note the participant, like "P3".
2. Put all stickies on a FigJam board without sorting.
3. Group similar stickies silently. Let clusters emerge; don't force categories.
4. Name each cluster as an insight sentence, not a topic. "Orders get lost in long WhatsApp chats" is better than "Communication".
5. Count how many participants appear in each cluster to prioritise.

## Writing problem statements

Turn your top insight into a problem statement:

> **[User]** needs a way to **[need]** because **[insight]**.

Example: "Home bakers in Jaipur need a way to see all confirmed orders for the week in one place, because order details are scattered across WhatsApp chats and they've missed deliveries."

A good problem statement is specific, based on evidence, and doesn't contain the solution. "Needs an app" is not a need.

From here, write two or three "How might we" questions, like "How might we help bakers confirm order details without leaving WhatsApp?" These become the starting point for your design ideas.

lessons.title: Usability testing with five users
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Usability testing checks whether people can complete real tasks with your design, not whether they like it.
- Write tasks as realistic scenarios, like "Your cousin's birthday is Saturday, order a 1kg chocolate cake".
- Ask participants to think aloud, and resist helping them when they get stuck.
- Track simple metrics: task success, time taken and where people hesitated.
- Fix the biggest issues and show the before and after in your case study.

## Transcript
Once you have a prototype, even a rough one, test it. Five users will reveal most of the big usability problems.

Here's how I run it. I share the Figma prototype link on a Google Meet call and ask the person to share their screen. Then I give a scenario, not instructions. I don't say "click on the order button". I say "your cousin's birthday is this Saturday, order a one kg chocolate cake for pickup". Big difference.

I ask them to think aloud. "Just tell me what you're looking at and what you're thinking." And then, the hardest part, I stay quiet. When they get stuck, I count to ten in my head. If they're still stuck, I ask "what are you looking for?" instead of pointing.

I note three things for each task: did they complete it, how long it took, and where they hesitated or said something like "hmm, where is..." Those hesitation moments are gold.

After five sessions, I list issues by how many people hit them. Fix the top two or three, then show the before and after in your case study. Dekho, a before and after with a clear reason is one of the most convincing things you can show a hiring manager.

lessons.title: Assignment: Research synthesis board
lessons.content: Clients and product teams don't pay for interviews, they pay for the clarity that comes out of them. A clean synthesis board shows you can turn messy conversations into decisions, which is the core skill behind every senior UX role.

assignment.brief:
## Your task

Run research on a real problem and synthesise it into clear insights.

## Steps

1. Pick a real, local problem space, for example: a Jaipur home bakery taking orders on WhatsApp, students finding PG accommodation in Pune, or a Kochi homestay handling bookings.
2. Interview **5 people** using a guide built on past behaviour (share the guide).
3. In FigJam, create an affinity map with at least 40 stickies, each tagged with a participant code (P1 to P5).
4. Name clusters as insight sentences and rank the top 3 by number of participants.
5. Write **one problem statement** and **three "How might we"** questions.

## Deliverable

A FigJam **view link** with your interview guide, affinity map, top insights and problem statement.

## Tips

- Anonymise participants. Use roles, not full names.
- Include 2 or 3 direct quotes. They make your insights believable.

rubric.criterion: Interview guide focuses on past behaviour and avoids leading questions
Affinity map is grounded in real observations with participant tags
Insights are specific, prioritised and supported by quotes
Problem statement and HMW questions are clear and solution-free

modules.title: Writing a Case Study That Gets You Hired

lessons.title: The one-minute case study structure
lessons.content:
## Write for the skimmer

A recruiter or founder will skim first and read only if hooked. Structure your case study so the first screen answers: what was the problem, what did you do, and what changed?

## A structure that works

1. **Header**: project name, your role, timeline, tools. "UX designer (solo), 3 weeks, Figma and FigJam."
2. **TL;DR**: 3 lines. Problem, approach, outcome. "Home bakers missed orders buried in WhatsApp. I interviewed 5 bakers and tested 2 prototype rounds. Task success for confirming an order rose from 2/5 to 5/5."
3. **The problem**: context and why it matters, with one strong quote.
4. **Research**: what you did and the top 3 insights. Show the affinity map as a cropped image, not the whole board.
5. **Decisions**: 2 or 3 key design decisions, each linked to an insight.
6. **Testing and iteration**: before and after screens with the reason for each change.
7. **Final design**: a few polished screens or a short prototype video.
8. **Reflection**: what you'd do differently and what you'd measure next.

> **Tip:** Be honest about scale. "Tested with 5 users" is respected. Inflated claims like "increased revenue by 300%" on a student project raise red flags.

Keep it under 1,500 words. Every section should earn its place.

lessons.title: Publishing and pitching your case study
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Publish where people can open it in one tap: a Behance project, a Notion page, or your own portfolio site built with Framer.
- Share a LinkedIn post that tells the story in 5 to 6 lines with one striking image and the link in the post.
- Apply to design roles on LinkedIn, Internshala and startup job boards with a short, specific note pointing to the most relevant case study.
- Two strong case studies beat six shallow ones; quality is what gets you shortlisted.

## Transcript
You've written your case study. Now let's get it in front of people.

First, where to publish. Behance is fine and has discovery. Notion is fast and clean. If you want a proper portfolio site, Framer has a free plan and looks great. Whatever you pick, make sure it loads well on mobile, because most recruiters will open your link on their phone.

Second, LinkedIn. Don't just post "Check out my new case study!" Tell the story. Something like: "Jaipur home bakers told me they lose orders in WhatsApp chats. I spent three weeks interviewing and testing to fix that. Here's what I learned." Then one clear before and after image, and the link. Indian design recruiters are very active on LinkedIn, so this works.

Third, applying. On LinkedIn, Internshala, or directly to startups, send a short note: "Hi, I saw you're building a booking product. I recently designed a booking flow for a Kochi homestay and tested it with five users. Here's the case study." Specific beats generic every time.

And remember, two strong case studies are enough to start. Chalo, finish yours and hit publish.

lessons.title: Assignment: Publish your case study
lessons.content: A published, well-structured case study is the single most important asset for getting a design internship, a job or a freelance client. This assignment turns your research and design work into something you can send out tomorrow.

assignment.brief:
## Your task

Write and publish a complete UX case study based on your research synthesis from Module 2 (and a design project of your choice).

## Steps

1. Follow the one-minute structure: Header, TL;DR, Problem, Research, Decisions, Testing, Final design, Reflection.
2. Include at least **one before and after** with the reason for the change.
3. Add real quotes and honest numbers (for example "4 of 5 participants").
4. Publish on Behance, Notion or your portfolio site.
5. Draft a LinkedIn post (5 to 6 lines) sharing the story.

## Deliverable

Submit the **public link** to your case study. Paste your LinkedIn post draft at the end of the case study page or in a linked doc.

## Tips

- Read it on your phone before submitting. Fix anything that's hard to read.
- Cut ruthlessly. If a section doesn't support a decision, remove it.

rubric.criterion: Clear TL;DR and problem framing that a recruiter understands in under a minute
Research insights clearly linked to design decisions
Evidence of testing and iteration with a convincing before and after
Honest reflection, readable layout and a well-written LinkedIn post

courses.title: Data Analytics with Excel & SQL
courses.subtitle: Turn messy sales exports into clear answers clients will pay for
courses.description: Learn the two tools every analyst job and freelance gig still runs on: Excel and SQL. You will clean a real-looking kirana and D2C sales dataset, summarise it with XLOOKUP, SUMIFS and pivot tables, then answer sharper questions with SQL joins and GROUP BY. We finish by turning numbers into a one-page insight report a small business owner actually reads.

mentor.name: Arvind Krishnan
mentor.headline: Data analyst turned freelance BI consultant

whatYouBuild: A cleaned, analysis-ready version of a 3-month kirana store sales sheet
A pivot-table summary of a D2C brand's orders by city, channel and product
A set of SQL queries answering repeat-customer and top-product questions
A one-page insight report for a Coimbatore D2C snack brand, ready to send on WhatsApp or email
requirements: A laptop with Microsoft Excel 2021/365 or free Excel for the web (XLOOKUP needs one of these)
No coding experience needed; we use a free online SQL editor
Comfort with basic school maths: percentages and averages
courses.outcome: Clean a messy dataset and report KPIs with Excel and SQL.
courses.whoFor: Beginners comfortable with numbers who want to work with data.

modules.title: Excel Foundations: Cleaning and Core Formulas

lessons.title: What analysts actually do for small businesses
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Most small-business clients do not need machine learning; they need clean numbers and three clear answers.
- A typical freelance analytics gig starts with a messy export from Tally, Shopify, Dukaan or a Google Sheet.
- Your value is in asking the right business question before touching a single formula.
- Excel handles cleaning and quick summaries, while SQL scales the same thinking to lakhs of rows.
- Every analysis in this course ends with a recommendation the owner can act on this week.

## Transcript
Vanakkam, hello everyone, I am Arvind. Before I went freelance, I spent years at Mu Sigma building analyses for large companies. But honestly, some of my most satisfying projects since then have been for small businesses: a kirana chain in Madurai, a D2C coffee brand in Bengaluru, a saree store in Hyderabad that sells on Instagram.

Let me tell you what these clients actually send me. It is usually an Excel file exported from Tally or Shopify, or a Google Sheet that three different people have typed into. Dates are in four formats. "Chennai" is also written as "chennai " with a trailing space and "Madras". Some prices have the rupee symbol typed in, so Excel treats them as text. And the owner's question is simple: "Which products are actually making me money?"

So dekho, the job is not fancy. The job is to take that mess, make it trustworthy, and answer the question clearly. That is exactly what this course trains you to do.

In the first two modules we live inside Excel. You will learn to clean data properly, use XLOOKUP to bring in product categories, use SUMIFS to total sales by any condition, and build pivot tables that summarise a whole month in seconds. Then in module three we move to SQL, because when a D2C brand has two lakh orders, Excel starts crying. SQL lets you ask the same questions, faster and repeatably.

Finally, we learn the part most courses skip: presenting. A client paying you ₹8,000 for an analysis does not want forty charts. They want three findings and what to do next.

One tip before we start: keep a notebook of every business question you hear. That list becomes your portfolio later. Chalo, let us open our first messy file.

lessons.title: Cleaning messy sales data in Excel
lessons.content:
## Why cleaning comes first

If your data is wrong, every chart built on it is wrong too. Analysts spend a large share of their time cleaning, and clients rarely see it, but it is what makes your numbers trustworthy. Here is the checklist I run on every new sales file.

## Step 1: Make it a proper table

Select your data and press **Ctrl + T** to convert it into an Excel Table. Tables auto-expand when new rows are added, give each column a name, and make formulas easier to read, for example `=[@Qty]*[@Price]` instead of `=C2*D2`.

Rules for a clean table:
- **One header row**, no merged cells, no blank rows in between.
- **One fact per column**: do not put "Rice 5kg - ₹420" in one cell; split product, pack size and price.
- **One row per transaction**, never subtotal rows mixed into the data.

## Step 2: Fix text problems

- `TRIM` removes extra spaces: `=TRIM(B2)` turns "Chennai " into "Chennai".
- `PROPER` fixes casing: `=PROPER(TRIM(B2))` turns "cHENNAI" into "Chennai".
- Use **Find & Replace (Ctrl + H)** to standardise spellings, for example replace "Madras" with "Chennai" and "Bangalore" with "Bengaluru".

> Tip: never overwrite the raw data. Keep the original sheet untouched and do your cleaning in a copy or in helper columns. Clients will ask "where did this number come from?" and you need the trail.

## Step 3: Fix numbers stored as text

If prices were typed as "₹420" or "420 ", Excel sees text and `SUM` ignores them. Fix it with:

```text
=VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(TRIM(D2),"₹",""))
```

A quick check: numbers align right by default, text aligns left. If a "price" column is left-aligned, investigate.

## Step 4: Fix dates

Dates from different systems arrive as "03/04/2025", "2025-04-03" and "3 Apr". Use **Data → Text to Columns → Date (DMY)** to convert Indian-style day-first dates. Then add helper columns:
- `=TEXT([@Date],"mmm-yyyy")` for month labels
- `=TEXT([@Date],"ddd")` for weekday, useful for spotting weekend sales spikes

## Step 5: Remove duplicates carefully

**Data → Remove Duplicates** is powerful but dangerous. Two rows with the same customer and amount might be two genuine purchases. Only dedupe on a true unique key like **Order ID**.

## Step 6: Flag, do not delete, suspicious rows

Add a column `Check` with a formula like `=IF(OR([@Qty]<=0,[@Price]=0),"Review","OK")` and filter on it. Then ask the client about those rows instead of silently dropping them.

### Your cleaning log

Keep a small sheet called **Notes** listing every change: "Standardised 14 city spellings, removed 6 duplicate Order IDs, flagged 3 zero-price rows". This log turns into the first paragraph of your client report and builds a lot of trust.

lessons.title: XLOOKUP, SUMIFS and COUNTIFS on real data
lessons.content:
## Key points
- XLOOKUP replaces VLOOKUP: it looks left or right, defaults to an exact match and lets you set a friendly "not found" value.
- SUMIFS adds up a column only where every condition you give it is true, so one formula can answer "sales of Snacks in Chennai in May".
- COUNTIFS counts rows matching conditions and is perfect for order counts and repeat-customer checks.
- Point your conditions at cells instead of typing them inside the formula so one formula can fill an entire summary grid.
- Use absolute references with $ (or Table column names) so formulas do not break when copied.

## Transcript
Okay, in this lesson we will use the three formulas I use in almost every client file.

First, XLOOKUP. Our kirana sales sheet has a product code in each row, but no category. The category lives in a separate Product Master sheet. So in a new column I write:

```text
=XLOOKUP([@ProductCode], Products[Code], Products[Category], "Not found")
```

Read it like a sentence: look for this product code in the Code column, and return the matching Category. If it is missing, write "Not found" instead of an ugly #N/A error. Then I filter for "Not found" and send that small list to the client. Usually it is new products they forgot to add to the master. Old VLOOKUP needed column numbers and could only look to the right; XLOOKUP has neither problem.

Next, SUMIFS. The owner asks, "How much Snacks did we sell in May?" I build a small summary grid: categories down the rows, months across the columns. In the first cell:

```text
=SUMIFS(Sales[Amount], Sales[Category], $A2, Sales[Month], B$1)
```

The first argument is what to add up. Then come pairs: which column to check, and what it should equal. Dekho, notice the dollar signs. $A2 locks the column so the category always comes from column A, and B$1 locks the row so the month always comes from row 1. Now I drag this formula across the whole grid and every cell is correct. One formula, forty answers.

Finally, COUNTIFS works the same way but counts rows. To count how many orders a customer placed, I use `=COUNTIFS(Sales[Phone], [@Phone])`. Any customer with a count above one is a repeat customer, and repeat rate is a number every D2C founder cares about.

Practice these three on the sample file before the quiz. Once they feel natural, you are already more useful than most people who list "Advanced Excel" on Naukri.

lessons.title: Quiz: cleaning and core formulas
lessons.content: Check that you can pick the right cleaning step and formula for common client problems. Think about why each answer works, not just which one it is.

questions.prompt: A price column shows values like "₹420" and SUM returns 0. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The column is formatted as Currency
The values are stored as text because of the typed rupee symbol
The sheet has calculation set to Manual

questions.explanation: Typing the ₹ symbol makes Excel store the value as text, which SUM ignores. Remove the symbol with SUBSTITUTE and convert with VALUE.

questions.prompt: You need total sales where Category is "Snacks" AND City is "Chennai". Which formula fits best?
questions.explanation: SUMIFS adds the Amount column only for rows meeting every condition. COUNTIFS would count orders, and XLOOKUP returns only the first match.

questions.prompt: When is it safe to use Remove Duplicates on an order sheet?

options.text: When deduplicating on a true unique key such as Order ID
Whenever two rows have the same customer name
Whenever two rows have the same amount on the same day

questions.explanation: The same customer can genuinely buy the same thing twice. Only an ID that should be unique per transaction proves a row is a duplicate.

questions.prompt: Why write $A2 and B$1 in a SUMIFS formula you plan to drag across a grid?

options.text: Dollar signs make the result display in currency format
They lock the category column and the month row so every copied cell reads the correct labels
They make the formula calculate faster
They are required for SUMIFS to accept text criteria

questions.explanation: Mixed references keep the label lookups anchored: the column of categories stays fixed for $A2, and the row of months stays fixed for B$1.

questions.prompt: XLOOKUP returns "Not found" for 12 rows. What should a good analyst do?

options.text: Delete those 12 rows so the totals look clean
Switch to VLOOKUP, which will find them
Fill in a category based on a guess from the product name
Filter those rows and confirm the missing product codes with the client

questions.explanation: Missing codes usually mean the product master is out of date. Asking the client keeps the analysis accurate and shows you are careful.

lessons.title: Pivot tables in 10 minutes
lessons.content:
## Key points
- A pivot table summarises thousands of rows by dragging fields into Rows, Columns, Values and Filters.
- Always build pivots from an Excel Table so new data is picked up with a simple Refresh.
- Change Value Field Settings to switch between Sum, Count and Average, and use "Show Values As % of Grand Total" for share-of-sales questions.
- Group dates by Month or Quarter and add Slicers so clients can click through cities or channels themselves.
- A pivot answers "what happened"; your job is to follow up with "why" and "so what".

## Transcript
Chalo, let us build our first pivot table. I have the cleaned D2C order sheet open: about six thousand rows of orders for a snack brand, with columns for Order Date, City, Channel, Product, Qty and Amount.

Click anywhere inside the Table, go to Insert, then PivotTable, and put it on a new sheet. On the right you see the field list. Think of it like this: Rows is what you want down the side, Columns is across the top, Values is what you want to measure, and Filters narrows everything.

Drag Product into Rows and Amount into Values. Instantly, total sales per product. Now sort it largest to smallest. Already we have a useful finding: in this data the top three products bring in more than half the revenue.

Now drag Channel into Columns. Suddenly you can see that Masala Makhana sells mostly on the website, but Banana Chips sell mostly through Amazon. That is a real business insight; the owner may want to price or promote differently on each channel.

Next, put Order Date into Rows above Product. Excel will offer to group it. Right-click, Group, and choose Months. Now you see monthly trends per product.

Two settings I use constantly. First, right-click the Amount values, choose Show Values As, then % of Grand Total. Owners understand "Makhana is 31% of sales" much faster than a raw rupee number. Second, add a Slicer for City from the PivotTable Analyze tab. Slicers are clickable buttons, and when you share the file, clients love playing with them.

One warning, dekho: when the client sends new data, paste it into the Table, then right-click the pivot and Refresh. If you built the pivot from a fixed range instead of a Table, new rows get ignored silently, and that is how wrong numbers end up in reports.

In the next lesson we will walk through a full kirana month analysis using exactly these moves.

lessons.title: Worked example: analysing a kirana store's quarter
lessons.content:
## The client and the question

Selvi Stores is a two-branch kirana in Coimbatore. The owner, Mr. Murugan, sent three months of billing exports and asked: **"Sales feel flat. Where should I focus?"** A vague question like this is normal. Your first job is to break it into answerable pieces.

### Turning a vague ask into questions
1. Is revenue actually flat, or is it shifting between branches or categories?
2. Which categories bring the most **margin**, not just revenue?
3. When do customers buy: which days and which hours?
4. Are digital payments (UPI) changing the picture?

## Building the analysis

After cleaning (see the previous module), add helper columns to the Table:
- `Month` with `=TEXT([@BillDate],"mmm")`
- `Weekday` with `=TEXT([@BillDate],"ddd")`
- `Margin` with `=[@Amount]-[@Qty]*XLOOKUP([@SKU],Products[SKU],Products[CostPrice])`

Now build four small pivots, each on its own sheet:

**Pivot 1: Branch by Month (Sum of Amount).** Total revenue barely moved, but Branch 2 grew while Branch 1 fell. "Flat" was hiding two opposite stories.

**Pivot 2: Category (Sum of Amount, Sum of Margin).** Staples like rice and atta are the biggest revenue, but margins are thin. Snacks, beverages and personal care are smaller in revenue yet bring a large share of the margin.

**Pivot 3: Weekday by Hour (Count of Bills).** Evenings between 6 and 9 pm and Sunday mornings are the peaks.

**Pivot 4: Payment Mode by Month.** UPI share is rising month on month.

> Tip: add a calculated field **Margin %** in the pivot (PivotTable Analyze → Fields, Items & Sets → Calculated Field) with `=Margin/Amount`. Owners think in margin, not revenue.

## From numbers to recommendations

Analysis is only useful when it changes a decision. For Selvi Stores the story becomes:

- **Branch 1 is losing customers, not prices.** Bill count fell while average bill value held steady. Worth checking for a new competitor or a quick-commerce dark store nearby.
- **Push high-margin categories at peak hours.** Place snacks and beverages near the counter between 6 and 9 pm.
- **Use UPI data for loyalty.** UPI bills often capture a phone number, which makes a WhatsApp Business broadcast list possible for repeat customers.

### What to deliver

Do not send the client your working file with ten sheets. Send a clean **Summary** sheet: three charts, three findings, three actions. Keep the pivots in the file for anyone who wants to dig deeper.

lessons.title: Assignment: clean and summarise a D2C order export
lessons.content: This is the most common paid analytics task on Internshala and freelance groups: "here is our export, tell us what is going on". Doing it end to end once gives you a portfolio piece you can show in interviews and client calls.

assignment.brief:
## The task
**Kaapi Kadai**, a Bengaluru D2C filter-coffee brand, has shared a 3-month order export (download the sample from the resources tab). It has inconsistent city names, prices typed as text, duplicate Order IDs and a separate Product Master sheet.

## Steps
1. Keep the raw sheet untouched; copy it to a new sheet and convert it to an Excel Table.
2. Clean city names (TRIM, PROPER, Find & Replace), fix text prices with `VALUE` and `SUBSTITUTE`, and convert dates.
3. Remove true duplicates on Order ID only. Flag any zero or negative quantity rows in a `Check` column.
4. Bring in the product category and cost price with `XLOOKUP`.
5. Build a SUMIFS grid of revenue by Category and Month.
6. Build at least two pivot tables: revenue by City and Channel, and monthly trend by Product. Add one Slicer.
7. Write a **Notes** sheet listing every cleaning change, with row counts.

## Deliverable
Upload the workbook to Google Drive or OneDrive and submit the view link. Include a **Summary** sheet with 3 findings written in plain English.

## Tips
- Name your sheets clearly: Raw, Clean, Products, Pivots, Summary, Notes.
- A finding has a number and a "so what", for example: "Mysuru orders doubled in March, mostly via Instagram; worth testing a city-specific offer."

rubric.criterion: Data cleaning is correct and documented in the Notes sheet
XLOOKUP and SUMIFS used correctly with sensible references
Pivot tables are accurate, well grouped and include a Slicer
Summary findings are specific, numeric and actionable

lessons.title: SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY
lessons.content:
## Key points
- SQL lets you ask questions of tables with lakhs of rows that would slow Excel down.
- SELECT chooses columns, FROM names the table, WHERE filters rows, and ORDER BY sorts the result.
- Text values go in single quotes, and dates are safest in the 'YYYY-MM-DD' format.
- Use IN for lists, BETWEEN for ranges and LIKE with % for partial text matches.
- Always use LIMIT while exploring a big table so you do not pull everything at once.

## Transcript
Welcome to SQL. If Excel is your calculator, SQL is how you talk to a database. Good news: the core of it reads almost like English.

Imagine our snack brand's orders are in a table called orders, with columns order_id, order_date, customer_id, city, channel and amount. Let us look at a few rows first:

```sql
SELECT order_id, order_date, city, amount
FROM orders
LIMIT 10;
```

SELECT says which columns, FROM says which table, and LIMIT keeps it small. I always start this way with a new client database, just to see what the data looks like.

Now the owner asks, "Show me big Chennai orders from April." That is a filter, so we use WHERE:

```sql
SELECT order_id, order_date, amount
FROM orders
WHERE city = 'Chennai'
  AND order_date BETWEEN '2025-04-01' AND '2025-04-30'
  AND amount >= 1000
ORDER BY amount DESC;
```

Dekho, a few things here. Text like 'Chennai' goes in single quotes. Dates are written year-month-day, which avoids all the day-first versus month-first confusion. AND means every condition must be true. ORDER BY amount DESC puts the biggest orders on top.

Two more filters you will use daily. IN checks a list, for example `WHERE city IN ('Chennai', 'Coimbatore', 'Madurai')`. And LIKE does partial matches: `WHERE product_name LIKE '%Makhana%'` finds every product with Makhana anywhere in the name.

One beginner mistake: writing `WHERE city = NULL`. It never works. Missing values need `WHERE city IS NULL`.

Practice in the free online editor linked in the resources. Write at least ten queries of your own before the next lesson. Typing them yourself is how SQL actually sticks.

lessons.title: GROUP BY and HAVING for business questions
lessons.content:
## From rows to summaries

Clients rarely want individual rows. They want totals and averages: revenue per city, orders per month, average bill per channel. In SQL, that is **GROUP BY** with **aggregate functions**. If you understood pivot tables, you already understand GROUP BY; it is the same idea in code.

### The aggregate functions
- `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` counts unique customers
- `SUM(amount)` totals a column
- `AVG(amount)` gives the average
- `MIN()` and `MAX()` give the smallest and largest values

## Revenue by city

```sql
SELECT city,
       COUNT(*)                     AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)  AS customers,
       SUM(amount)                  AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(amount), 0)        AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

The rule to remember: **every column in SELECT must be either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate.** If you select `city` and `channel` but group only by `city`, the database does not know which channel to show, so it throws an error (or worse, in some databases it silently picks one).

## Monthly trend

Most databases have a function to cut a date down to its month. In PostgreSQL:

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
ORDER BY month;
```

In MySQL you would use `DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m')` instead. Check which database your client uses before writing date logic.

## WHERE versus HAVING

This confuses almost everyone at first:
- **WHERE** filters rows *before* grouping.
- **HAVING** filters groups *after* aggregating.

"Show cities with more than ₹5 lakh revenue from Instagram orders" needs both:

```sql
SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE channel = 'Instagram'
GROUP BY city
HAVING SUM(amount) > 500000
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

> Tip: the logical order SQL runs in is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. Once you remember that, most "why is this not working" moments make sense, including why you cannot use a SELECT alias inside WHERE.

### Practice questions
1. Which channel has the highest average order value?
2. How many unique customers ordered each month?
3. Which products sold fewer than 50 units in the quarter? (Hint: HAVING.)

lessons.title: JOINs explained with orders and customers
lessons.content:
## Why JOINs exist

Real databases split information across tables so nothing is typed twice. A D2C brand might have:
- `customers`: customer_id, name, phone, city, signup_date
- `orders`: order_id, customer_id, order_date, channel, amount
- `order_items`: order_id, product_id, qty, price
- `products`: product_id, product_name, category, cost_price

A JOIN connects them using matching keys, exactly like XLOOKUP did in Excel, but for every row at once.

## INNER JOIN: only matching rows

```sql
SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, c.name, c.city, o.amount
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c
        ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
```

`o` and `c` are **aliases**, short names that keep queries readable. INNER JOIN returns only orders whose customer_id exists in customers. If an order has a missing or wrong customer_id, it silently disappears, which matters when you are totalling revenue.

## LEFT JOIN: keep everything on the left

```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
       ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;
```

This keeps **every customer**, even those with zero orders. Customers who signed up but never bought are a goldmine for a WhatsApp re-engagement campaign. Notice we use `COUNT(o.order_id)` not `COUNT(*)`, so customers with no orders show 0 instead of 1.

To find only the never-buyers, add `WHERE o.order_id IS NULL`.

## Joining several tables

Revenue and margin by category needs three tables:

```sql
SELECT p.category,
       SUM(oi.qty * oi.price)                    AS revenue,
       SUM(oi.qty * (oi.price - p.cost_price))   AS margin
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY margin DESC;
```

## Common JOIN mistakes

- **Row explosion.** Joining orders to order_items repeats each order once per item. If you then `SUM(o.amount)`, revenue is double or triple counted. Sum at the item level, or aggregate before joining.
- **Forgetting the ON condition.** Without it you get every row matched with every other row: a cross join of millions of rows.
- **Wrong join type.** Ask yourself: "Do I need rows that have no match?" If yes, LEFT JOIN.

> Tip: after any join, compare the row count and total with the original table. If revenue suddenly jumped 40%, you have a duplication problem, not a great quarter.

lessons.title: Quiz: SQL fundamentals
lessons.content: These questions test whether you can choose the right SQL clause for a real business question. Read each query carefully before answering.

questions.prompt: You want cities whose total revenue exceeds ₹2,00,000. Where does the condition SUM(amount) > 200000 belong?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after SUM is calculated.

questions.prompt: Which query finds customers who signed up but never placed an order?

options.text: customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE c.name IS NULL
customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id = NULL

questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, and unmatched ones get NULL order columns. IS NULL (not = NULL) then filters to never-buyers. An INNER JOIN would drop them entirely.

questions.prompt: After joining orders to order_items, SUM(o.amount) shows revenue 2.5x higher than expected. Why?

options.text: Each order row is repeated once per item, so order amounts are counted multiple times
The JOIN removed orders with no items

questions.explanation: A one-to-many join duplicates the 'one' side. Sum item-level values (qty * price) or aggregate orders before joining.

questions.prompt: Which query runs without error in standard SQL?

options.text: SELECT city, channel, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY city
SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE revenue > 1000 GROUP BY city
SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY city ORDER BY revenue DESC
SELECT city, amount FROM orders GROUP BY city

questions.explanation: ORDER BY runs after SELECT so it can use the alias. The others select ungrouped columns or use an alias inside WHERE, which runs before SELECT.

questions.prompt: What does COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) tell you that COUNT(*) does not?

options.text: The number of unique customers rather than the number of rows or orders
The number of customers with missing IDs
The number of new customers this month
Nothing different; they always return the same value

questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row, so a customer with five orders counts five times. DISTINCT counts each customer once, which you need for repeat-rate analysis.

lessons.title: Answering a D2C founder's questions with SQL
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Founders ask business questions like "are customers coming back?"; your job is translating them into precise metrics.
- Repeat rate is the share of customers with two or more orders in a period, and it is often the most important D2C health metric.
- A CTE (WITH clause) breaks a hard question into readable steps, which makes your query easier to check and explain.
- Always sanity-check results against a number the client already knows, such as total monthly revenue from their Shopify dashboard.
- Save your queries with comments so you can rerun the same analysis next month as a retainer.

## Transcript
In this lesson I want to show you how a real client conversation becomes SQL. Last year, the founder of a Coimbatore snack brand called me and said, "Arvind, Instagram ads are getting expensive. Are my customers even coming back?"

That is a great question, but it is not yet a metric. So I asked two follow-ups: over what period, and what counts as "coming back"? We agreed: in the last six months, a returning customer is anyone with two or more orders.

Now we can write SQL. I like using a CTE, the WITH clause, because it lets me build the answer in steps:

```sql
WITH customer_orders AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         COUNT(*)    AS orders,
         SUM(amount) AS total_spent
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers,
       SUM(CASE WHEN orders >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS repeat_customers,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN orders >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS repeat_rate_pct,
       ROUND(AVG(total_spent), 0) AS avg_spend
FROM customer_orders;
```

Step one summarises each customer. Step two summarises those summaries. Dekho, the CASE WHEN is just an IF statement inside SQL. And I multiply by 100.0, not 100, so the division gives decimals instead of rounding down to zero in some databases.

For this brand the repeat rate came out around 22 percent. Then I split it by first-order channel with one more join, and found customers acquired through WhatsApp referrals came back far more often than Instagram-ad customers. That single finding moved part of their ad budget into a referral offer.

Before presenting anything, I always cross-check. I ran total revenue for January and compared it with their Shopify dashboard. It matched within a few hundred rupees, which I could explain by refunds. If it had been way off, I would fix my query before saying anything to the client.

Finally, save the query with comments. Next month they will ask the same question, and rerunning it in two minutes is how one project becomes a monthly retainer.

lessons.title: Presenting insights: the one-page client report
lessons.content:
## Clients buy decisions, not dashboards

A small business owner reading your report is busy, possibly on a phone, possibly between customers. If they need ten minutes to find the point, you have lost them. The fix is a **one-page insight report** built on a simple structure.

## The structure

### 1. Headline (one sentence)
Lead with the answer. Not "Sales Analysis Q1 2025", but:

> Repeat customers drive 48% of revenue, but only 22% of buyers come back. Improving retention is your biggest lever.

### 2. Three findings
Each finding gets a **number**, a **comparison**, and a **chart** at most.
- "Average order value on the website is ₹612 versus ₹438 on Amazon."
- "Sunday orders are 1.6x the weekday average, mostly between 7 and 10 pm."
- "Customers from WhatsApp referrals reorder at nearly twice the rate of Instagram-ad customers."

A number alone is not a finding. A number with a comparison is.

### 3. Recommendations
One action per finding, written so someone could start tomorrow:
- Offer free shipping above ₹599 on the website to lift order value further.
- Schedule Instagram posts and WhatsApp broadcasts for Sunday evening.
- Launch a "refer a friend, both get ₹100 off" offer via WhatsApp Business.

### 4. Data notes (small print)
Date range, data source, what was cleaned or excluded. This protects you and builds trust.

## Charts that work for owners

- **Bar charts** for comparing categories; sort them largest first.
- **Line charts** for trends over months.
- **Avoid** 3D charts, pie charts with more than four slices, and dual axes.
- Title every chart with the takeaway: "Website orders are worth 40% more than Amazon orders", not "AOV by Channel".
- Highlight the one bar that matters in a strong colour; keep others grey.

## Delivering it

- Export the page as a **PDF**; it opens cleanly on WhatsApp and email.
- Send a short message with it: the headline plus "happy to walk you through it in a 15-minute call".
- On the call, talk through recommendations, not methodology. Keep your Excel and SQL ready in case they ask "how did you get this?"

> Tip: end the call by asking, "Which of these would you like me to track every month?" That question is how analysts turn one-time projects into ₹5,000 to ₹15,000 monthly retainers.

## A quick self-check before sending
- Can the owner understand the headline without reading anything else?
- Does every chart title state a conclusion?
- Is every recommendation specific, cheap to test, and tied to a finding?

lessons.title: Capstone: insight report for a Coimbatore snack brand
lessons.content: This capstone mirrors a real first project: a founder shares their data and a worry, and you return answers they can act on. A strong submission here is exactly what you will show when pitching your first analytics client on LinkedIn or Catalance.

assignment.brief:
## The scenario
**Kongu Crunch** is a Coimbatore D2C snack brand selling on its website, Amazon and Instagram. The founder writes: *"Revenue grew last quarter but profit did not. Ad costs are up. What is going on and what should I do?"*

You get a SQLite database (resources tab) with `customers`, `orders`, `order_items` and `products` tables.

## Steps
1. Explore every table with `SELECT ... LIMIT 10` and note row counts.
2. Write SQL to answer at least four of these:
   - Revenue and margin by month and by channel
   - Margin by product category (join `order_items` and `products`)
   - Repeat rate overall and by acquisition channel (use a CTE)
   - Top 10 customers by total spend and their share of revenue
   - Average order value by channel
3. Cross-check one total against a simple Excel pivot of the exported orders table.
4. Build 3 clean charts in Excel or Google Sheets.
5. Write a one-page report: headline, three findings, three recommendations, data notes.

## Deliverable
Submit a Google Drive folder link containing: `queries.sql` (commented), the chart workbook, and the report as a PDF.

## Tips
- Comment each query with the business question it answers.
- Watch for row explosion when joining orders to order_items.
- Recommendations should be cheap to test, such as a free-shipping threshold or a WhatsApp referral offer.

rubric.criterion: SQL queries are correct, readable and commented with the business question
Results are cross-checked and data notes explain cleaning and scope
Findings are specific, numeric and compared against a baseline
Recommendations are actionable and tied to findings
Report and charts are clear enough for a busy owner to read in two minutes

courses.title: Power BI Dashboards for Clients
courses.subtitle: Build interactive, refreshable dashboards small businesses will pay for monthly
courses.description: Go beyond one-off Excel reports and build Power BI dashboards clients open every Monday. You will shape messy files with Power Query, write your first DAX measures for revenue, margin and growth, and design a clean single-page dashboard for a real-style Indian retail client. Ideal if you already know Excel basics and want a skill that turns into monthly retainers.

mentor.name: Arvind Krishnan
mentor.headline: Data analyst turned freelance BI consultant

A star-schema model with a date table and core DAX measures
A one-page sales dashboard for a Hyderabad apparel store, published and shareable
