lessons.title: AIDA and PAS in plain words
lessons.content:
## Key points
- AIDA stands for Attention, Interest, Desire, Action and works well for landing pages and longer ads.
- PAS stands for Problem, Agitate, Solution and works well when the reader already feels a pain.
- Frameworks are skeletons for your thinking, not templates to fill blindly.
- Always start from the customer's words, gathered from reviews, DMs and sales calls.

## Transcript
Welcome! Let's begin with two frameworks I use almost every day. First, AIDA. Attention: stop the scroll. Interest: show why this matters to them. Desire: make them picture life with the product. Action: tell them exactly what to do next.

Second, PAS. Problem: name the pain. Agitate: show what it costs them. Solution: present the product as the relief. Here's PAS for a Pune tiffin service: "Skipping lunch again because the canteen food is oily? By 4 pm you're tired and snacking on chips. Ghar ka khana, delivered to your Hinjewadi office by 1 pm, Rs 120 a meal."

Dekho, the framework didn't write that. The customer's words did. "Oily canteen food" came from real reviews. So before writing copy, read reviews, DMs and comments. Then use the framework to arrange what you find.

lessons.title: Features vs benefits
lessons.content:
## Features tell, benefits sell

A **feature** is what the product has. A **benefit** is what that does for the customer. Beginners list features; good copy translates them.

### The "so what?" test

Take any feature and ask "so what?" until you reach something the customer cares about.

- **Feature:** 5,000 mAh battery.
- So what? Lasts two days.
- So what? **No hunting for a charger on a Mumbai-Pune Volvo trip.**

That last line is the benefit worth writing.

### More examples

- "256-bit encryption" becomes "Your customers' UPI details stay private."
- "Eggless recipes" becomes "Everyone at the family party can have a slice."
- "Live doubt classes" becomes "Get stuck at 9 pm? Get unstuck by 9:15."

> Tip: Keep the feature nearby as proof. "Lasts two days (5,000 mAh battery)" combines emotion with evidence.

Benefits go in headlines and first lines. Features go in bullets and specs, where serious buyers look for details.

lessons.title: Frameworks quiz
lessons.content: Three quick questions to check you can apply AIDA, PAS and benefits, not just name them.

questions.prompt: Your client's customers already complain loudly about late salary-day payouts. Which framework fits best for their ad?
questions.explanation: PAS works when the pain is already felt. Naming and agitating it makes the solution land.

questions.prompt: Which line is a benefit rather than a feature?

options.text: Clear photos of your kids even in dim restaurant lighting

questions.explanation: It describes what the feature does for the customer in a real situation.

questions.prompt: Where should you find the words you use inside a framework?

options.text: Customer reviews, DMs, comments and sales calls
The company's internal product specs only

questions.explanation: Copy that mirrors the customer's own language feels instantly relevant.

lessons.title: Five headline formulas that work
lessons.content:
## Why headlines matter most

Most people read only the headline. If it fails, the rest of your copy is never seen. Here are five formulas to start with.

### 1. Outcome + timeframe
"Speak confident English in 60 days." Specific and measurable.

### 2. How to + benefit
"How to file your ITR without a CA, in 30 minutes."

### 3. Question that names the pain
"Still paying Rs 2,000 a month for software you barely use?"

### 4. Number + specific promise
"7 GST mistakes that cost small shops thousands."

### 5. Social proof
"Why 12,000 Kolkata parents trust us for school pickups."

## Make it sharper

- Swap vague words for numbers: "fast" becomes "in 10 minutes".
- Cut the brand name unless it is famous; the benefit matters more.
- Read it as a busy stranger would. Would you stop?

> Tip: Never promise what the product cannot deliver. Clickbait raises clicks but kills conversions and trust.

Write at least ten headlines for every piece. The fourth or seventh is often the winner.

lessons.title: Testing headlines like a pro
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Your opinion of a headline matters less than data from real readers.
- A/B testing means showing two versions to similar audiences and comparing one metric.
- Test big differences in angle first, then fine-tune wording later.
- Small Indian brands can test cheaply with Meta ads, email subject lines or WhatsApp broadcasts.

## Transcript
Here's a humbling truth: my favourite headline loses about half the time. So I test. A/B testing simply means showing version A to one group and version B to another similar group, then checking one number, like click rate.

You don't need fancy tools. For a Jaipur bakery, we ran two Meta ads at Rs 300 each. A: "Eggless cakes, baked fresh daily." B: "The birthday cake your whole family can eat." B got almost double the clicks. Same product, different angle.

Test big differences first: price angle versus family angle versus speed angle. Once you find the winning angle, then play with words. And give each test enough people, at least a few hundred views, before you decide. Chalo, write bold variations, not tiny tweaks.

lessons.title: Write and rank 10 headlines
lessons.content: Clients often hire copywriters just for headline and hook options. This exercise builds the volume-and-judgement muscle that makes you fast and valuable.

assignment.brief:
## The product
**StudyNest**, a Rs 299-a-month app from Bengaluru that gives college students recorded lectures plus live doubt sessions every evening.

## Task
1. Write **10 headlines** using at least four of the five formulas.
2. Label which formula each one uses.
3. Pick your **top 2** and explain in 2-3 lines each why they would win.
4. Suggest how you would A/B test them cheaply.

## Deliverable
Paste everything as text in your submission.

## Tip
Read real student reviews of similar apps on the Play Store for language you can borrow.

rubric.criterion: Range: ten distinct headlines across at least four formulas
Clarity and specificity: concrete benefits, numbers, customer language
Sound reasoning for top picks and a practical test plan

lessons.title: Anatomy of a high-converting landing page
lessons.content:
## Key points
- The hero section needs a benefit headline, a supporting line and one clear call-to-action button.
- Follow with the problem, the solution, how it works, proof, pricing and FAQs.
- Objections should be answered in FAQs and near the button, not ignored.
- One page, one goal: every section should push toward the same action.

## Transcript
Let's walk through a landing page top to bottom. The hero is the first screen. It needs a headline with the main benefit, one supporting line and one button. "Start your 7-day free trial", not "Submit".

Next, the problem section, using PAS. Then the solution and a simple "how it works" in three steps. Then proof: testimonials with real names and cities, ratings, logos of clients. Indians trust word of mouth, so a line like "Riya, Pune: lost 6 kg in 3 months" works hard.

Then pricing, clearly in rupees, and mention payment options like UPI and Razorpay. Then FAQs that answer objections: "Can I cancel anytime?" "Is my data safe?" Finally, repeat the call to action. Dekho, one page, one goal. If you add five different links, you leak conversions.

lessons.title: Meta and Google ad copy within limits
lessons.content:
## Different platforms, different mindsets

On **Google Search**, people are actively looking. Match their query and be direct. On **Meta (Instagram and Facebook)**, people are scrolling, so you must interrupt with a hook.

## Google Search ads

Responsive search ads use **headlines of up to 30 characters** and **descriptions of up to 90 characters**. Write several of each so Google can mix them.

- Headline: "Eggless Cakes in Jaipur"
- Headline: "Same-Day Delivery by 8 pm"
- Description: "Fresh eggless cakes from Rs 450. Order on WhatsApp and get same-day delivery across Jaipur."

Include the keyword, a specific offer and a reason to act now.

## Meta ads

The **primary text** shows about 125 characters before "more", and the **headline** under the image works best around 40 characters.

- Primary text: "Your mom's birthday is Sunday. Order a fresh eggless cake today, delivered by 8 pm."
- Headline: "Order on WhatsApp"

> Tip: Write five variations of each element and let the platform test them. Keep the image and copy telling the same story.

Always check claims against ad policies: no guaranteed health results, no misleading "free" offers.

lessons.title: Landing page copy for FitKadam
lessons.content: Landing page copy is one of the best-paid projects for intermediate copywriters, often Rs 8,000 to Rs 25,000 per page. This assignment gives you a full sample to show clients.

assignment.brief:
## The client
**FitKadam** is a Pune startup with a walking-and-strength app for busy professionals aged 28-45. Plans cost Rs 249 a month or Rs 1,999 a year, with a 7-day free trial. Users get 20-minute home workouts, step challenges with friends and a WhatsApp coach check-in every week.

## Task
Write full landing page copy:
1. Hero: headline, subheadline, CTA button text
2. Problem section using PAS
3. How it works in 3 steps
4. Three benefit blocks (benefit headline + 2 lines)
5. Two sample testimonials, clearly marked as placeholders for real ones
6. Pricing section
7. Four FAQs answering real objections
8. Final CTA

Then write **two Google headlines (30 characters max)** and **one Meta primary text** for the page.

## Deliverable
A Google Doc link with comment access, sections clearly labelled.

rubric.criterion: Hero and headline: clear benefit, strong CTA, instantly understandable
Structure follows a logical persuasion flow with one goal
Objections handled honestly in FAQs and pricing
Ad copy fits platform limits and matches the page

modules.title: Design Principles That Make Work Look Right

lessons.title: Why Some Posters Just Work: Contrast and Hierarchy
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Contrast is the difference between elements, and it is the fastest way to tell the viewer what matters most.
- Every design needs one clear hero element; if everything is big and bold, nothing stands out.
- You can create contrast with size, weight, colour, spacing and shape, not just with bright colours.
- Squint at your design: whatever you still see clearly is your true hierarchy.
- Aim for three levels of hierarchy on most posters: headline, supporting info, and fine print.

## Transcript
Hi everyone, I am Meghna, and for the last nine years I have been designing brands and posters from my small studio in Kolkata. Let me start with a confession. My first paid poster, for a Durga Puja cultural night, was a disaster. I had seven fonts, four colours, and every line of text was shouting. The client was polite, but nobody at the pandal could read the date.

What was missing? Contrast. Contrast is simply difference. A big headline next to small body text. A dark background with light type. A heavy bold word next to a thin one. When things are different, the eye knows where to go first.

Dekho, here is the test I still use every single day. Step back from your screen and squint until everything goes blurry. Whatever you can still see is your hierarchy. If you see five blobs of equal weight, your viewer will feel confused, even if they cannot explain why.

On most posters I want three levels. Level one is the hero: usually the event name or offer, like "Flat 30% Off". Level two is the supporting info: date, venue, what to do next. Level three is the fine print: address, phone number, terms. Each level should look clearly different from the next, not just slightly different. A 48pt headline next to a 44pt subheading is not contrast; it is a mistake that looks accidental.

One more tip. Contrast is not only about colour. You can use size, weight, spacing, even shape. A single circle in a layout full of rectangles grabs attention instantly.

Chalo, in the next lesson we will look at the other three principles that work hand in hand with contrast: alignment, repetition and proximity.

lessons.title: Alignment, Repetition and Proximity in Practice
lessons.content:
## The three quiet principles

Contrast grabs attention. Alignment, repetition and proximity make a design feel **organised and trustworthy**. Clients rarely notice them when they are right, but they always notice when they are wrong.

## Alignment: nothing placed by accident

Every element on the page should line up with something else. When text and images float randomly, the design feels amateur even if each piece looks nice on its own.

- **Pick one strong edge.** Left-aligned text is easiest to read and creates a clean vertical line.
- **Avoid centring everything.** Centred text works for short headlines and wedding invites, but a centred paragraph of six lines is hard to scan.
- **Use the guides.** In Canva, turn on rulers and guides; in Illustrator, use Smart Guides and the Align panel.

> Tip: Draw an imaginary line down the left of your poster. Count how many elements touch it. More touching points usually means a calmer layout.

## Repetition: build a visual system

Repetition means reusing the same fonts, colours, shapes and spacing across a design or a series. It is what makes a brand feel consistent.

- Use the **same heading style** for every heading.
- Repeat a **signature element**, like a rounded corner, a mustard underline or a leaf motif.
- In a carousel or post series, keep the logo in the **same corner** every time.

When a Pune café posts twenty Instagram posts with the same two fonts and colour palette, followers start recognising their posts before reading the name. That is repetition doing its job.

## Proximity: group what belongs together

Items that are related should sit close together; unrelated items should have clear space between them. The viewer reads distance as meaning.

### A common mistake

On event posters, beginners often space the date, time and venue evenly down the page, mixed in with the headline and sponsor logos. Instead:

1. Group **date, time and venue** into one tight block.
2. Put **contact details** in a separate block near the bottom.
3. Keep **sponsor logos** together in a strip.

Now the poster has three clear chunks instead of twelve loose pieces.

## Putting them together

Before you export anything, run a quick check:

- Does everything align to at least one other element?
- Are fonts, colours and spacing repeated consistently?
- Are related items grouped, with breathing room between groups?
- Is there one clear hero thanks to contrast?

If you can say yes to all four, your design is already ahead of most posters you see on WhatsApp forwards.

lessons.title: Typography and Colour Basics for Beginners
lessons.content:
## Typography: choosing and pairing fonts

Fonts carry personality before anyone reads a word. A wedding planner and a gym should not use the same headline font.

### The main families

- **Serif** fonts (like Playfair Display, Lora) have small feet on the letters. They feel classic, elegant, editorial.
- **Sans serif** fonts (like Poppins, Inter, Montserrat) are clean and modern. Great for tech, startups and body text on screens.
- **Script** fonts (like Great Vibes) imitate handwriting. Use them sparingly, only for one or two words.
- **Display** fonts are decorative and loud. Perfect for a festive headline, terrible for paragraphs.

### Simple pairing rules

1. **Two fonts maximum** for most projects: one for headings, one for body.
2. **Pair contrast, not conflict.** A bold serif heading with a simple sans serif body works well. Two different script fonts fight each other.
3. **Use weights for variety.** Instead of adding a third font, use the bold, medium and light versions of the one you have.
4. **Check Indian scripts.** If your client needs Hindi or Bengali text, pick fonts with good Devanagari or Bangla support, such as Mukta, Hind or Noto Sans.

> Tip: Body text on Instagram should rarely go below 24px on a 1080px wide post. People read on small phones while scrolling fast.

## Colour: less is more

### Start with a limited palette

A practical palette has:

- **One primary colour** that represents the brand.
- **One accent colour** for buttons, offers and highlights.
- **Neutrals** such as off-white, warm grey and near-black for backgrounds and text.

The **60-30-10 rule** helps: roughly 60% neutral or dominant colour, 30% secondary, 10% accent.

### Colour meaning in India

Colour associations are cultural. Saffron, marigold and deep red feel festive and auspicious. Green connects with freshness and organic food. White can mean purity, but in some contexts it is associated with mourning, so be careful with all-white festive designs.

### Contrast and accessibility

Light grey text on a white background might look elegant on your large monitor, but it is unreadable on a budget phone in sunlight. Use a free contrast checker (Canva and many websites have them) and aim for strong contrast between text and background.

## Quick checklist

- Two fonts or fewer, with clear weights
- Body text large enough for phones
- A palette of three to five colours, written down with hex codes
- Text readable on its background in bright sunlight

Save your chosen fonts and hex codes in a note. In the next module, you will turn them into a Canva Brand Kit.

lessons.title: Quiz: Design Principles Check
lessons.content: Let us check that the core principles have clicked. These questions are based on real situations you will face with clients.

questions.prompt: A client's sale poster has the headline, discount, date and phone number all in the same bold 40pt font. What is the main problem?

options.text: The font is not trendy enough
There is no contrast, so there is no clear hierarchy
The phone number should be removed

questions.explanation: When every element has the same size and weight, nothing stands out. Varying size and weight creates contrast and tells the viewer what to read first.

questions.prompt: On an event poster, the date, time and venue are scattered across different corners. Which principle would fix this best?

options.text: Proximity: group related details into one block
Colour: make each detail a different colour
Script fonts: make the details more decorative

questions.explanation: Related information should sit together. Grouping date, time and venue lets the viewer grab all the event details in one glance.

questions.prompt: A Kolkata bookstore wants a warm, literary feel for its posts. Which font pairing is the most sensible starting point?

options.text: A decorative display font for both headings and paragraphs
A serif font for headings and a clean sans serif for body text

questions.explanation: A serif heading brings a classic, bookish personality, and a sans serif body keeps longer text readable on phones. Two fonts with clear roles is the safest pairing.

questions.prompt: Using the 60-30-10 rule, where should the bright accent colour usually go?

options.text: Small high-priority elements like the offer badge or call to action

questions.explanation: The accent is the 10%. Keeping it rare means it pulls attention to the most important action, such as 'Order on WhatsApp' or '30% Off'.

questions.prompt: Why does a carousel feel more professional when the logo sits in the same corner on every slide?

options.text: Repetition creates consistency and makes the brand recognisable
It improves the contrast of the headline

questions.explanation: Repeating placement, fonts and colours builds a visual system. Followers start recognising the brand before they even read the name.

modules.title: Canva for Social Posts and Client Templates

lessons.title: Setting Up Canva Like a Pro: Brand Kit, Grids and Guides
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Create a separate Brand Kit for every client so fonts, colours and logos are always one click away.
- Always start from the correct size: 1080x1350 for Instagram portrait posts and 1080x1920 for Stories and Reels covers.
- Turn on rulers, guides and margins so every design shares the same safe area and alignment.
- Name your designs and folders clearly, like "Bakery_IG_Launch_Post01", so clients and teammates can find them.
- Use Canva's "Resize" carefully: it is a starting point, but always fix the layout by hand afterwards.

## Transcript
Chalo, let us open Canva together. Most beginners jump straight into the template gallery, pick something pretty, and change the text. That is fine for your own birthday invite, but for client work it creates chaos. Today I want you to set up Canva the way I set it up in my studio.

First, the Brand Kit. In Canva Pro or Canva for Teams, go to Brand and create a new kit for your client. Upload their logo in both colour and white versions, add their hex codes, and set the heading, subheading and body fonts. Now when you design for, say, a Jaipur bakery, you are not guessing their pink every time. If you are on the free plan, just keep a simple "Brand Sheet" design with the colours and fonts and copy from it.

Second, size. For Instagram feed posts I now default to 1080 by 1350, the portrait 4:5 size, because it takes up more of the screen than a square. For Stories and Reel covers, 1080 by 1920. Do not design a square and stretch it later. Start right.

Third, guides. Go to File, then Settings, and turn on Show rulers and guides, and Show margins. I add guides about 80 pixels in from each edge. Text and logos never cross that line. This keeps everything aligned and safe from Instagram's profile icons and buttons covering it on Stories.

Fourth, naming. Dekho, when a client sends a WhatsApp message saying "Can you change the Thursday post?", you do not want to scroll through forty designs called "Untitled". Name them like Bakery underscore IG underscore Launch underscore Post 01. Use a folder per client.

Finally, the Resize button. It is useful to turn a post into a Story, but it never gets the layout perfectly right. Treat it as a first draft and adjust spacing by hand. That last ten percent of care is what clients pay for.

lessons.title: Designing Instagram Posts and Stories That Get Saved
lessons.content:
## Design for the scroll

Your post has under two seconds to stop someone scrolling. That means the hierarchy you learnt in Module 1 matters even more on Instagram.

## The anatomy of a strong post

1. **A hook headline** of 3 to 7 words, large enough to read on a small phone.
2. **One focal visual**: a product photo, an illustration or a bold shape.
3. **Supporting text** only if needed, kept short.
4. **A brand signature**: logo or handle in a consistent spot.
5. **A clear action** where relevant: "Order on WhatsApp", "Link in bio", "Save for later".

> Tip: If your post needs a paragraph to make sense, it probably wants to be a carousel instead.

## Post types that work for local businesses

### Product spotlight
A clean photo of the product with a short headline and price. For a bakery: "Mango Cheesecake, ₹180 a slice". Use plenty of empty space around the product.

### Offer post
The offer is the hero. "Buy 2 Get 1" in your accent colour, with conditions in small text. Keep terms readable; hiding them looks shady.

### Carousel tips
Educational carousels get **saved and shared**, which helps reach. Structure:

- Slide 1: a bold promise, such as "5 cakes you can order for Raksha Bandhan".
- Slides 2 to 6: one idea per slide, same layout each time.
- Last slide: a call to action and the handle.

### Stories
Stories are casual and quick. Use large text, keep important content within the safe area, and leave space at the bottom for stickers like polls or links.

## Photos make or break the post

Most small clients will send you photos shot on a phone. A few quick fixes in Canva:

- Use **Edit photo** to straighten and crop. A tilted cake looks unappetising.
- Slightly increase **brightness** and **warmth** for food.
- Use **Background Remover** (Pro) for product cut-outs on a solid colour.
- Never stretch a photo; always scale proportionally.

## Consistency across the grid

Clients judge your work by how their profile grid looks as a whole. Plan posts in sets of three or six, alternating between photo-heavy and text-heavy designs, so the grid feels balanced. Reuse the same two fonts and palette from the Brand Kit on every post.

## Before you send to the client

- Check spelling, prices and phone numbers twice
- View the post on your phone, not only on your laptop
- Export as PNG for text-heavy posts and JPG for photo-heavy ones
- Name files in the order they will be posted

lessons.title: Building Reusable Templates for Clients
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Templates let small business owners update their own posts, which turns a one-time gig into an ongoing relationship.
- Lock the elements clients should not touch, such as logos, background shapes and frames.
- Design 4 to 6 core layouts (offer, product, quote, announcement, carousel) instead of thirty random ones.
- Use clear placeholder copy that explains what goes there, like "Product name, max 4 words".
- Share templates with a "Use as template" link so the client always gets a fresh copy and never edits your master.

## Transcript
One of the most profitable services in my studio is not one-off posts. It is template packs. Let me explain why.

A homestay owner in Kochi cannot pay a designer every single time they want to post "Rooms available this weekend". But they will happily pay you once, say ₹6,000 to ₹10,000, for a set of beautiful templates they can edit themselves on their phone. And when they need something bigger, like a Onam campaign, who do you think they will call? You.

So how do we build a good template? Start with a small set of core layouts. I usually make five: an offer post, a product or room spotlight, a customer review quote, an announcement, and a three-slide carousel. Each one follows the Brand Kit strictly.

Next, lock things. In Canva, select an element, click the lock icon, and the client cannot accidentally drag the logo off the page or delete your background shape. Lock the frames too, so they can swap a photo without breaking the layout.

Then, placeholder copy. Never leave "Lorem ipsum" or "Your text here". Write guidance instead, like "Headline, max 5 words" or "Price in rupees". Dekho, the client is not a designer. If the instructions are in the template itself, they will use it correctly.

Finally, sharing. Do not share the edit link to your master file. Use Share, then More, then Template link. Every time the client clicks it, Canva makes them a fresh copy. Your original stays safe.

I also record a quick three-minute screen video showing how to swap a photo and change text, and send it on WhatsApp. Clients love it, and it saves you from ten "how do I change this?" calls.

lessons.title: Assignment: Instagram Launch Set for a Jaipur Bakery
lessons.content: Small businesses are the biggest source of first gigs for new designers, and almost every one of them asks for Instagram posts. This assignment mirrors a real brief so the result goes straight into your portfolio.

assignment.brief:
## The client

**Gulaab Oven** is a home bakery in Jaipur's Malviya Nagar, run by a mother and daughter. They are moving from WhatsApp-only orders to Instagram and want a launch set. Their vibe: warm, handmade, a little royal. Signature items are rose-pistachio cake, eggless brownies and nankhatai.

## Your task

Create a **6-post Instagram launch set** in Canva at 1080x1350, plus **2 reusable templates** the owners can edit themselves.

### Steps

1. Set up a Brand Kit (or a brand sheet design on the free plan) with a palette of 3 to 5 colours and two fonts.
2. Design these six posts:
   - "We are now on Instagram" announcement
   - Three product spotlights with price in ₹
   - One launch offer post (for example, 10% off the first order on WhatsApp)
   - One "How to order" post explaining the WhatsApp Business ordering steps
3. Turn the product spotlight and the offer post into templates with locked elements and helpful placeholder copy.
4. Arrange the six posts in a 2x3 grid mockup to show how the profile will look.

## Deliverable

A **link** to a Google Drive folder or Behance project containing the six PNG/JPG exports, the grid mockup, and the two Canva template links.

## Tips

- Use free stock photos from Pexels or Unsplash if you do not have bakery photos, and mention this in your notes.
- Keep the logo in the same position on every post.
- Check your designs on your phone before submitting.

rubric.criterion: Clear hierarchy and contrast on every post
Consistent use of fonts, colours and layout across the set
Templates are locked correctly and easy for a non-designer to edit
Accurate, readable copy and correct export sizes

modules.title: Illustrator Basics: Shapes, Pen Tool and Vectors

lessons.title: Your First Hour in Illustrator: Artboards, Shapes and Pathfinder
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Illustrator creates vector graphics, built from mathematical paths, so they scale to any size without blurring.
- Artboards are your pages; you can have many in one file, such as a logo, a business card and a social icon.
- Every shape has a fill and a stroke; press X to switch between them and Shift+X to swap their colours.
- The Shape Builder tool and the Pathfinder panel let you combine and cut simple shapes into complex icons.
- Use the Selection tool (V) to move whole objects and the Direct Selection tool (A) to edit individual anchor points.

## Transcript
Canva is fantastic for fast social content, but when a client needs a logo, an icon set or a print-ready packaging label, you need Illustrator. Do not be scared by all the panels. Today we only need about five tools.

Create a new document. Choose the Print or Web preset, and notice the Artboards option. An artboard is like a page. I usually make one file per client with several artboards: logo, logo variations, business card, and a social media icon.

Now press M for the Rectangle tool and draw a shape. On the right, in the Properties panel, you will see Fill and Stroke. Fill is the inside colour, stroke is the outline. Press X to switch which one you are editing, and Shift plus X to swap them. Hold Shift while drawing to get a perfect square or circle.

Here is where the magic starts. Draw a circle and a smaller circle overlapping it, the way you would draw a crescent moon. Select both, press Shift plus M for the Shape Builder tool, then hold Alt and click on the overlapping part. It disappears, and you have a crescent. Perfect for an Eid post or a night-market logo.

The Pathfinder panel, under Window, does similar jobs with buttons: Unite, Minus Front, Intersect, Exclude. Try making a simple chai cup icon: a rounded rectangle for the cup, a circle for the handle, then Minus Front a smaller circle to hollow the handle. Unite them, and you have a clean, scalable icon.

Last, the two selection tools. The black arrow, V, moves whole objects. The white arrow, A, selects individual anchor points so you can reshape them. Dekho, ninety percent of beginner frustration in Illustrator is using the wrong arrow. Once you get this, everything else feels much easier.

lessons.title: The Pen Tool Without Tears
lessons.content:
## Key points
- The pen tool draws paths with anchor points; a click makes a sharp corner and a click-and-drag makes a smooth curve.
- Use as few anchor points as possible: fewer points mean smoother curves and cleaner files.
- Place anchor points at the extremes of a curve (top, bottom, left, right) for the most natural shapes.
- Hold Alt while dragging a handle to break it and turn a smooth point into a corner.
- Practise by tracing simple shapes and logos on a locked, faded image layer.

## Transcript
Every designer I know remembers their first week with the pen tool. Mine involved a lot of tea and some bad words in Bengali. So if it feels hard, you are completely normal. Let us break it down.

Press P for the pen tool. Click once, move the mouse, and click again. You have drawn a straight line between two anchor points. Click again and again and you get sharp corners. Click back on the first point and the path closes into a shape.

Now the important part: curves. Instead of just clicking, click and drag. Two handles come out of the point. These handles control the direction and depth of the curve. Longer handles mean a rounder curve. Drag in the direction you want the path to travel next.

Here is the rule that changed everything for me. Put anchor points at the extremes of the curve: the very top of an arch, the very bottom of a loop. Not in the middle of a slope. If you are tracing the letter O, you need only four points: top, right, bottom, left. Beginners put twenty points on a circle and it comes out wobbly.

What if you want a curve, then a sharp corner? Like the top of a leaf or the tip of a paan? After drawing the curved point, hold Alt and drag the handle. That breaks it, so the next segment can go in a completely different direction.

How to practise? Place a simple image, like a sketch of a mango or a logo, then lower its opacity to about 30% and lock its layer. Make a new layer on top and trace it with the pen tool. Do this for ten minutes a day for one week. Honestly, that is all it takes. By Sunday your curves will look smooth and confident.

Chalo, pause the video now and trace a leaf before moving on.

lessons.title: Vectors vs Raster, and Exporting the Right Files
lessons.content:
## Vector and raster: what is the difference?

**Raster** images (JPG, PNG, WebP) are made of pixels. Zoom in far enough and you see little squares. They are perfect for photographs but get blurry when you enlarge them.

**Vector** graphics (AI, SVG, EPS, PDF) are made of paths and points described by maths. You can scale a vector logo from a visiting card to a 20-foot shop hoarding and it stays perfectly sharp.

> Tip: Logos should always be designed as vectors. If a client sends you their logo as a blurry WhatsApp JPG, offer to redraw it in Illustrator. It is a quick, paid job.

## Before you export: a clean-up checklist

1. **Outline your fonts** for final logo files: select the text and use Type, Create Outlines. The client's printer may not have your font installed. Keep an editable copy too.
2. **Expand strokes** if the logo will be resized a lot (Object, Expand), so line thickness scales correctly.
3. **Delete stray points**: Object, Path, Clean Up removes empty text boxes and lonely anchor points.
4. **Fit artboard to artwork**: Object, Artboards, Fit to Artwork Bounds, so there is no awkward empty space.

## Which file for which job?

### SVG
Best for websites and apps. Tiny file size, crisp at every size. Use File, Export, Export As, and choose SVG.

### PDF
Best for printers and for sharing with clients who do not have Illustrator. Use File, Save As, Adobe PDF, and pick the **High Quality Print** or **PDF/X-1a** preset when it is going to a press.

### PNG
Best for social media, presentations and WhatsApp. Supports transparent backgrounds. Export at 2x or 3x for sharp results on phones.

### JPG
Best for photos and posters without transparency. Smaller than PNG but no transparent background.

## RGB vs CMYK

- **RGB** is for screens: Instagram, websites, presentations.
- **CMYK** is for printing: flyers, banners, visiting cards, packaging.

Switch with File, Document Colour Mode. Bright neon greens and electric blues often look dull in CMYK, so always warn clients that printed colours can differ slightly from the screen.

## A naming system clients love

Use names that explain themselves:

- `gulaab-oven-logo-primary-colour.svg`
- `gulaab-oven-logo-white.png`
- `gulaab-oven-logo-print-cmyk.pdf`

Group them into folders named **Print**, **Web** and **Social**. A tidy delivery folder makes you look far more professional than a single ZIP of mystery files.

modules.title: Client Work: Briefs, Revisions, Delivery and Pricing

lessons.title: Reading a Brief and Asking the Right Questions
lessons.content:
## Why briefs matter

Most design disputes are not about design. They are about **expectations that were never written down**. A client says "make a poster for our sale", you deliver something lovely, and they say "but we wanted it for the newspaper, not Instagram". A good brief prevents this.

## What a good brief covers

Many small clients will not send you a brief at all. They will send a WhatsApp voice note. Your job is to turn that into a written brief using a few questions.

### 1. The goal
- What should this design make people **do**? Visit the shop, call, order online, attend an event?
- How will you know it worked?

### 2. The audience
- Who is it for? College students, families, corporate buyers?
- Which language should the copy be in: English, Hindi, Bengali, or a mix?

### 3. Deliverables and sizes
- Exactly which items? "One A3 poster, one Instagram post, one Story" is a brief. "Some posters" is not.
- Where will it appear: print, Instagram, WhatsApp Status, a newspaper ad?

### 4. Content
- Who provides the text, logo and photos?
- Are prices, dates and phone numbers final?

### 5. Style
- Ask for two or three **examples they like** and one they dislike. This saves hours of guessing.
- Any brand colours or fonts already in use?

### 6. Timeline and approvals
- When is the final deadline? When is the print or posting date?
- Who gives final approval? The owner, or their son who "knows Instagram"?

> Tip: Always ask who the final decision-maker is. Many revision loops happen because a second person sees the design only at the end.

## Turn it into a one-page summary

After the call, send a short written summary on WhatsApp or email:

1. Project and goal in one line
2. Deliverables with sizes
3. Content the client will send, and by when
4. Number of revision rounds included
5. Price, advance amount and deadline

Ask the client to reply "Confirmed". This simple message protects you if the scope changes later.

## Red flags

- "Just make something nice, you are the designer." Ask for references anyway.
- "Can you do a free sample first?" Offer a paid mini-task or show your portfolio instead.
- No clear decision-maker or deadline.

Clients who answer your questions properly are usually the clients who pay on time. Treat the brief as the first step of the design, not paperwork before it.

lessons.title: Handling Revisions and Delivering Files Professionally
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Include a fixed number of revision rounds (usually two) in every quote and charge for extra rounds.
- Collect all feedback for one round in a single message instead of reacting to every WhatsApp text separately.
- Share watermarked or low-resolution previews until the final payment is received.
- Deliver final files in organised folders (Print, Web, Social) with clear file names and a short usage note.
- Close every project with a thank-you message and a request for a testimonial or Google review.

## Transcript
Let me tell you about a mehendi artist in Howrah I designed for early in my career. I said "unlimited changes" because I wanted the job. Thirty-one versions later, we were changing the shade of green for the fourth time. I earned maybe ₹40 an hour. Please, learn from my mistake.

Rule one: revision rounds go in the quote. I include two rounds. A round means the client gives all their feedback at once, I make the changes, and send it back. A third round is charged, usually ₹300 to ₹800 depending on the job. When you state this upfront, clients actually become more thoughtful with their feedback.

Rule two: consolidate feedback. Clients love sending one change at a time: "Make the logo bigger." Ten minutes later: "Also change the date." I reply politely: "Got it! Please send all changes for this round together and I will update everything in one go." It saves both of you time.

Rule three: when feedback is vague, like "make it pop", ask a follow-up question. Do they mean brighter colours, bigger headline, or more contrast? Show two small options if needed.

Rule four: protect your work. Until the balance payment arrives via UPI or Razorpay, I share previews as low-resolution JPGs with a light watermark. This is normal and professional, not rude.

Finally, delivery. Dekho, delivery is where you look like a studio instead of a student. I share a Google Drive folder with three subfolders: Print, Web and Social. Files are named clearly, like "diwali-poster-01-a3-print.pdf". I add a short text note explaining which file to use where.

After delivery, send a thank-you message and ask for a short testimonial or a Google review. Those reviews will win you your next three clients.

lessons.title: Pricing a Festive Diwali Poster Pack
lessons.content:
## Festivals are peak season

From Navratri to Diwali, every sweet shop, jeweller, salon and coaching centre wants festive creatives. Demand is high and deadlines are tight, which makes it the best time for beginners to earn, as long as you price properly.

## Three ways to price

### Per piece
Simple for clients to understand: "₹500 per Instagram post". The risk is underpricing complex pieces.

### Per pack
Bundle related items: "Diwali Pack: 5 posters for ₹3,500". Clients feel they are getting value, and you plan the work as one system, which is faster.

### Per hour
Useful for open-ended edits, but small business owners rarely like hourly billing. Use it internally to check your pack price makes sense.

## Working out your pack price

Let us price a **5-poster Diwali pack** for a sweet shop in Lucknow. Deliverables: five Instagram posts at 1080x1350, each also resized into a Story, plus one A4 print poster for the counter.

1. **Estimate hours.** Brief and moodboard: 1 hour. First design and system: 3 hours. Remaining four posts: 4 hours. Resizes: 1.5 hours. Print poster: 1.5 hours. Two revision rounds: 2 hours. Total: about **13 hours**.
2. **Choose an hourly target.** As a beginner with a portfolio, ₹250 to ₹400 per hour is reasonable. At ₹300, that is ₹3,900.
3. **Add a rush factor** if the client wants it within 48 hours: 25 to 50% extra.
4. **Round to a clean number.** Quote **₹3,999**, or offer two tiers.

> Tip: Offer tiers. Clients like choosing, and many pick the middle option.

- **Basic, ₹2,499:** 3 posts, no Stories
- **Standard, ₹3,999:** 5 posts + Stories + A4 print poster
- **Premium, ₹6,499:** Standard + 3 editable Canva templates + a short animated Reel cover

## Payment terms

- Take **50% advance** before starting, via UPI or a Razorpay payment link.
- Balance before final high-resolution files.
- State revision rounds and extra charges in writing.
- Mention that stock images or paid fonts, if needed, are billed separately.

## Do not compete only on price

On Instagram and freelance platforms you will always find someone offering posters for ₹99. Do not chase that. Instead, sell **reliability and results**: on-time delivery before the festival, files that print correctly, and designs that bring customers to the shop. Clients who value that will happily pay ₹3,999 and come back for Holi, Eid and Christmas.

assignment.brief:
## The client

**Mishti Mahal** is a 40-year-old sweet shop in Kolkata's Gariahat, now run by the founder's grandson. They want to announce Diwali gift boxes (₹499, ₹999 and ₹1,999) and take orders through WhatsApp Business. Tone: festive and premium, not cluttered.

## Your task

### Part 1: Brief and quote
Write a one-page brief summary (goal, audience, deliverables, content, timeline, revision rounds) and a **tiered quote** in ₹ with payment terms.

### Part 2: Design
1. In Illustrator, create a simple vector diya or rangoli motif and export it as SVG and PNG.
2. In Canva, use that motif to design **5 Instagram posts** at 1080x1350:
   - Diwali greeting
   - Three gift box posts, one per price point
   - "Order on WhatsApp" post with the ordering steps and last order date
3. Resize **one** post into a Story and **one** into an A4 print poster (CMYK PDF).

### Part 3: Delivery
Organise the files into Print, Web and Social folders with clear names, and write the WhatsApp delivery message you would send the client.

## Deliverable

A **link** to a Google Drive folder or Behance project containing the brief, the quote, all design files and the delivery message.

## Tips

- Use one festive accent colour, not five. Let gold or marigold be the 10%.
- Make sure prices and the WhatsApp number are readable in two seconds.
- Keep the motif, logo position and fonts consistent across every poster.

modules.title: Discovery: Understanding the Business Before the Logo

lessons.title: Why Identity Projects Start With Questions, Not Sketches
lessons.content:
## Key points
- A brand identity is a system that expresses a business's personality, not just a logo.
- Discovery uncovers the audience, competitors and values so design choices have reasons behind them.
- A strategy summary approved by the client makes logo feedback objective instead of personal taste.
- Charging for discovery positions you as a partner and raises the value of the whole project.

## Transcript
When a client tells me "I just need a logo", I smile, because that is almost never true. A Pune café owner does not need a logo. She needs college students to choose her café over the three chains on the same road.

That is why I never open Illustrator in week one. Discovery comes first: a 60 to 90 minute conversation, plus some homework for the client. Who are your customers? Who are your competitors? What do you want people to feel when they walk in? If your brand were a person, how would they talk?

From this, I write a one-page strategy summary and ask the client to approve it. Dekho, this is the secret. Later, when they say "I don't like this purple", I can ask, "Does it feel youthful and welcoming, like we agreed?" The conversation becomes about goals, not taste.

And yes, discovery is paid. It is part of the project fee, and it is why my identity projects cost ₹25,000 and not ₹2,500.

lessons.title: Running a Discovery Session and Writing the Strategy Summary
lessons.content:
## Before the session

Send a short questionnaire on Google Forms a few days ahead, so the meeting is a discussion, not an interview.

## Questions that matter

- **Business:** What do you sell, and what makes you different from nearby options?
- **Audience:** Who is your ideal customer? Age, location, budget, where they spend time online.
- **Competitors:** Name three. What do you like and dislike about their branding?
- **Personality:** Pick three adjectives. Also ask for three words the brand should **never** be.
- **Practical needs:** Signage, packaging, Instagram, WhatsApp Business, uniforms?

> Tip: Ask "What would a customer say about you to a friend?" The answers are often better than any tagline.

## The strategy summary

Condense everything into one page:

1. **Positioning line:** "For working professionals in Baner, Kaapi Theory is the quiet café where you actually get work done."
2. **Audience snapshot** in two or three lines.
3. **Personality:** three adjectives, plus the "never" words.
4. **Competitor gap:** what everyone else looks like, and where you can stand out.
5. **Touchpoints** the identity must work on.

Get written approval before you sketch anything.

lessons.title: From Sketches to Shortlist: Exploring Concepts
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Start with fast pencil sketches and aim for quantity, at least 30 to 50 rough ideas.
- Explore different routes: wordmark, lettermark, symbol plus wordmark, and emblem.
- Test every shortlisted idea in black and white at very small sizes before adding colour.
- Present two or three strong concepts shown in context, never ten options.

## Transcript
Chalo, notebooks out. The best logo ideas I have ever had came from page four of my sketchbook, not page one. The first ideas are always the obvious ones: a coffee cup for a café, a house for a homestay.

So I set a timer for 30 minutes and push for quantity. Wordmarks, lettermarks, symbols, emblems. For a Kochi homestay, I might explore the shape of a Chinese fishing net, a coconut frond, the curve of a backwater boat, and a simple monogram.

Then I pick around eight and redraw them in Illustrator, in black only. Colour hides weak ideas. I shrink each one to the size of a WhatsApp profile picture. If it turns into a blob, it goes.

Finally, I present just two or three concepts, each shown on real mockups: the signboard, an Instagram profile, a coffee cup or a room key tag. Clients judge logos in context, so show them in context.

lessons.title: Refining the Logo and Building Variations
lessons.content:
## Refinement is where quality shows

Once the client picks a direction, the real craft begins.

### Optical adjustments
- **Kerning:** adjust spacing letter by letter. Pairs like "AV" or "To" usually need tightening.
- **Overshoot:** round letters and shapes should extend slightly beyond flat ones so they look the same size.
- **Stroke consistency:** keep line weights intentional and consistent.

### Clean construction
Use as few anchor points as possible, align key shapes to a grid, and make sure there are no stray or overlapping paths.

## The logo system

One logo is not enough. Deliver:

1. **Primary logo:** the full version for signage and the website.
2. **Secondary layout:** horizontal or stacked, for tight spaces.
3. **Icon or monogram:** for Instagram and WhatsApp profile pictures and favicons.
4. **Monochrome versions:** one-colour black and white for stamps, embossing and newspaper ads.

> Tip: Define a **minimum size** for each version, for example 24px for the primary logo on screens.

Export every version as SVG, PNG and PDF, in RGB and CMYK.

lessons.title: Assignment: Logo System for a Kochi Homestay
lessons.content: Identity clients pay for a system, not a single file. This assignment takes you from strategy to a refined, presentation-ready logo family, exactly as you would deliver it to a paying client.

assignment.brief:
## The client

**Kaayal Stays** is a four-room heritage homestay in Fort Kochi run by a retired couple. Guests are mostly international backpackers and young Indian couples. Personality: calm, warm, rooted in Kerala. Never: flashy, corporate.

## Your task

1. Write a one-page strategy summary (positioning line, audience, personality, competitor gap, touchpoints).
2. Sketch at least 30 rough ideas and photograph your best sketch page.
3. Develop **two concepts** in black and white, then refine **one** in colour.
4. Build the system: primary logo, secondary layout, icon, and monochrome versions.
5. Show the logo on three mockups: entrance signboard, Instagram profile, and a room key tag.

## Deliverable

A **link** to a Behance project or PDF presentation with the strategy, sketches, concepts, final system and mockups.

## Tips

- Test the icon at 32px before finalising.
- Explain in one or two lines how each concept connects back to the strategy.

modules.title: Brand Guidelines That Clients Actually Use

lessons.title: What Goes Into a Brand Guidelines Document
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Brand guidelines explain how to use the identity correctly so it stays consistent without you.
- For local businesses, a focused 10 to 15 page PDF is more useful than a 60 page manual.
- Cover logo usage, clear space, colour codes, typography, imagery style and real application examples.
- Include a short "do and don't" page, because that is the page clients and printers actually look at.

## Transcript
Here is something painful. Six months after delivering a beautiful identity, you walk past the client's shop and the signboard has your logo stretched sideways in a different font. It happens because nobody told the printer the rules.

Brand guidelines fix that. But for a local bakery or homestay, do not make a 60 page corporate manual. Nobody will read it. I make a 10 to 15 page PDF.

What goes in? The logo and its variations, with clear space and minimum sizes. Colour codes in HEX, RGB and CMYK. The two typefaces, with sizes for headings and body. A few lines on photography style. Then real applications: Instagram post, visiting card, signboard. And the most important page: do and don't. Don't stretch, don't recolour, don't add shadows.

Dekho, that one page saves more brands than all the others combined.

lessons.title: Writing Clear Rules: Colour, Type and Logo Usage
lessons.content:
## Write for non-designers

Your guidelines will be read by the owner, their nephew managing Instagram, and the local printer. Write simply and show examples.

## Logo usage
- **Clear space:** define it using part of the logo, such as "the height of the letter K on all sides".
- **Minimum size:** for example 25mm in print and 120px on screen for the primary logo.
- **Backgrounds:** show which version to use on light, dark and photo backgrounds.

## Colour
List every colour with **HEX, RGB and CMYK** values, and a Pantone reference if the budget allows. State the proportions, such as "Backwater Teal is the main colour; Turmeric Yellow is only for highlights".

## Typography
- Name the fonts and where to download them (Google Fonts is ideal for small clients).
- Give a clear hierarchy: headline, subheading, body.
- Suggest a fallback system font for Word and WhatsApp documents.

> Tip: Include ready-to-use Canva templates with the guidelines. Clients follow rules more easily when the rules are already built in.

## Do and don't
Show 6 to 8 visual examples: stretched logo, wrong colours, busy photo backgrounds, added effects. Mark each with a clear tick or cross.

lessons.content: Final check: make sure your guidelines will survive contact with real printers and real Instagram managers.
