lessons.title: Why viewers swipe away in the first two seconds
lessons.content:
## Key points
- On Reels and Shorts, the first one to two seconds decide whether the video gets watched or swiped, so the edit must earn attention immediately.
- Every video, even a 30-second reel, needs a simple story shape: a hook, a build-up of value, and a payoff that matches the promise.
- Retention graphs in YouTube Studio and Instagram Insights show exactly where viewers drop, and editors should study them after every upload.
- Cutting dead air, filler words and slow intros is the single fastest way to improve retention for most creators.
- Your job as an editor is not to show off effects; it is to make the creator's message land as clearly and quickly as possible.

## Transcript
Hi everyone, Farhan here. Before we touch Premiere Pro or CapCut, I want to talk about the one thing that separates editors who get paid ₹500 a reel from editors who get paid ₹5,000 a reel. It is not plugins. It is understanding attention.

Dekho, when someone is scrolling Instagram at 11 pm, their thumb is moving faster than their brain. You get maybe one and a half seconds. If the first frame is the creator saying "Hi guys, so today I wanted to talk about...", that reel is already dead. The viewer is gone.

So every edit I make starts with one question: what is the promise of this video, and how fast can I show it? If a finance creator is explaining how to save ₹10,000 a month on a ₹40,000 salary, I want that number on screen in the first second. Not the intro, not the logo. The promise.

After the hook, we build. Each section should give one piece of value and then move on. And at the end, we pay off the promise, so the viewer feels the time was worth it. Hook, build, payoff. Even a 20-second reel follows this.

Now here is a habit that changed my career. After a video goes live, open the retention graph. On YouTube Studio it is under Analytics, and on Instagram it is in the reel insights. Look for the steep drops. Usually you will find a slow sentence, a pause, or a section where nothing changes visually. That is feedback on your edit, free of cost.

Chalo, in the next lesson we will look at specific hook formulas you can use tomorrow with any creator.

lessons.title: Hook formulas that work for Indian creators
lessons.content:
## What a hook actually is

A hook is the first one to three seconds of a video, combining **what is said**, **what is shown** and **what is written on screen**. Most beginners only think about the spoken line. Strong editors stack all three so the viewer gets the promise even with the sound off, which is how a large share of people watch Reels in public places, offices and metro rides.

## Five hook formulas you can reuse

### 1. The result first
Show the end result before explaining how. A food creator in Jaipur shows the finished dal baati plate, then cuts back to the raw ingredients. On screen text: **"Restaurant-style dal baati at home in 30 minutes"**.

### 2. The bold number
Numbers are specific and believable. "I paid off ₹3 lakh of education loan in 14 months" beats "How I paid off my loan" every time. Put the number in large text in the first frame.

### 3. The mistake callout
"Stop doing this in your resume" or "You are using UPI wrong". People hate being wrong, so they stay to check. Use this carefully; the video must deliver a real mistake, not clickbait.

### 4. The pattern interrupt
Start mid-action: a door slamming, a laptop closing, a quick zoom on the creator's face. Movement in the first frame stops the thumb.

### 5. The relatable situation
"When your mummy asks what you actually do as a freelancer..." Relatability works brilliantly for Hinglish comedy and lifestyle creators.

## How to edit a hook

- **Cut the first sentence the creator recorded.** It is almost always a warm-up. The real hook is often sentence two or three.
- **Move the best line to the top.** It is completely fine to take a line from the middle of the video and open with it, then continue normally.
- **Add text within the first 10 frames.** Keep it to six to eight words, high contrast, inside the safe area so the Instagram UI does not cover it.
- **Add motion.** A slight punch-in (scale from 100% to 110%) or a quick b-roll flash keeps the first second alive.

> Tip: Write three alternative hooks for every reel you edit and send them to the creator as options. Clients remember the editor who thinks about growth, not just cuts.

## Checklist before you export

1. Does the first frame make sense with sound off?
2. Is the promise clear within two seconds?
3. Is there zero dead air before the first word?
4. Does the ending actually deliver what the hook promised?

If all four are a yes, your hook is ready.

lessons.title: Pacing: controlling the rhythm of an edit
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Pacing is how often something changes on screen: a cut, a zoom, a b-roll shot, a text pop or a sound effect.
- Short-form content usually needs a visual change every two to four seconds, while long-form YouTube can breathe more but still needs variety.
- Remove pauses, breaths and filler words, but leave tiny gaps after punchlines and important points so they land.
- Change pace deliberately: speed up during lists and setup, slow down during the emotional or key moment.
- Music tempo should support the pace; cutting on the beat makes even simple edits feel professional.

## Transcript
Okay, let us talk about pacing, which is honestly the thing creators notice most even if they cannot name it. When a creator says "the edit feels slow", they mean the pacing.

Pacing is simply how often something changes. A new cut, a zoom, a b-roll clip, a caption pop, a sound effect. Each change resets the viewer's attention. For a Reel, I aim for some visual change every two to four seconds. For a 12-minute YouTube video, you can stay on a shot longer, maybe eight to ten seconds, but not a full minute of the same frame.

The first step is always the rough cut. I go through the talking-head footage and remove every "umm", every long breath, every repeated sentence. In Premiere I use the Razor tool with the C key and ripple delete with Shift plus Delete. In CapCut, you split and delete, and there is also an auto-remove pauses option, but always check it manually because it sometimes cuts words in half.

But here is the mistake beginners make. They cut so tight that the video feels like a machine gun. No space to breathe. When the creator delivers a punchline or a big number, leave five to eight frames of silence after it. Let it land. Then move.

Think of pace like a song. Verses are faster, the chorus hits harder. In a video, setup and lists can be quick, with jump cuts and punch-ins. The key insight, the emotional moment, deserves a slower shot, maybe a gentle zoom.

One more trick: cut on the beat of the music. Put markers on the beat in Premiere by pressing M while the music plays, then snap your cuts to them. Even simple edits suddenly feel polished. Practice this with any trending audio and you will feel the difference.

lessons.title: Quiz: hooks, story and pacing
lessons.content: Let us check whether the ideas about attention, hooks and pacing have clicked. Think like an editor who wants the creator's reel to perform.

questions.prompt: A creator's raw footage starts with "Hi guys, welcome back, so today..." followed by a strong line about saving ₹10,000 a month. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the intro because it builds a personal connection
Cut the warm-up and open with the saving line plus matching on-screen text
Add a logo animation before the intro to look professional
Speed up the intro to 2x so it is shorter

questions.explanation: The promise must appear in the first one to two seconds. Warm-up lines lose viewers; the strongest line should open the video, supported by text for sound-off viewers.

questions.prompt: Why should hook text be readable with the sound off?

options.text: Because Instagram removes audio from Reels after 24 hours
Because many people scroll with sound muted, so the promise must work visually too
Because music copyright rules require text

questions.explanation: A large share of viewers watch without sound in public. Stacking spoken, visual and written hooks makes sure the promise lands either way.

questions.prompt: A creator says the edit "feels tiring" even though every pause is removed. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Leave a few frames of breathing room after key points and punchlines
Add more transitions between every cut

questions.explanation: Cutting too tight removes the space that lets important moments land. Good pacing varies speed and leaves small gaps after key beats.

questions.prompt: Where should you look to find exactly which part of your edit is losing viewers?

options.text: The number of likes on the post
The audience retention graph in YouTube Studio or Instagram insights

questions.explanation: Retention graphs show second-by-second drop-offs, pointing to slow lines or visually static sections in your edit.

questions.prompt: In a 40-second educational reel, what is a sensible rhythm of visual change?

options.text: One static shot for the full 40 seconds
A cut, zoom, b-roll or text change roughly every two to four seconds
A new transition effect every half second

questions.explanation: Short-form content benefits from frequent but purposeful changes every few seconds. Constant effects every half second feel chaotic.

modules.title: Editing Workflow in Premiere Pro & CapCut

lessons.title: Project setup: folders, sequences and proxies
lessons.content:
## Key points
- A consistent folder structure (Footage, Audio, Music, Graphics, Exports, Project) saves hours when a creator asks for changes weeks later.
- Create a 1080x1920 vertical sequence for Reels and Shorts, and 1920x1080 horizontal for YouTube, matching the frame rate of the footage.
- Proxies are lightweight copies of heavy 4K files that make editing smooth on a normal laptop, and Premiere swaps back to full quality on export.
- In CapCut desktop, set the canvas ratio to 9:16 before importing so your framing decisions are correct from the start.
- Name files and versions clearly, like "CreatorName_Reel12_v2", so revisions never get mixed up.

## Transcript
Chalo, let us open the software. I will show this in Premiere Pro, and I will mention the CapCut equivalent as we go, because many of you will start on CapCut and that is perfectly fine. I have edited reels that crossed 10 million views entirely in CapCut.

First, before opening any app, I create a folder for the project. Inside it: Footage, Audio, Music, Graphics, Exports and Project. Every single client gets this structure. When a creator messages me two months later saying "bhai, can you change the caption on reel 12", I find it in ten seconds.

Now in Premiere, create a new project and save it inside the Project folder. Import footage. Right-click your main clip and choose New Sequence From Clip so the frame rate matches. For a Reel, go to Sequence Settings and change the frame size to 1080 by 1920. For YouTube, keep 1920 by 1080.

Most creators shoot on phones or mirrorless cameras in 4K. On a laptop with 8GB RAM, 4K playback will stutter. So we make proxies. In the Ingest settings, tick Create Proxies and choose a low-resolution preset. Premiere edits with the light files and exports from the originals. Your laptop will thank you.

In CapCut desktop, choose the 9:16 ratio first, then import. On mobile CapCut, the ratio option is at the bottom under Format.

Last thing: versioning. Every time you send an edit, export it with a version number, like Ananya_Reel12_v1, then v2 after feedback. Never overwrite. Trust me, this habit alone makes you look like a professional.

lessons.title: Cuts, J-cuts and L-cuts explained
lessons.content:
## The basic cut

A **hard cut** simply ends one clip and starts the next. It is the most used edit in the world, and it is invisible when done well. For talking-head content, you will mostly use **jump cuts**: removing a section from the same shot so the creator seems to "jump" slightly. Jump cuts are accepted on YouTube and Reels because they keep the pace tight.

### Making jump cuts look smooth
- Alternate between the original frame and a **punch-in** (scale 110-120% on the next segment). This hides the jump and adds energy.
- Cut on a natural pause or the start of a word, never in the middle of a syllable.
- In Premiere, press `C` for the Razor tool, `V` to return to Selection, and use **Ripple Delete** (`Shift + Delete` on Windows) to close gaps automatically.

## J-cuts and L-cuts

These are named after the shape the audio and video make on the timeline.

### J-cut: audio leads
The **audio of the next clip starts before its video**. You hear the next scene before you see it. Example: while the creator is still on screen, you start hearing pressure cooker whistles, and then cut to the kitchen. It pulls the viewer forward.

### L-cut: audio lingers
The **audio of the current clip continues after the video changes**. The creator keeps talking about their Goa trip while the picture cuts to beach b-roll. This is the most common use of b-roll in YouTube content.

### How to make them in Premiere Pro
1. Unlink audio and video if needed, or hold `Alt` and drag just the audio or video edge.
2. Use the **Rolling Edit** tool (`N`) to move the cut point on one track without changing the overall duration.
3. For an L-cut, extend the A-roll audio under the next clip; for a J-cut, pull the next clip's audio earlier.

### How to make them in CapCut
Select the clip, tap **Extract audio** (or use the separated audio track on desktop), then trim the audio and video edges independently.

## When to use what

- **Hard/jump cuts**: talking-head reels, fast tips, lists.
- **L-cuts**: covering explanations with b-roll, vlogs, interviews.
- **J-cuts**: transitions between locations or topics, building anticipation.

> Tip: Watch any good documentary on YouTube with headphones and notice how often you hear the next scene before you see it. Once you notice J-cuts, you will see them everywhere.

## Common beginner mistakes

1. Cutting mid-word, which creates an unnatural click.
2. Using a fancy transition (spin, glitch) to hide a bad cut instead of fixing the timing.
3. Forgetting to add a 2-frame audio crossfade at cuts, which causes small pops.

Master these three cut types and you can edit eighty percent of creator content without a single transition preset.

lessons.title: B-roll that earns its place
lessons.content:
## Key points
- B-roll is any footage that supports what the creator is saying, such as screen recordings, product shots, stock clips or reaction memes.
- Good b-roll shows the specific thing being said, not a generic visual, so match it to keywords in the script.
- Use b-roll to hide jump cuts, illustrate numbers or steps, and reset attention every few seconds.
- Free sources like Pexels, Pixabay and the creator's own phone gallery are usually enough; always check licences for brand work.
- Keep most b-roll clips between one and three seconds in Reels, and slightly longer in YouTube videos.

## Transcript
Let me tell you a story. One of my first clients was a Pune-based tech creator. His videos were good but retention was low. I added b-roll, but generic stuff: someone typing on a laptop, city timelapses. Retention barely moved.

Then I changed my approach. When he said "open your Razorpay dashboard", I showed a screen recording of the Razorpay dashboard. When he said "I was earning only ₹18,000 at my first job", I put a quick shot of a salary slip with the number blurred except ₹18,000. Retention jumped. Why? Because the b-roll was specific. It proved what he was saying.

So here is my rule: read the script, underline the nouns and numbers, and find a visual for each important one. Product, place, app, amount, person.

Where do you get b-roll? First, ask the creator. Most creators have hundreds of clips in their phone gallery and do not realise they are useful. Second, screen recordings, which you can make yourself. Third, free stock from Pexels or Pixabay. For brand deals, check the licence, because some brands are strict.

In Reels, keep b-roll short, one to three seconds, often placed on an upper track over the A-roll with the creator's audio continuing underneath. That is the L-cut we just learned. On YouTube, you can hold b-roll longer, especially during explanations.

One warning: do not cover the creator's face during emotional or funny moments. People follow creators for their face and expressions. B-roll supports the creator; it does not replace them.

lessons.title: Captions people actually read
lessons.content:
## Why captions matter

Captions are not just accessibility, though that matters too. On Reels and Shorts, captions **keep the eyes busy**, help sound-off viewers follow along, and make Hinglish or fast speech easier to understand across India's many language audiences.

## Generating captions quickly

### In Premiere Pro
1. Open the **Text** panel and choose **Transcribe sequence**. Pick English or Hindi as the language.
2. Click **Create captions**, then set maximum characters per line around 20-25 for vertical video.
3. Correct the transcript manually. Auto-transcription often gets names, brand words and Hinglish wrong.

### In CapCut
Use **Text > Auto captions**. CapCut handles Hindi and English well and has ready-made animated styles. Again, proofread every line.

## Style rules that work

- **Short lines.** Two to four words per caption on Reels. Viewers read in quick bursts.
- **High contrast.** White or yellow text with a black stroke or soft shadow. Avoid thin fonts.
- **Safe area.** Keep captions in the middle third of the frame. The bottom 20% is covered by the caption, likes and username on Instagram.
- **Highlight keywords.** Colour or scale up the important word: numbers, brand names, the "aha" word.
- **One font family.** Bold sans-serif fonts like Montserrat, Poppins or The Bold Font are safe choices. Consistency across a creator's videos builds brand recall.

> Tip: Build a caption preset for each client. In Premiere, save it as a **Track Style**; in CapCut, save it to favourites. Your third reel for the same creator will take half the time.

## Hinglish and Hindi captions

Ask the creator which script their audience prefers. Many Hinglish creators prefer **Roman script** ("kya scene hai") because their audience reads it faster than Devanagari on a phone. Others targeting Hindi heartland audiences prefer Devanagari. Never guess; it is a branding decision.

## Proofreading checklist

1. Brand names spelled exactly as the brand writes them.
2. Numbers match what is said, including ₹ and lakh/crore formatting.
3. No caption hides the creator's mouth or a product being shown.
4. Captions are synced to within a few frames of the spoken word.

Clean captions are often what clients notice first. A single spelling mistake in a brand deal can cost a creator money, so treat captions as part of the edit, not an afterthought.

lessons.title: Assignment: edit a 45-second reel
lessons.content: Real creator work starts with raw, messy footage: pauses, repeated lines, no b-roll. This assignment simulates your first paid reel, so treat it exactly as you would treat a client's file.

assignment.brief:
## Your task
Record or source 2-3 minutes of talking-head footage (yourself, a friend, or a creator who gives permission) on any topic, for example "3 apps every college student should use". Edit it into a **45-second vertical Reel**.

## Steps
1. Set up the project folder structure and a 1080x1920 sequence.
2. Do a rough cut: remove filler words, pauses and repeated lines.
3. Rewrite the opening so the hook lands in the first two seconds, with on-screen text.
4. Add at least **4 specific b-roll shots** (screen recordings, gallery clips or stock).
5. Use at least one **L-cut or J-cut** and alternate punch-ins on jump cuts.
6. Add styled, proofread captions inside the safe area.
7. Export and upload as an unlisted YouTube Short or a Google Drive link.

## Deliverable
A link to the final reel plus a 3-4 line note explaining your hook choice and where you used the L/J-cut.

## Tips
- Watch it once on your phone with the sound off before submitting.
- If you cannot decide between two hooks, export both and mention it in your note, just like you would for a client.

rubric.criterion: Hook lands in the first two seconds with clear on-screen text
Pacing: tight rough cut with purposeful punch-ins and breathing room
Specific, well-timed b-roll including an L-cut or J-cut
Captions are accurate, readable and inside the safe area

lessons.title: Audio first: levels, noise and music ducking
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Viewers forgive average visuals but quickly leave videos with bad audio, so clean voice audio is the top priority.
- Keep dialogue peaking around -6 dB to -3 dB on the meters and aim for roughly -14 LUFS integrated loudness for YouTube and Reels.
- Use noise reduction gently (Premiere's Essential Sound "Reduce Noise" or CapCut's "Reduce noise") to remove fan hum without making the voice sound robotic.
- Duck background music 15-20 dB under the voice so every word stays clear.
- Add small crossfades at audio cuts to avoid clicks and pops.

## Transcript
I will say something that surprises a lot of new editors: audio matters more than video. A slightly soft image is fine. But if the voice is echoey, too quiet, or the music drowns the words, people swipe immediately.

So after my rough cut, I fix audio before anything else. In Premiere, select the dialogue clips, open the Essential Sound panel, and tag them as Dialogue. Then use Loudness, Auto-Match. It brings the voice to a standard level. On the audio meters, I want speech peaking somewhere around minus six to minus three dB. Never touching zero, because that clips and distorts.

Most Indian creators record at home. Ceiling fan, cooler, traffic, pressure cooker from the kitchen. Under Repair in Essential Sound, tick Reduce Noise and start low, around 3 to 5. Too much and the voice sounds like it is underwater. In CapCut, tap the clip and use Reduce noise. Same idea, use it, then listen with headphones.

Now music. The music should support the mood, never compete with the voice. Tag music clips as Music in Essential Sound and turn on Ducking. Premiere automatically lowers the music when the creator speaks. I usually want music about 15 to 20 dB below the voice.

For the final loudness, platforms normalise to around minus 14 LUFS. You can check this using the Loudness Meter effect on the master track. If your video is much quieter, it will sound weak next to other reels.

Last tip: always add a tiny audio crossfade, two or three frames, on every cut. Ctrl plus Shift plus D in Premiere applies default transitions to selected clips. No more clicks. Listen to the whole edit once with headphones and once on phone speakers before you export.

lessons.title: Colour basics: correction before grading
lessons.content:
## Correction vs grading

**Colour correction** makes footage look natural and consistent: right exposure, accurate white balance, true skin tones. **Colour grading** adds a creative look on top, like warm and golden, or cool and moody. Always correct first. Grading badly exposed footage just makes bad footage stylish.

## A simple correction workflow in Premiere Pro

Open the **Lumetri Color** panel and work top to bottom in **Basic Correction**.

1. **White balance.** Use the eyedropper on something that should be white or grey, like a wall or a shirt. Indian homes often have warm yellow bulbs, so footage may look orange; the temperature slider fixes this.
2. **Exposure.** Adjust until the face is bright and clear without blown-out highlights.
3. **Contrast.** Add a little contrast for punch, usually +5 to +15.
4. **Highlights and shadows.** Pull highlights down if a window behind the creator is blown out; lift shadows slightly to recover detail.
5. **Saturation.** Small changes only. Over-saturated skin looks orange and fake.

Use the **Lumetri Scopes** (Waveform and Vectorscope) to check your work. On the vectorscope, skin tones of every complexion should sit near the **skin tone line**. This is the most reliable way to protect natural skin colour.

## In CapCut

Select the clip and open **Adjust**. You get temperature, tint, brightness, contrast, highlights, shadows and saturation. The same order applies. CapCut's filters are grading, not correction, so apply them after the basics, and keep filter intensity low, around 20-40%.

## Matching shots

When a creator records over two days, colour shifts between clips. In Premiere, **Color Match** under Lumetri's Color Wheels section can match one shot to a reference. Always check by eye afterwards.

## A light grade that suits most creators

- Slightly warm highlights, slightly cool shadows for a clean, modern look.
- Gentle contrast curve, not crushed blacks.
- Save it as a preset or **Adjustment Layer** so every video from the same creator looks consistent.

> Tip: Never grade on max screen brightness or night mode. Set your laptop to a neutral brightness and check the export on a phone, because most viewers will watch on one.

Good colour is mostly invisible. If nobody comments on the colour but the creator says "this looks so clean", you have done it right.

lessons.title: Export settings: Reels vs YouTube
lessons.content:
## Why export settings matter

Instagram and YouTube both re-compress your video. If you upload a poorly exported file, it gets compressed twice and looks blurry. The goal is to give each platform a clean, high-quality file in the format it expects.

## Instagram Reels

- **Resolution:** 1080x1920 (9:16 vertical).
- **Frame rate:** same as your footage, usually 30 fps (25 fps is fine if shot that way).
- **Codec:** H.264, MP4.
- **Bitrate:** VBR, target around 15-20 Mbps.
- **Audio:** AAC, 48 kHz, 320 kbps.
- **Length:** keep within Instagram's current Reel length limit, and remember shorter usually performs better.

Upload from the phone app with **"Upload at highest quality"** turned on in Instagram's media quality settings. Many creators forget this and blame the editor.

## YouTube (long-form)

- **Resolution:** 1920x1080 at minimum. Uploading in 4K (3840x2160), even from 1080p footage, often gets better compression on YouTube's side.
- **Codec:** H.264, MP4.
- **Bitrate:** around 12-16 Mbps for 1080p, 35-45 Mbps for 4K.
- **Audio:** AAC, 48 kHz, 320 kbps.

## YouTube Shorts

Same as Reels: 1080x1920 vertical. Keep important text away from the right edge and the bottom, where the buttons and title sit.

## A quick preset reference

```text
REELS / SHORTS  -> H.264 | 1080x1920 | 30 fps | VBR 1-pass 16 Mbps | AAC 320 kbps
YOUTUBE 1080p   -> H.264 | 1920x1080 | match source | VBR 1-pass 14 Mbps | AAC 320 kbps
YOUTUBE 4K      -> H.264 | 3840x2160 | match source | VBR 1-pass 40 Mbps | AAC 320 kbps
```

### Saving presets in Premiere Pro
In the Export window, set the options once, then click **Save Preset** and name it, for example "Reels_1080x1920_16Mbps". Next time, it is one click.

### Exporting in CapCut
Choose **1080p**, frame rate **30**, and on desktop set bitrate to **Higher** or a custom value. On mobile, the export menu has the same resolution and frame rate options.

> Tip: Before sending to a creator, watch the exported file once on your phone. Check that captions are not cut off, audio is in sync, and the first frame is not black.

## File naming for delivery

Use a clear name like `Ananya_Reel14_v2_FINAL.mp4` and share through Google Drive or WeTransfer, not WhatsApp, because WhatsApp compresses video heavily. If the creator insists on WhatsApp, send it as a **document** instead of a video so the quality stays intact.

lessons.title: Quiz: audio, colour and export
lessons.content: Finishing is where amateur and professional edits separate. Answer these as if a creator just sent you a complaint about their video.

questions.prompt: A creator complains their reel looks blurry on Instagram even though your edit looked sharp. What is the most likely cause to check first?

options.text: The colour grade was too warm
The file was sent over WhatsApp as a video or uploaded without the highest quality setting
The captions used the wrong font

questions.explanation: WhatsApp video compression and Instagram's default data-saving upload both reduce quality. Send files via Drive or as a WhatsApp document and enable high-quality uploads.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of working on colour?

options.text: Apply a cinematic LUT first, then fix exposure
Grade first, then correct white balance at the end
Correct white balance and exposure first, then apply a creative grade
Only use filters; correction is not needed for Reels

questions.explanation: Correction makes footage accurate and consistent; grading on top of uncorrected footage amplifies its problems.

questions.prompt: Background music keeps covering the creator's words. What is the best fix?

options.text: Duck the music 15-20 dB under the voice whenever the creator speaks
Remove all music from the video
Increase the voice to peak at 0 dB
Add more noise reduction to the voice

questions.explanation: Ducking keeps the music present but clearly under the voice. Peaking at 0 dB causes clipping and distortion.

questions.prompt: Which export setting is correct for an Instagram Reel?

options.text: 1080x1920, H.264 MP4, around 15-20 Mbps, AAC audio

questions.explanation: Reels are 9:16 vertical. H.264 MP4 at a healthy bitrate with AAC audio gives Instagram a clean file to re-compress.

modules.title: Working with Creators: Briefs, Revisions & Pricing

lessons.title: Reading a creator brief like a pro
lessons.content:
## Key points
- A good brief covers the goal of the video, target platform, length, reference videos, style rules, deadline and number of revisions.
- If a creator does not send a brief, send them a short questionnaire so expectations are clear before you start.
- Reference videos are the most valuable part of a brief; study them for pacing, caption style, music and transitions.
- Confirm the deadline in writing, including time and timezone, especially for brand deals with fixed posting dates.
- Ask for all raw files, logos, fonts and brand guidelines in one shared Google Drive folder.

## Transcript
Let us talk about the business side, because editing skill alone does not get you repeat clients. Communication does.

Most creators will not send you a proper brief. They will send a WhatsApp voice note saying "bhai, make it viral" and a Drive link. That is normal. Your job is to turn that into a clear brief.

So I always send five questions. One: what is the goal of this video? Followers, brand deal, product sales, or community? Two: which platform and what length? Three: share two or three reference videos you love. Four: any style rules, like fonts, colours, words to avoid? Five: when exactly do you need it, date and time?

The reference videos are gold. When a Bengaluru fitness creator sent me three references, I immediately understood she wanted fast cuts, bold yellow captions and phonk music. Without references, I would have guessed and wasted a revision.

For brand deals, ask for the brand's guidelines. Brands often have rules like "logo must be visible for three seconds" or "do not use competitor colours". Missing one of these can delay payment for the creator, and that will reflect on you.

Also, confirm the deadline in writing. "I will deliver v1 by Thursday 6 pm" in the WhatsApp chat. This protects both of you.

Finally, ask for everything in one Google Drive folder: raw footage, logos, fonts, music. Chasing files across chats wastes so much time. Clear briefs mean fewer revisions, happier creators, and more referrals. Most of my clients came through referrals from other creators.

lessons.title: Revisions, turnaround and feedback etiquette
lessons.content:
## Set the rules before the first edit

Unlimited revisions are the fastest way to burn out as a freelance editor. Agree on terms at the start, in writing:

- **Revisions included:** two rounds per video is standard for reels; three for long YouTube videos.
- **What counts as a revision:** changes to the existing edit, like trimming, caption fixes or music swaps. A completely new direction or new footage is a **new edit** and is charged separately.
- **Turnaround:** for example, 24-48 hours for a reel, 3-5 days for a 10-minute YouTube video, and 24 hours per revision round.

## Getting clear feedback

Vague feedback like "make it more engaging" wastes everyone's time. Make it easy for creators to be specific.

### Ask for timestamped notes
Request feedback in the format **"0:12 - remove this line"**. Tools like **Frame.io** or Google Drive comments let creators click on the exact moment and type. If they prefer WhatsApp voice notes, write down the timestamps yourself and send a summary back to confirm.

### Send numbered versions
Always label exports `v1`, `v2`, `v3`. When feedback comes in, reply with a checklist:

1. 0:04 - hook text changed to "₹500 to ₹50,000"
2. 0:18 - b-roll replaced with app screen recording
3. 0:31 - music volume lowered

This shows professionalism and avoids "I told you to change this already" arguments.

## Handling difficult feedback

- **Do not take it personally.** The creator knows their audience; you know editing. Both matter.
- **Explain your choice once, then respect their decision.** "I kept this pause so the joke lands, but happy to tighten it."
- **Push back politely on scope creep.** "Happy to do this, it is outside our two revision rounds, so it would be ₹300 extra."

> Tip: Keep a running Google Doc per client with their preferences: fonts, caption colours, words they hate, music they love. Your edits will need fewer revisions every month.

## Turnaround reality

Creators post on schedules. A reel promised for Friday evening is useless on Sunday. If you are going to be late, inform the creator **before** the deadline, with a new time. Silence is what loses clients, not a one-time delay.

## Payment terms

For new clients, ask for **50% advance via UPI** and the rest on final delivery. For monthly retainers, invoice at the start of the month. Send the final high-quality file only after payment clears; a watermarked preview is fine for review.

lessons.title: Pricing your edits per reel in ₹
lessons.content:
## Why per-reel pricing works

Creators think in content units, not hours. "How much per reel?" is the first question you will get. Per-reel pricing is easy to compare, easy to budget, and rewards you for getting faster.

## Typical market ranges in India

These are rough ranges for freelance editors and vary by city, niche and creator size:

- **Beginner (first 3-6 months, small creators):** ₹300 - ₹800 per reel.
- **Intermediate (solid portfolio, 100K+ creators):** ₹1,000 - ₹2,500 per reel.
- **Advanced (motion graphics, storytelling, million-plus creators):** ₹3,000 - ₹8,000+ per reel.
- **YouTube long-form (8-15 minutes):** ₹3,000 - ₹15,000+ per video depending on complexity.

## How to calculate your own price

1. **Estimate time.** How long does one reel take you, including revisions? Say 2.5 hours.
2. **Pick an hourly target.** If you want ₹30,000 a month working about 100 billable hours, that is ₹300 per hour.
3. **Multiply.** 2.5 hours x ₹300 = ₹750 per reel.
4. **Adjust for value.** A brand-deal reel that earns the creator ₹50,000 justifies a higher price than a casual meme reel.

## Packages beat single reels

Offer monthly packages so income is predictable:

- **Starter:** 8 reels/month, 2 revisions each - ₹6,000
- **Growth:** 15 reels/month, captions + thumbnails for 2 YouTube videos - ₹14,000
- **Pro:** 30 reels/month, priority 24-hour turnaround - ₹30,000

Discount slightly for volume, but never so much that you resent the work.

## Add-ons to charge separately

- Rush delivery within 12 hours: +30-50%.
- Extra revision rounds: ₹200-500 each.
- Thumbnails: ₹300-1,500 each.
- Script or hook writing: ₹200-500 per reel.

> Tip: Never quote on a call immediately. Say "Let me look at the footage and send you a quote in an hour." Then send a clear message with scope, revisions, turnaround and price.

## Getting paid safely

- 50% advance via **UPI** for new clients; full payment before files for one-off jobs.
- Use **Razorpay payment links** or a simple invoice for agencies and brands.
- Track everything in a Google Sheet: client, reel, date, amount, paid or pending.

## When to raise prices

Raise your rates when you are booked more than 80% of the month, when a client's channel has grown a lot with your edits, or every six months as your skills improve. Inform existing clients a month in advance. Good creators expect their editors to grow.

lessons.title: Assignment: build your rate card and pitch
lessons.content: Most editors lose work not because of skill but because their pitch is vague and their pricing is unclear. In this assignment you will create the exact documents you will send to your first paying creators.

assignment.brief:
## Your task
Create a **one-page rate card** and a **pitch message** for a real creator you would like to work with (e.g. a 50K-follower food creator in Indore or a tech YouTuber in Hyderabad).

## Steps
1. Calculate your per-reel price using time per reel and a monthly income target. Show the working.
2. Design 2-3 monthly packages with reel counts, revisions, turnaround and price in ₹.
3. List at least 3 add-ons (rush delivery, thumbnails, extra revisions) with prices.
4. Write your terms: revision rules, payment (advance via UPI), delivery format.
5. Write a WhatsApp or Instagram DM pitch (under 120 words) to the creator. Mention one specific idea to improve their recent reel and link your portfolio reel from Module 2.

## Deliverable
Paste the rate card (as text) and the pitch message in the submission box.

## Tips
- Specific beats generic: "Your reel on Indore street food lost viewers at 0:06, I would open with the jalebi shot" is far stronger than "I can make your reels better".
- Keep the rate card readable on a phone screen.

rubric.criterion: Pricing is calculated logically from time and income target
Packages and add-ons are clear, realistic and priced in ₹
Terms cover revisions, turnaround and payment
Pitch is short, personalised and includes a specific improvement idea

courses.title: Advanced Premiere Pro: Story & Pace
courses.subtitle: Shape long-form YouTube edits that hold viewers from first frame to last.
courses.description: For editors who already know the tools and want their work to feel like storytelling, not just cutting. We break down story structure, retention editing, sound design and finishing workflows I use for creators with 5M+ subscribers, all inside Premiere Pro.

mentor.name: Farhan Ali
mentor.headline: Video editor for creators with 5M+ subs

whatYouBuild: A restructured 8-minute YouTube edit with a clear three-act arc and open loops
A sound design pass with risers, whooshes and room tone that lifts retention
A reusable Premiere Pro finishing template with adjustment layers and export presets

A laptop with 16GB RAM recommended for long-form timelines

lessons.title: Finding the story inside raw footage
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Before cutting, watch all footage and write a one-line story: who wants what, what stands in the way, and what changes.
- Use a paper edit or text-based editing in Premiere's Transcript panel to rearrange the story before touching the timeline.
- Every long-form video needs a setup, rising tension and a payoff, even tutorials and vlogs.
- Cut anything that does not move the story forward, however beautiful the shot is.

## Transcript
At the advanced level, the biggest shift is this: you stop being a cutter and start being a storyteller. A creator gives you two hours of footage from a Manali trip. Beginners cut it in order. Storytellers find the story first.

So I watch everything once, without touching the timeline, and write one line. "Rohan wants to reach the summit before sunset, the bike breaks down, and he learns to enjoy the detour." Now I know what to keep.

Next, I use Premiere's text-based editing. Transcribe the footage, then highlight the lines that build the story and insert them into a sequence directly from the transcript. It is a paper edit, inside the software. Rearrange freely here; it is much faster than dragging clips.

The hardest part, honestly, is killing good shots. That gorgeous drone shot? If it does not move the story, it goes, or it becomes a two-second transition. Dekho, viewers do not remember shots. They remember how the video made them feel.

lessons.title: Open loops, three acts and the retention curve
lessons.content:
## Three acts in a YouTube video

- **Act 1 (first 10-15%)**: the hook and the promise. Establish what the viewer will get and why it matters.
- **Act 2 (middle 70%)**: rising stakes. Each section answers one question and raises another.
- **Act 3 (last 15%)**: the payoff, delivered fully, then a quick end. Long outros kill session time.

## Open loops

An **open loop** is a question you raise and deliberately answer later: "But the third mistake cost me ₹2 lakh, and we will get to that." Viewers stay to close the loop. Place a new loop before the previous one closes, especially around the 30% mark, where most retention graphs dip.

## Reading the curve

> Tip: Compare the retention graph against your timeline markers. If drops line up with sections that lack a loop or a visual change, your structure, not your cutting, needs fixing.

Restructure in a duplicate sequence so you can always return to the original.

lessons.title: Quiz: structure decisions
lessons.content: Test your structural instincts on real long-form scenarios.

questions.prompt: A vlog's retention drops sharply at 35%. The section has nice visuals but no new question. What is the strongest fix?

options.text: Add a colour grade to make it prettier
Plant an open loop before this section so viewers have a reason to stay

questions.explanation: Mid-video dips usually come from a lack of tension. An open loop gives viewers a question to stay for.

questions.prompt: What should you do first with two hours of raw travel footage?

options.text: Watch everything and write a one-line story before editing
Pick music and cut to the beat

questions.explanation: Knowing the story first tells you what to keep and what to cut.

questions.prompt: Why keep Act 3 short after the payoff?

options.text: Long outros cause viewers to leave, hurting watch time and session time
Endings are not counted in analytics

questions.explanation: Once the promise is delivered, viewers leave. A short ending keeps retention high and points them to the next video.

lessons.title: Retention editing: pattern interrupts with purpose
lessons.content:
## Key points
- A pattern interrupt is any deliberate change that resets attention: angle change, zoom, graphic, sound or music shift.
- Tie every interrupt to the meaning of the line, not to a timer, or the edit feels gimmicky.
- Use music changes to mark chapters and shifts in emotion.
- Use nested sequences to manage complex sections and keep the main timeline readable.

## Transcript
Many editors learn "add something every three seconds" and then stuff zooms everywhere. The edit becomes noisy. At an advanced level, every interrupt has a reason.

If the creator says "and then everything changed", that is where the music drops out. If they reveal a number, that is where a graphic appears with a sound hit. If they are being sarcastic, a quick punch-in on their face sells the joke.

I also use music as chapter markers. New section, new track or a switch in energy. Viewers feel the structure even if they never notice it.

For heavy sections, like a 40-second montage, I build it in its own sequence and nest it into the main timeline. Right-click, Nest. The main timeline stays clean and I can tweak the montage separately. On a 20-minute edit for a big creator, this keeps you sane.

lessons.title: Sound design that people feel but don't notice
lessons.content:
## Layers of a good soundscape

1. **Dialogue**: clean, levelled, always on top.
2. **Room tone**: a quiet bed of ambient sound under jump cuts so silence never feels "dead".
3. **Music**: ducked under dialogue, cut to phrase endings, not mid-bar.
4. **Sound effects**: whooshes on transitions, risers before reveals, soft clicks on text pops.

## Practical rules

- Keep SFX subtle, roughly -18 dB to -24 dB, so they are felt more than heard.
- Place a **riser** 1-2 seconds before a big reveal and cut it exactly on the reveal.
- Use **silence** as an effect. Dropping all music for one line makes it hit hard.
- Organise tracks: A1-A2 dialogue, A3 room tone, A4-A5 music, A6-A8 SFX. Use Premiere's **track targeting** and label tracks.

> Tip: Build an SFX library folder (whoosh, riser, hit, click, pop) once and reuse it for every creator. Royalty-free sources include YouTube Audio Library and licensed packs; always check licences for brand work.

lessons.title: Assignment: re-pace a long-form edit
lessons.content: Senior editors are hired to fix videos that "feel slow". This assignment trains exactly that: improving someone else's edit through structure, pace and sound.

assignment.brief:
## Your task
Take an existing 6-10 minute video (your own older edit, or footage a creator permits) and produce a re-paced version.

## Steps
1. Write the one-line story and mark Acts 1-3 with timeline markers.
2. Add at least two open loops and remove sections that do not serve the story.
3. Add purposeful pattern interrupts and a full sound design pass (room tone, music changes, SFX).
4. Export both versions and upload them as unlisted YouTube videos.

## Deliverable
A Google Doc link containing both video links, your one-line story, and 5 timestamped notes explaining key changes.

## Tips
Show your reasoning; reviewers care more about why than about effects.

rubric.criterion: Clear story structure with acts and open loops
Purposeful pacing and pattern interrupts
Layered, balanced sound design
Quality of timestamped reasoning notes

lessons.title: Adjustment layers, presets and a finishing pass
lessons.content:
## Key points
- Use adjustment layers for the overall grade so one change updates the whole video.
- Save Lumetri looks, caption styles and export settings as presets for each creator.
- Run a final finishing pass: audio loudness, colour consistency, spelling, safe areas and black frames.
- Export a high-bitrate master before making platform-specific versions.

## Transcript
Finishing is where big creators judge you. They have seen hundreds of edits; small mistakes stand out.

I put my grade on an adjustment layer across the whole timeline. Shot-level corrections stay on the clips, but the look lives in one place. If the creator says "a bit warmer", it is one slider, not two hundred clips.

Then my finishing pass, always in the same order. Loudness check on the master track, aiming around minus 14 LUFS. Colour consistency by scrubbing through. Every caption and on-screen text read once for spelling. Safe areas checked. And I scan the timeline for gaps or stray black frames.

Finally, I export a high-quality master and then create versions from it: YouTube, a vertical cut-down for Shorts. Chalo, one master, many outputs.

lessons.title: Team workflows: Productions, handoffs and archiving
lessons.content:
## When you work with a team

Big creators often have multiple editors, a thumbnail designer and a manager. Your workflow must be easy for others to pick up.

## Premiere Pro Productions

**Productions** split a large project into multiple linked projects in a shared folder. One editor works on the main video while another builds the Shorts, without conflicts.

## Clean handoffs

- Use consistent track layout and labelled tracks.
- Colour-label clips: for example green for approved, red for needs fixing.
- Use **Project Manager** (File > Project Manager) to collect and copy only used media into a new folder.

## Archiving

After final delivery and payment, archive the trimmed project to an external drive or cloud storage, with the version number and date in the folder name.

> Tip: Write a short README note in the project folder: fonts used, music licences and where the master export is. Future you will be grateful.

lessons.title: Quiz: finishing and workflow
lessons.content: A final check on finishing and professional workflow habits.

questions.prompt: The creator asks for the whole video to look warmer. What setup makes this fastest?

options.text: Applying the grade separately to every clip
Keeping the overall look on one adjustment layer
